sessions.title: Coastal to shelfal environments: Processes and products
sessions.conveners: Kyungsik Choi, Xin Shan
sessions.description:
Coastal to shelfal systems record the complex interaction of river discharge, tidal currents, waves dynamics, and episodic storm events. Interpreting these depositional successions remains challenging because depositional controls operate across multiple spatial and temporal scales, including variations in relative sea level, climate, tectonic subsidence, and sediment supply. The interplay of these processes can obscure the dominant mechanisms that preserve sedimentary signatures in the stratigraphic record.

Refining our understanding of coastal-to-shelfal systems is essential for advancing sedimentological and stratigraphic models. Moreover, it supports resource management, such as energy resources, aggregates, and Carbon Capture and Storage, while providing the scientific basis to navigate increasing anthropogenic and environmental pressures.

This session invites contributions exploring coastal and shelfal depositional systems across modern analogue and ancient successions. Studies based on field and outcrop observations, subsurface data, remote sensing, laboratory experiments, and numerical modelling are welcome across all climatic and tectonic settings. Submissions from early-career scientists are particularly encouraged.

sessions.title: Antarctic Ocean-Ice-Climate Interactions I: Paleoceanographic perspectives
sessions.conveners: Min Kyung Lee, Sunghan Kim
sessions.description:
This session focuses on paleoceanographic perspectives of Antarctic ocean–ice–climate interactions, highlighting the role of the Southern Ocean in past climate variability. We invite contributions that reconstruct shifts in ocean circulation, sea-ice extent, and Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) stability using marine sediment archives, geochemical proxies, and climate modeling approaches.

The session aims to bring together studies that address key processes shaping the Antarctic climate over geological timescales, including ocean circulation, cryosphere dynamics, and carbon cycling. Contributions spanning different time intervals—from glacial–interglacial cycles to longer-term climate transitions—are encouraged.

Topics include, but are not limited to:
- Southern Ocean circulation and water-mass changes
- Sea ice variability and its role in ocean-atmosphere exchange
- Antarctic ice-sheet evolution and ocean interactions
- Carbon cycle and deep ocean processes
- Marine sediment records and proxy development
- Past long-term climate transitions and their variability

sessions.title: Unravelling Arctic fjord and coastal change: Paleoenvironmental records, modern observations, and future perspectives
sessions.conveners: Jung-Hyun Kim, Young Jin Joe, Dahae Kim
sessions.description: Arctic fjords and adjacent coastal zones are highly sensitive environments where glaciers, ocean circulation, atmospheric forcing, terrestrial inputs, and increasing human activities interact. These systems provide key archives of past climate variability, yet they are undergoing rapid transformation driven by both natural variability and anthropogenic forcing. However, our understanding of their long-term evolution and future response to ongoing environmental and human pressures remains incomplete, highlighting the need for integrated approaches across disciplines and time scales. This session invites contributions on Arctic fjord and coastal systems, including Svalbard and the broader Arctic–North Atlantic and North Pacific regions. We welcome studies on sedimentary archives, glacier–fjord interactions, freshwater fluxes and hydrography, ocean circulation, sea-ice variability, and climate–ocean–cryosphere dynamics. Contributions addressing human impacts (e.g., shipping, resource development), as well as proxy development, numerical modeling, and data–model integration, are particularly encouraged. This session aims to foster interdisciplinary and international collaboration toward a deeper understanding of Arctic fjord and coastal change.

sessions.title: Sediment dynamics and geomorphodynamics in tidal environments
sessions.conveners: Sun Min Choi, Joohee Jo, Jun Young Seo
sessions.description:
Sediment dynamics and geomorphological evolution in tidal environments are inextricably linked through continuous feedback loops, requiring an integrated research approach to understand their co-evolution. These dynamics are temporally and spatially controlled by periodic tidal forcing, alongside seasonal fluvial and wave processes along longitudinal gradient. In the face of increasing human activities and extreme atmospheric events, these multiple impacts can significantly alter sediment dynamics –erosion, transport, and deposition– thereby disrupting long-term morphodynamic equilibrium.

Such shifts trigger fundamental morphodynamic feedback, where altered sediment transport patterns drive morphological changes, which in turn redefine the hydrodynamic and sedimentological behavior of the environment. It is no longer sufficient to study these processes in isolation; rather, understanding the coupled feedback between hydrodynamic forcing and subsequent bedform evolution is essential for grasping the trajectory of coastal system. Such integrated approaches will improve our ability to predict future coastal evolution and are fundamental to enhancing the resilience and adaptive capacity of coastal systems under future climate change.

This session welcomes contributions from field, laboratory, numerical, and theoretical studies that investigate sediment dynamics and geomorphology across micro- to macrotidal environments. We also encourage contributions that introduce new methods for observing sediment dynamics and geomorphology, as well as studies focused on predictive modeling that aim to bridge the gap between traditional observations and models.

sessions.title: Arctic paleoceanography and cryosphere dynamics: High-frequency variability and global climate linkage during the Quaternary
sessions.conveners: Kwangchul Jang, Xiaotong Xiao, Kwangkyu Park, Wenshen Xiao
sessions.description: The Arctic Ocean and sub-Arctic regions have been key drivers of the Earth’s climate system through the growth and decay of ice sheets, freshwater discharge, and associated ocean and atmospheric circulation. This session explores the reconstruction of Arctic and subarctic paleoceanography and cryosphere dynamics, with particular emphasis on the glacial-interglacial variability. We seek to elucidate the mechanisms governing ice-shelf stability, sea-ice oscillations, and the Arctic’s role in modulating global ocean circulation. We invite contributions that utilize marine sediment archives to investigate glacial dynamics, sea-ice extent, ocean circulation, meltwater discharge events, carbon cycles, and sediment provenance etc. A primary objective of this session is to integrate multi-proxy (e.g., sedimentological, micropaleontological, geochemical) records with numerical modeling simulations. Such integration is essential for refining the timing and magnitude of Quaternary glacial-interglacial climate transitions and for identifying potential tipping points within the Arctic (and sub-Arctic) climate system. We particularly welcome studies that bridge the gap between regional circum-Arctic glacial history and broader Northern Hemisphere climate sensitivity. By bringing together sedimentary records and modeling approaches, this session aims to provide a comprehensive perspective on how the Arctic responds to and drives global climate change through the Quaternary.

sessions.title: Sedimentary environment evolution of Asian continental margin and compilation of related maps
sessions.conveners: Xuefa Shi, Minoru Ikehara, Tae Soo Chang, Shuqing Qiao
sessions.description: The Asian continental margin, located at the convergent and collisional boundaries of the Eurasian, Pacific, and Indo-Australian plates, is a globally unique composite continental margin. This region is characterized by the world's most representative systems of monsoons, rivers, marginal seas, ocean currents, and sea ice, creating diverse sedimentary environments such as deltas, continental shelves, submarine canyons, trenches, and basins. This special session explores characteristics, mechanisms and evolutionary models of these environments across various spatio-temporal scales. Central to this research is the development of diverse thematic maps, including sediment types, submarine topographic and geomorphologic maps, horizontal and vertical hydrological profiles, and shoreline evolution maps. Driven by science and technological advancements, research on the sedimentary evolution of the Asian continental margin now integrates remote sensing, GIS, numerical modeling, and AI to transform vast amounts of observational and analytical datasets into sophisticated visual maps. By synthesizing these advancements, this session aims to refine our theoretical understanding of margin evolution while providing critical scientific support for resource management, environmental protection, disaster mitigation, and sustainable development. We welcome a diverse range of presentations on these themes. We anticipate that this session will serve as a platform for productive dialogue regarding the evolution of the Asian continental margin.

sessions.title: Western Pacific paleoceanography I: Past and future
sessions.conveners: Li Lo, Kyung Eun Lee, Takuya Sagawa, Helen Bostock
sessions.description:
The Western Pacific Ocean, the largest and most dynamic ocean basin on Earth, plays a pivotal role in global heat redistribution, carbon cycling, and climate variability from tropical to polar regions. Its unique configuration—connecting major marginal seas, large continental landmasses, and deep-water formation regions—governs energy and material exchange across the Earth system. Over recent decades, extensive paleoceanographic research in the Western Pacific has generated transformative insights into monsoon evolution, ENSO dynamics, ocean circulation, tectonic–climate interactions, and marine ecosystem responses from the Neogene to the Quaternary.

This session aims to bring together new findings and emerging perspectives in Western Pacific paleoceanography. We welcome contributions presenting high-resolution proxy reconstructions, innovative analytical developments, multiproxy approaches, and improved chronological frameworks. Studies addressing paleo-ecology, biodiversity evolution, species adaptation, and extinction dynamics in response to climatic transitions are encouraged as well. We also invite research exploring land–ocean coupling, sedimentary processes, hydroclimate variability, and the role of tectonics in shaping oceanographic conditions.

Given the Pacific’s central importance in global energy transport and biogeochemical cycling, we strongly encourage contributions integrating data–model comparisons and paleo-numerical simulations from a Pacific-centered perspective. Abstracts proposing future drilling strategies, reanalysis of legacy cores, and interdisciplinary approaches linking physical, chemical, and biological oceanography are highly welcome.

By fostering cross-disciplinary dialogue, this session seeks to synthesize accumulated knowledge and stimulate new ideas on how Western Pacific paleo-records can inform our understanding of large-scale ocean reorganization and future climate change in a rapidly evolving Earth system.

sessions.title: Marine Geohazards, Tectonics and Geophysics
sessions.conveners: Soojung An, Hyeon-Seob Kim, Kyoungjin Kim, Donggeun Yoo
sessions.description:
Fault architecture controls the evolution of subsurface systems through interactions among deformation, fluid flow, and energy transport. Variations in crustal strength and mechanical stratigraphy influence fault growth, segmentation, and connectivity, which define permeability structure and fluid pathways. Fault-controlled heterogeneity plays a key role in governing subsurface dynamics across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales.

Coupled processes involving geomechanics, multiphase fluid flow, and thermal transport are critical for subsurface energy applications. Carbon sequestration, hydrogen storage, and geothermal energy development require an improved understanding of fault-controlled permeability, caprock integrity, and fluid migration under evolving stress conditions. The interaction between fault architecture and coupled physical processes directly impacts storage efficiency, injectivity, and long-term stability.

This session invites contributions that explore the relationships between fault architecture and coupled processes in subsurface systems. Topics include field observations, laboratory experiments, and numerical modeling studies addressing fault development, segmentation, permeability evolution, fluid transport, and thermal effects. Contributions focusing on integrated approaches that link structural geology with fluid and thermal processes in energy-related systems are particularly encouraged.

sessions.title: Source-to-Sink transport and fate across atmosphere-land-river-ocean-sediment system
sessions.conveners: Hoi-Soo Jung
sessions.description: This session focuses on source-to-sink (S2S) transport, transformation, and fate of materials across coupled atmosphere–land–river–coastal–ocean–sediment systems. We welcome contributions examining how diverse materials—including atmospheric dust, sediments, nutrients, organic matter, greenhouse gases, contaminants, and other natural or anthropogenic substances—are transported, transformed, exchanged, and ultimately stored or released across interconnected Earth surface environments. Topics include atmospheric deposition, riverine transport of sediments and pollutants, estuarine and coastal trapping and redistribution, air–water–sediment exchanges of CO₂ and CH₄, cross-shelf sediment dispersal, and long-term burial or remobilization in marine sinks. Field observations, geochemical and isotopic tracing, remote sensing, monitoring, and modeling studies are all encouraged.

sessions.title: Carbon cycling and subsurface CO2 storage
sessions.conveners: Sookwan Kim, Byung-Dal So
sessions.description:
Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) is a critical technology for mitigating anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and achieving net-zero climate targets. Among various storage options, offshore sub-seabed geological storage provides a highly promising and scalable solution, utilizing the vast capacities of continental shelves and marginal sea basins. To unlock this immense potential, comprehensive exploration and a deep understanding of the sub-seabed environment are essential.

The successful and safe implementation of offshore CCS projects fundamentally depends on robust marine geosciences. The core expertise of marine geoscientists is indispensable across the entire project lifecycle, particularly in site evaluation, predictive numerical modeling, and long-term marine observation. Interpreting complex geological frameworks, simulating dynamic CO2 behavior, predicting potential seabed leakage, and deploying advanced monitoring systems are critical steps for ensuring permanent CO2 containment and mitigating geohazards.

This session aims to bring together marine geoscientists, researchers, and industry professionals to discuss the latest scientific advancements, technological innovations, and field experiences in offshore geological CO2 storage. We invite abstract submissions on various marine geological studies related to offshore CCS.

Topics of interest include:
- Site screening, selection, and comprehensive marine geological/geophysical characterization.
- Numerical modeling and simulation of CO₂ behavior and migration within geological formations.
- Predictive modeling and risk assessment of potential CO₂ leakage at the seabed.
- Advanced marine observation networks and Measurement, Monitoring, and Verification (MMV) technologies, including environmental baseline surveys.
- Stratigraphic, sedimentological, and geomechanical assessments of reservoir quality and caprock integrity.
- Geochemical interactions among injected CO₂, formation fluids, and marine sediments.
- Case studies, pilot projects, and interdisciplinary approaches to offshore CCS.

Through this session, we hope to share valuable insights and discuss the future direction of marine geological research for safe and effective offshore CCS deployment.

sessions.title: Transport and burial of particulate organic matter in the ocean
sessions.conveners: Baozhi Lin, Minkyoung Kim, Shigeyoshi Otosaka
sessions.description: Transport and burial of particulate organic matter (POM) in the ocean transfer CO₂ from the atmosphere to the deep ocean, thereby regulating Earth’s climate on decadal to millennial time scales. The POM in the sea are not only derived from the marine organisms, but also from the terrestrial plants, soils, and bedrocks delivered predominantly via river discharge. The sink and burial of biospheric POM (marine organisms, terrestrial plant and soil) represent a net sink for atmospheric CO2. In contrast, the burial of petrogenic POM (terrestrial bedrock) has no effect in regulating the atmospheric CO2 concentration. In this session, we invite contributions that advance our understanding of the source to sink processes of POM in continental marginal seas and the open ocean. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, the molecular and isotopic characterization fingerprinting of sinking and buried POM, quantification of sources, fluxes, and fate of POM across the water column and in marine sediments, interactions and mixing between marine- and terrestrial-derived POM pool, environmental and biogeochemical factors affecting the transport, degradation, and preservations of POM, geoengineering and enhancing carbon sequestration of POM, from the modern ocean to the geological past.

sessions.title: New-Era Scientific Ocean Drilling: To improve collaboration in Asian Marine Geology
sessions.conveners: Minoru Ikehara, Yoon-Mi Kim, Zhifei Liu, Ron Hackney
sessions.description:
Scientific Ocean Drilling, which continues to generate diverse scientific findings, entered a new era in 2025. In addition to the International Ocean Drilling Programme (IODP3), a collaboration between Japan, ECORD (European Consortium), and ANZIC (Australia and New Zealand Consortium), China will soon launch the Deep Ocean Drilling Program (DODP). The US has also established a Scientific Ocean Drilling Coordination Office (SODCO) in readiness for new, US-led expeditions. These ocean drilling programs are based on internationally focused marine geological and geophysical investigations.

We aim to use the opportunity at ICAMG10 to further advance international collaboration by sharing the outcomes of recently completed IODP3 projects and future drilling plans from all programs and consortia, thereby facilitating open information exchange. Presentations on new and existing ideas for scientific drilling in the Pacific and Indian Oceans are welcome from around the world, especially those that facilitate cooperation between existing and emerging programs.

Advances in Scientific Ocean Drilling rely not only on drilling expeditions but also on the utilization of six decades of legacy cores stored in global repositories. For example, projects are already underway and generating results through the Japanese community activity ReCoRD (Repository Core Re-Discovery Program), while the first IODP3 SPARC (Scientific Projects using Ocean Drilling Archives) expeditions are commencing in 2026, and the US National Science Foundation already accepts proposals for Legacy Asset Projects.

Outreach and training for young researchers is also essential. In addition to established ECORD summer schools in Europe and USSSP-supported initiatives in the US, regular international core schools are planned in Japan. We therefore encourage submissions that share and discuss recent information about outreach and training activities related to Scientific Ocean Drilling.

sessions.title: Deep-sea sedimentary dynamic processes: Combining observations and sedimentary records
sessions.conveners: Zhifei Liu, Jang Jun Bahk, Andrew Tien-Shun Lin
sessions.description:
Research on deep-sea sediments has evolved from the early perception that the deep sea is a “tranquil world” to the current understanding that there are complex and diverse dynamic processes. Gravity-driven processes (including turbidity currents, debris flows, and grain flows) along with bottom currents (including contour currents, tidal bottom currents, and internal waves) together shape the deep-sea sedimentary system. The key to understanding sedimentary dynamic processes lies in combining modern ocean observations with sedimentary records. Modern observational technologies (i.e., deep-sea mooring observation, benthic boundary layer monitoring) reveal details of deep-sea sedimentary dynamic processes, while sedimentary records (i.e., surface sediments and sedimentary cores) provide evidence of sedimentary evolution over multiple timescales. The combined study of these two aspects helps us understand the formation mechanisms from microscopic sedimentary structures to macroscopic geomorphological forms (such as submarine canyons, channel-levee systems, and sediment drifts).

This session focuses on the latest advances in modern observation and sedimentary record studies of various sedimentary dynamic processes from the continental shelf to deep-sea basins, especially in the Asian marginal seas. We encourage, but are not limited to, submissions in the following research topics: sediment source-to-sink transport processes, observation and simulation of deep-sea sediment dynamics, paleoenvironmental applications of sediment records, deep-sea sediment and global change responses, comparative studies of modern observations and paleo records, and application of new technologies and methods in deep-sea sediment research (such as granulometry). Through exchanges in this session, we expect to advance research in deep-sea sedimentology and provide new sedimentological perspectives for the development of Earth system science.

sessions.title: Sedimentary processes in the Asian marginal seas and marine environmental evolution
sessions.conveners: Chuanxiu Luo, Sui Wan, Yi Zhong, Shuhuan Du
sessions.description:
Asian Marginal seas are dynamic interfaces between continents and open oceans, serving as critical archives of source-to-sink sediment transport, ocean-atmosphere interactions, ocean circulation changes, sea-level fluctuations, and biological productivity. Their sedimentary records preserve high-resolution evidence of land-ocean interactions and past climate variability, offering unique insights into the mechanisms driving regional and global environmental change.

In the context of accelerating global warming and increasing human impacts, understanding how Asian marginal seas respond to past climate perturbations—such as glacial-interglacial cycles, abrupt climate events, and monsoon shifts—has become critically important for predicting future changes in coastal and marine environments.

This special session aims to synthesize cutting-edge research on sedimentary processes and paleoenvironmental evolution in Asian marginal seas, with a focus on reconstructing past climate variability, identifying sediment sources and transport mechanisms, and evaluating the implications for future climate scenarios. The collection of studies will highlight how Asian marginal seas record and modulate global climate signals and how sedimentary archives can be used to constrain model predictions of future change. Key themes addressed in this special session include but are not limited to: (1) Sediment provenance, transport, and accumulation in marginal seas; (2) Marginal seas record and amplify global climate signals; (3) Evolution of monsoon systems and related mechanisms.

sessions.title: Formation and exploration of marine mineral resources: Crusts, nodules, and hydrothermal deposits
sessions.conveners: Youngjae Kim, Jung-Woo Park, Sang-Mook Lee, Kiho Yang
sessions.description:
Marine mineral resources, such as ferromanganese (Fe–Mn) crusts, polymetallic nodules, and hydrothermal vent systems (including seafloor massive sulfide deposits), form through distinct yet interconnected geological, oceanographic, and geochemical processes across the seafloor. Understanding how these deposits grow, how they concentrate metals, and how their occurrence varies from local to regional scales is essential for interpreting seafloor mineral systems and improving exploration strategies.

This session invites contributions that advance (1) formation mechanisms and controls on metal enrichment and deposit architecture, and (2) exploration and characterization approaches that constrain deposit distribution, thickness, and grade. We broadly welcome observational studies (e.g., field mapping, sampling, and in situ measurements), experimental and analytical work (e.g., mineralogy, geochemistry, paleoceanographic proxies, and geochronology), and related modeling studies. We also encourage submissions on exploration workflows using marine geophysics and seafloor mapping (e.g., AUV/ROV surveys, acoustic and optical imaging, and data integration/analytics) that link deposit-forming processes to prospectivity.

sessions.title: Marine sedimentary records supporting climate systems-models
sessions.conveners: Shu Gao, James T. Liu
sessions.description: In the research field of systems-theory based climate models, the existing GCM-type global climate models rely mainly on instrumental data, but the instrumental period is limited to a temporal scale of 10² years. Some additional data sets are available from historical written records, which cover a temporal scale of 10³ years with low spatial and temporal resolutions. As such, simulations on longer timescales face the problem of data scarcity. To date, the progress made in climate change research has been in the ice age-interglacial cycle and the effect of human carbon dioxide emissions; recently, short-term climate changes other than these two channels are being considered. An even more ambitious goal is to investigate and analyze the climate changes throughout Earth’s history, on various spatial-temporal scales and with different controlling mechanisms. For these efforts, the development of future climate system models requires data from sedimentary records. Oceans represent the main water body that receives sediment from the various sources; thus, the sedimentary records formed by modern and ancient oceans contain rich data information, including both climate change information and related process information, which await to be further explored. Hence, the purpose of this session is to discuss how marine sedimentary records can support future climate system models, with the following key themes: (1) the diversity, temporal and spatial distribution patterns, and resolution characteristics of climate information contained in marine sedimentary records; (2) climate change data derived from marine sedimentary records; (3) information on changes in external and internal drivers of the climate system contained in marine sedimentary records; (4) normal climate factor data obtained from the analysis of marine sedimentary records to reveal the “emergent” phenomena of climate change; (5) methodology to establish the process-product relationship of climate datasets; and (6) examples of deep-time climate simulations driven by marine sedimentary records.

The POM in the sea are not only derived from the marine organisms, but also from the terrestrial plants, soils, and bedrocks delivered predominantly via river discharge. The sink and burial of biospheric POM (marine organisms, terrestrial plant and soil) represent a net sink for atmospheric CO2. In contrast, the burial of petrogenic POM (terrestrial bedrock) has no effect in regulating the atmospheric CO2 concentration. In this session, we invite contributions that advance our understanding of the source to sink processes of POM in continental marginal seas and the open ocean. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, the molecular and isotopic characterization fingerprinting of sinking and buried POM, quantification of sources, fluxes, and fate of POM across the water column and in marine sediments, interactions and mixing between marine- and terrestrial-derived POM pool, environmental and biogeochemical factors affecting the transport, degradation, and preservations of POM, geoengineering and enhancing carbon sequestration of POM, from the modern ocean to the geological past.

sessions.title: Source-to-Sink Transport and Fate Across Atmosphere-Land-River-Ocean-Sediment Systems
sessions.conveners: Hoi-Soo Jung
sessions.description: This session focuses on source-to-sink (S2S) transport, transformation, and fate of materials across coupled atmosphere–land–river–coastal–ocean–sediment systems. We welcome contributions examining how diverse materials—including atmospheric dust, sediments, nutrients, organic matter, greenhouse gases, contaminants, and other natural or anthropogenic substances—are transported, transformed, exchanged, and ultimately stored or released across interconnected Earth surface environments. Topics include atmospheric deposition, riverine transport of sediments and pollutants, estuarine and coastal trapping and redistribution, air–water–sediment exchanges of CO₂ and CH₄, cross-shelf sediment dispersal, and long-term burial or remobilization in marine sinks. Field observations, geochemical and isotopic tracing, remote sensing, monitoring, and modeling studies are all encouraged.

sessions.title: Marine sedimentary records supporting climate systems-models
sessions.conveners: Shu Gao, James T. Liu
sessions.description: In the research field of systems-theory based climate models, the existing GCM-type global climate models rely mainly on instrumental data, but the instrumental period is limited to a temporal scale of 10² years. Some additional data sets are available from historical written records, which cover a temporal scale of 10³ years with low spatial and temporal resolutions. As such, simulations on longer timescales face the problem of data scarcity. To date, the progress made in climate change research has been in the ice age-interglacial cycle and the effect of human carbon dioxide emissions; recently, short-term climate changes other than these two channels are being considered. An even more ambitious goal is to investigate and analyze the climate changes throughout Earth’s history, on various spatial-temporal scales and with different controlling mechanisms. For these efforts, the development of future climate system models requires data from sedimentary records. Oceans represent the main water body that receives sediment from the various sources; thus, the sedimentary records formed by modern and ancient oceans contain rich data information, including both climate change information and related process information, which await to be further explored. Hence, the purpose of this session is to discuss how marine sedimentary records can support future climate system models, with the following key themes: (1) the diversity, temporal and spatial distribution patterns, and resolution characteristics of climate information contained in marine sedimentary records; (2) climate change data derived from marine sedimentary records; (3) information on changes in external and internal drivers of the climate system contained in marine sedimentary records; (4) normal climate factor data obtained from the analysis of marine sedimentary records to reveal the “emergent” phenomena of climate change; (5) methodology to establish the process-product relationship of climate datasets; and (6) examples of deep-time climate simulations driven by marine sedimentary records.

sessions.title: Western Pacific Paleoceanography: Past and Future
sessions.conveners: Li Lo, Kyung Eun Lee, Takuya Sagawa, Helen Bostock
sessions.description:
The Western Pacific Ocean, the largest and most dynamic ocean basin on Earth, plays a pivotal role in global heat redistribution, carbon cycling, and climate variability from tropical to polar regions. Its unique configuration—connecting major marginal seas, large continental landmasses, and deep-water formation regions—governs energy and material exchange across the Earth system. Over recent decades, extensive paleoceanographic research in the Western Pacific has generated transformative insights into monsoon evolution, ENSO dynamics, ocean circulation, tectonic–climate interactions, and marine ecosystem responses from the Neogene to the Quaternary.

This session aims to bring together new findings and emerging perspectives in Western Pacific paleoceanography. We welcome contributions presenting high-resolution proxy reconstructions, innovative analytical developments, multiproxy approaches, and improved chronological frameworks. Studies addressing paleo-ecology, biodiversity evolution, species adaptation, and extinction dynamics in response to climatic transitions are encouraged as well. We also invite research exploring land–ocean coupling, sedimentary processes, hydroclimate variability, and the role of tectonics in shaping oceanographic conditions.

Given the Pacific’s central importance in global energy transport and biogeochemical cycling, we strongly encourage contributions integrating data–model comparisons and paleo-numerical simulations from a Pacific-centered perspective. Abstracts proposing future drilling strategies, reanalysis of legacy cores, and interdisciplinary approaches linking physical, chemical, and biological oceanography are highly welcome.

By fostering cross-disciplinary dialogue, this session seeks to synthesize accumulated knowledge and stimulate new ideas on how Western Pacific paleo-records can inform our understanding of large-scale ocean reorganization and future climate change in a rapidly evolving Earth system.

sessions.title: New-Era Scientific Ocean Drilling: To improve collaboration in Asian Marine Geology
sessions.conveners: Minoru Ikehara, Yoon-Mi Kim, Zhifei Liu, Ron Hackney
sessions.description:
Scientific Ocean Drilling, which continues to generate diverse scientific findings, entered a new era in 2025. In addition to the International Ocean Drilling Programme (IODP3), a collaboration between Japan, ECORD (European Consortium), and ANZIC (Australia and New Zealand Consortium), China will soon launch the Deep Ocean Drilling Program (DODP). The US has also established a Scientific Ocean Drilling Coordination Office (SODCO) in readiness for new, US-led expeditions. These ocean drilling programs are based on internationally focused marine geological and geophysical investigations.

We aim to use the opportunity at ICAMG10 to further advance international collaboration by sharing the outcomes of recently completed IODP3 projects and future drilling plans from all programs and consortia, thereby facilitating open information exchange. Presentations on new and existing ideas for scientific drilling in the Pacific and Indian Oceans are welcome from around the world, especially those that facilitate cooperation between existing and emerging programs.

Advances in Scientific Ocean Drilling rely not only on drilling expeditions but also on the utilization of six decades of legacy cores stored in global repositories. For example, projects are already underway and generating results through the Japanese community activity ReCoRD (Repository Core Re-Discovery Program), while the first IODP3 SPARC (Scientific Projects using Ocean Drilling Archives) expeditions are commencing in 2026, and the US National Science Foundation already accepts proposals for Legacy Asset Projects.

Outreach and training for young researchers is also essential. In addition to established ECORD summer schools in Europe and USSSP-supported initiatives in the US, regular international core schools are planned in Japan. We therefore encourage submissions that share and discuss recent information about outreach and training activities related to Scientific Ocean Drilling.

sessions.title: Interplay Between Fault Architecture and Coupled Processes in Subsurface Systems
sessions.conveners: Soojung An, Jia-Jyun Dong, Hyeon-Seob Kim, and Byung-Dal So
sessions.description:
Fault architecture controls the evolution of subsurface systems through interactions among deformation, fluid flow, and energy transport. Variations in crustal strength and mechanical stratigraphy influence fault growth, segmentation, and connectivity, which define permeability structure and fluid pathways. Fault-controlled heterogeneity plays a key role in governing subsurface dynamics across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales.

Coupled processes involving geomechanics, multiphase fluid flow, and thermal transport are critical for subsurface energy applications. Carbon sequestration, hydrogen storage, and geothermal energy development require an improved understanding of fault-controlled permeability, caprock integrity, and fluid migration under evolving stress conditions. The interaction between fault architecture and coupled physical processes directly impacts storage efficiency, injectivity, and long-term stability.

This session invites contributions that explore the relationships between fault architecture and coupled processes in subsurface systems. Topics include field observations, laboratory experiments, and numerical modeling studies addressing fault development, segmentation, permeability evolution, fluid transport, and thermal effects. Contributions focusing on integrated approaches that link structural geology with fluid and thermal processes in energy-related systems are particularly encouraged.

sessions.title: Unraveling Arctic Fjord and Coastal Change: Paleoenvironmental Records, Modern Observations, and Future Perspectives
sessions.conveners: Jung-Hyun Kim, Young Jin Joe, Dahae Kim
sessions.description: Arctic fjords and adjacent coastal zones are highly sensitive environments where glaciers, ocean circulation, atmospheric forcing, terrestrial inputs, and increasing human activities interact. These systems provide key archives of past climate variability, yet they are undergoing rapid transformation driven by both natural variability and anthropogenic forcing. However, our understanding of their long-term evolution and future response to ongoing environmental and human pressures remains incomplete, highlighting the need for integrated approaches across disciplines and time scales. This session invites contributions on Arctic fjord and coastal systems, including Svalbard and the broader Arctic–North Atlantic and North Pacific regions. We welcome studies on sedimentary archives, glacier–fjord interactions, freshwater fluxes and hydrography, ocean circulation, sea-ice variability, and climate–ocean–cryosphere dynamics. Contributions addressing human impacts (e.g., shipping, resource development), as well as proxy development, numerical modeling, and data–model integration, are particularly encouraged. This session aims to foster interdisciplinary and international collaboration toward a deeper understanding of Arctic fjord and coastal change.

sessions.title: Antarctic Ocean–Ice–Climate Interactions: Paleoceanographic Perspectives
sessions.conveners: Sunghan Kim, Min Kyung Lee
sessions.description:
This session focuses on paleoceanographic perspectives of Antarctic ocean–ice–climate interactions, highlighting the role of the Southern Ocean in past climate variability. We invite contributions that reconstruct shifts in ocean circulation, sea-ice extent, and Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) stability using marine sediment archives, geochemical proxies, and climate modeling approaches.

The session aims to bring together studies that address key processes shaping the Antarctic climate over geological timescales, including ocean circulation, cryosphere dynamics, and carbon cycling. Contributions spanning different time intervals—from glacial–interglacial cycles to longer-term climate transitions—are encouraged.

Topics include, but are not limited to:
- Southern Ocean circulation and water-mass changes
- Sea ice variability and its role in ocean-atmosphere exchange
- Antarctic ice-sheet evolution and ocean interactions
- Carbon cycle and deep ocean processes
- Marine sediment records and proxy development
- Past long-term climate transitions and their variability

sessions.title: Arctic Paleoceanography and Cryosphere Dynamics: High-frequency variability and global climate linkage during the Quaternary
sessions.conveners: Kwangchul Jang, Xiaotong Xiao, Kwangkyu Park, Wenshen Xiao
sessions.description: The Arctic Ocean and sub-Arctic regions have been key drivers of the Earth’s climate system through the growth and decay of ice sheets, freshwater discharge, and associated ocean and atmospheric circulation. This session explores the reconstruction of Arctic and subarctic paleoceanography and cryosphere dynamics, with particular emphasis on the glacial-interglacial variability. We seek to elucidate the mechanisms governing ice-shelf stability, sea-ice oscillations, and the Arctic’s role in modulating global ocean circulation. We invite contributions that utilize marine sediment archives to investigate glacial dynamics, sea-ice extent, ocean circulation, meltwater discharge events, carbon cycles, and sediment provenance etc. A primary objective of this session is to integrate multi-proxy (e.g., sedimentological, micropaleontological, geochemical) records with numerical modeling simulations. Such integration is essential for refining the timing and magnitude of Quaternary glacial-interglacial climate transitions and for identifying potential tipping points within the Arctic (and sub-Arctic) climate system. We particularly welcome studies that bridge the gap between regional circum-Arctic glacial history and broader Northern Hemisphere climate sensitivity. By bringing together sedimentary records and modeling approaches, this session aims to provide a comprehensive perspective on how the Arctic responds to and drives global climate change through the Quaternary.

sessions.title: Formation and Exploration of Marine Mineral Resources: Crusts, Nodules, and Hydrothermal Deposits
sessions.conveners: YoungJae Kim, Jung-Woo Park, Sang-Mook Lee, Kiho Yang
sessions.description:
Marine mineral resources, such as ferromanganese (Fe–Mn) crusts, polymetallic nodules, and hydrothermal vent systems (including seafloor massive sulfide deposits), form through distinct yet interconnected geological, oceanographic, and geochemical processes across the seafloor. Understanding how these deposits grow, how they concentrate metals, and how their occurrence varies from local to regional scales is essential for interpreting seafloor mineral systems and improving exploration strategies.

This session invites contributions that advance (1) formation mechanisms and controls on metal enrichment and deposit architecture, and (2) exploration and characterization approaches that constrain deposit distribution, thickness, and grade. We broadly welcome observational studies (e.g., field mapping, sampling, and in situ measurements), experimental and analytical work (e.g., mineralogy, geochemistry, paleoceanographic proxies, and geochronology), and related modeling studies. We also encourage submissions on exploration workflows using marine geophysics and seafloor mapping (e.g., AUV/ROV surveys, acoustic and optical imaging, and data integration/analytics) that link deposit-forming processes to prospectivity.

sessions.title: Offshore Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS): Marine Geological Perspectives and Challenges
sessions.conveners: Sookwan Kim and Byung-Dal So
sessions.description:
Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) is a critical technology for mitigating anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and achieving net-zero climate targets. Among various storage options, offshore sub-seabed geological storage provides a highly promising and scalable solution, utilizing the vast capacities of continental shelves and marginal sea basins. To unlock this immense potential, comprehensive exploration and a deep understanding of the sub-seabed environment are essential.

The successful and safe implementation of offshore CCS projects fundamentally depends on robust marine geosciences. The core expertise of marine geoscientists is indispensable across the entire project lifecycle, particularly in site evaluation, predictive numerical modeling, and long-term marine observation. Interpreting complex geological frameworks, simulating dynamic CO2 behavior, predicting potential seabed leakage, and deploying advanced monitoring systems are critical steps for ensuring permanent CO2 containment and mitigating geohazards.

This session aims to bring together marine geoscientists, researchers, and industry professionals to discuss the latest scientific advancements, technological innovations, and field experiences in offshore geological CO2 storage. We invite abstract submissions on various marine geological studies related to offshore CCS.

Topics of interest include:
- Site screening, selection, and comprehensive marine geological/geophysical characterization.
- Numerical modeling and simulation of CO₂ behavior and migration within geological formations.
- Predictive modeling and risk assessment of potential CO₂ leakage at the seabed.
- Advanced marine observation networks and Measurement, Monitoring, and Verification (MMV) technologies, including environmental baseline surveys.
- Stratigraphic, sedimentological, and geomechanical assessments of reservoir quality and caprock integrity.
- Geochemical interactions among injected CO₂, formation fluids, and marine sediments.
- Case studies, pilot projects, and interdisciplinary approaches to offshore CCS.

Through this session, we hope to share valuable insights and discuss the future direction of marine geological research for safe and effective offshore CCS deployment.

sessions.title: Geoheritage in Asian Waters: Scientific Value, Conservation, and Sustainable Use
sessions.conveners: Jongyun Jung
sessions.description:
This session invites contributions on the identification, assessment, conservation, interpretation, and sustainable use of marine and coastal geoheritage. Marine and coastal geoheritage is considered broadly here, encompassing coastal landforms, tidal flats, sedimentary and stratigraphic records, paleontological resources, and other geological features preserved within UNESCO World Heritage properties, National and Global Geoparks, marine parks, national monuments, and related areas. Special attention is welcome for Getbol, the Korean Tidal Flats, and other sites that illuminate earth system processes, sea-level changes, paleoenvironmental history, biodiversity, and human-environmental interactions.

Geoheritage shapes professional practice, public awareness, and personal connections to place. In marine and coastal settings, it contributes not only to ongoing research in marine geology, but also to conservation, place-based education, interpretation, and sustainable tourism. By making the link between geoheritage and cultural heritage tangible and teachable, place-based education and interpretation can improve earth system literacy and motivate diverse people to explore, value, care for, and protect significant coastal and marine landscapes.

We welcome interdisciplinary studies and case-based discussions on geoheritage inventory and assessment, criteria for scientific significance, conservation and monitoring, management with World Heritages or Geoparks, the role of geoheritage in tourism, and community engagement. This session aims to advance discussion on how marine geoheritage can be more effectively recognized, conserved, and activated as a scientific resource, a public asset, and a foundation for sustainable regional development.

abstracts.title: Morphodynamic evolution of a macrotidal open-coast tidal flat driven by decadal migration of a major estuarine tidal channel
abstracts.text: Open-coast tidal flats are shaped by the interaction of tides, waves, sediment supply, and channel dynamics, yet the role of adjacent larger channels in driving long-term tidal-flat morphodynamics remains poorly constrained. This study examines a channelized macrotidal open-coast tidal flat on southwestern Ganghwa Island, west coast of Korea, located adjacent to Sukmo Channel, a bedrock-confined distributary channel of the Han River estuary. Using repeated cross-shore topographic transects from 2009 to 2026, satellite imagery, surface sediment observations, and Empirical Orthogonal Function analysis, we investigate how decadal-scale migration of the Sukmo Channel influenced channel development and morphodynamic adjustment across the tidal flat. Long-term transect analysis reveals progressive intensification of channel morphology in the lower tidal flat. Between 2009 and 2011, two intertidal channels separated by a mid-channel bar occupied the lower flat. These channels merged into a larger channel between 2012 and 2015, after which the merged channel migrated and deepened between 2015 and 2018. From 2022 to 2026, the main channel shifted seaward, while the former point-bar area evolved into smaller channels and mid-channel bars, accompanied by notable bar accretion between 3600 and 3800 m. EOF analysis indicates that the leading morphologic mode represents large-scale channel migration, channel merging, and bar accretion, whereas the second mode captures channel deepening, bar dissection, and secondary channelization, including increasing channel development across the 2400–3200 m tidal-flat sector. These changes are interpreted as a response to the decadal-scale migration of Sukmo Channel. Its southward migration likely enhanced ebb-current influence across the tidal flat, promoting channel incision, expansion, and reorientation. Initially, intertidal channels were dominantly east–west oriented, but they progressively transformed into more north–south-oriented channel networks, consistent with increasing control by ebb-directed drainage across the flat. These results suggest that migration of a major estuarine distributary channel can reorganize tidal-flat flow pathways and drive progressive channelization of adjacent open-coast tidal flats over decadal timescales.

abstracts.title: A journey into Antarctica’s past: SWAIS 2C Project
abstracts.text: Response of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) to projected warming remains a significant uncertainty in sea level rise projections. This project will focus on understanding past and current drivers, mechanisms and feedbacks that influence retreat of ice sheets, to reduce uncertainty in numerical model projections of future changes. The SWAIS 2C (Sensitivity of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet to 2 Degrees Celsius) Project will address the overarching question: How will marine-based ice sheets respond to a 2°C increase in global temperature and what are the local, regional, and global environmental consequences of this response if temperatures ultimately exceed this 2°C increase? The Antarctic science platform is partnering internationally an exciting scientific drilling project aiming to address the following questions: 1) How will marine-based ice sheets respond to a 2oC increase in global temperature?, 2) Under what climatic conditions does the WAIS collapse?, and 3) What are the local, regional, and global environmental consequences of melting ice sheets? Given the far-reaching and international consequences of Antarctica's future contribution to global sea level rise, this project was developed through international collaboration to better forecast the size and timing of future changes. The project scientists will collect and study geological (rocks), glaciological (ice), and geophysical (earth physical properties) data and provide new information to guide the development of climate and ice sheet numerical models to better understand and predict how the ice sheet on West Antarctica will contribute to future sea level rise. As part of this project, the KOPRI paleoceanographic group will be working with other SWAIS2C researchers to study the stratigraphy of new drill core (length: about 227 m) beneath Kamb Ice Stream on Ross Sea Ice Shelf, focusing on how paleo-proxies can be used to infer paleoenvironments and ice sheet changes.

abstracts.title: Mercury isotopes reveal seasonal PBM variability and daily PBM–snow dynamics during early Arctic AMDEs
abstracts.text:
During the Arctic spring transition following polar sunrise, atmospheric mercury depletion events (AMDEs) are driven by rapid halogen-mediated oxidation of atmospheric Hg(0) to Hg(II), promoting its transfer to snow and other surfaces. Concurrent observations of atmosphere–snowpack Hg exchange during AMDE onset and seasonal shifts in atmospheric Hg isotope composition are important for distinguishing the initial delivery of Hg to the Arctic from subsequent recycling pathways. Here, we analyzed the Hg stable isotope compositions of year-round particulate-bound mercury (PBM) collected in 2022–2023 and daily PBM and surface snow collected in Svalbard in March 2024, shortly after polar sunrise, to assess seasonal changes in atmospheric Hg sources and short-term atmosphere–snowpack Hg exchange during early AMDEs development.

Daily surface snow Δ199Hg decreased from -0.20‰ to -2.49‰ over time and was strongly correlated with daily integrated UV-B radiation (r2 = 0.96, p < 0.01), indicating rapid photoreduction and Hg(0) re-emission from surface snow. Daily PBM Δ199Hg showed no significant temporal trend during the early AMDEs period in March (r² = 0.03, p > 0.05). The lack of a corresponding shift in daily PBM despite the marked change in surface snow suggests that Hg(0) re-emitted from surface snow did not measurably alter PBM isotope composition over this interval. Instead, the slightly negative Δ200Hg of daily PBM (−0.03 ± 0.07‰), together with a Δ199Hg/Δ201Hg slope (1.43 ± 0.32) close to those for Br- and Cl-mediated Hg(0) oxidation (1.64 ± 0.30 and 1.89 ± 0.18, respectively), is consistent with near-surface halogen oxidation, a major Hg(0) oxidation pathway during AMDEs. These isotope signatures suggest that PBM during the early AMDE was derived primarily from externally supplied Hg(0) that underwent halogen oxidation during transport over marine surfaces.

Over broader seasonal timescales, mean Δ199Hg of year-round PBM shifted from -0.24‰ during polar night to 0.20‰ during midnight sun. Unlike the daily PBM record, this seasonal shift suggests that year-round PBM captured the cumulative influence of photochemical processing, potentially including photoreduction of particle-associated Hg, as solar radiation increased. Overall, surface snow recorded rapid, local post-depositional processing, whereas PBM reflected the seasonally integrated photochemical evolution of atmospheric Hg.

abstracts.title: Transverse and longitudinal asymmetries of a mixed-energy strait: The Holocene Bohai Strait
abstracts.text: Depositional models for straits have predominantly focused on symmetric systems in both the longitudinal (along-strait) and transverse (across-strait) directions. This framework overlooks straits characterised by significant asymmetry, specifically those displaying profound imbalances in both directions regarding topography, hydrodynamics and sediment supply. Bohai Strait, connecting the Bohai and Yellow Seas, serves as an important example to investigate this topic. Transversely, it features a deep, tide-dominated northern passageway that contains little mobile sediment operating in parallel with a shallow, wind-driven southern margin receiving the immense fine-grained load of the Yellow River. Longitudinally, the strait exhibits an asymmetry, characterised by a larger flood-tidal delta that contrasts with a much smaller ebb-tidal delta. The asymmetric products of the Bohai Strait result primarily from a three-stage evolution throughout the late Pleistocene and Holocene. The incipient strait (~11.6 to 10.3 ka cal BP) was characterised by the discharge of the Yellow River into the central Bohai Sea, which deposited the paleo-Shandong Mud Wedge. A critical reorganisation probably started at ~10.3 ka cal BP, driven by two factors: the widening of the strait and the cutoff of mud supply due to the southward avulsion of the Yellow River. This event triggered a spatial contrast, causing a widespread depositional hiatus in the south while initiating the tide-dominated channel with its sandy flood-tidal delta in the north. After ~6.5 ka cal BP, the return of the Yellow River to Bohai Sea amplified this spatial divergence between the deeply scoured northern tide-dominated system and the shallow southern supply-dominated system. Overall, the northern half of the Strait experiences net input of locally eroded sand to the Bohai Sea (i.e. it is flood-tide dominated), whereas the southern half exports mud to the Yellow Sea. The Bohai Strait highlights that longitudinal and transverse asymmetries in sedimentary processes and products require a broader framework beyond the simplified tidal-strait models. Keywords: Bohai Strait, coastal mud belt, depositional asymmetry, flood-tidal delta, mixed-energy environment, strait, subaqueous delta, tidal strait.

abstracts.title: Glaciovolcanic processes between the Campbell glacier and Mt. Melbourne volcano, Antarctica: Ice and fire
abstracts.text:
The application of cosmogenic nuclides (in-situ 10Be and 26Al) for surface exposure dating has provided valuable chronological constraints on the evolution of Antarctic terrestrial glaciers. Building on previously published exposure ages from Campbell Glacier moraines that indicate moraine formation during Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 5, we analyzed palaeo-subglaciated bedrock to further constrain glacier thinning history. The newly obtained exposure ages (49.8–35.3 ka; MIS 3) indicate continued glacier surface lowering throughout the Late Quaternary, including the Last Glacial Period (MIS 4–2). Notably, our results suggest that the Local Last Glacial Maximum (LLGM) occurred at elevations of approximately 150–90 m a.s.l. during MIS 4 rather than MIS 2.

The new and recalculated exposure-age dataset for Campbell Glacier is distinct from those of other outlet glaciers draining into Terra Nova Bay. This pattern suggests that volcanic activity associated with Mt. Melbourne may have influenced glacial behaviour through glaciovolcanic interactions during the Late Quaternary, in addition to climatic and oceanic forcing. Further investigation of palaeo-glaciovolcanic interactions across the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) could provide important insights into the role of volcanic forcing in glacier evolution. Such studies may also improve predictions of future glacier change and sea-level rise, particularly considering the numerous subglacial volcanoes beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS).

abstracts.title: The last collapse of the northern Svalbard continental margin
abstracts.text: The Hinlopen Megaslide, located north of Svalbard, is one of the largest submarine landslides in the Arctic Ocean and is characterized by multiple phases of retrogressive slope failure following the main slide event. While the main failure is considered to have occurred at approximately 30 ka BP, the timing and triggering mechanisms of the subsequent retrogressive failures remain poorly constrained. This study focuses on the headwall area at the southern part of the Hinlopen Megaslide, which is interpreted to represent one of the youngest retrogressive failure stages. We present two sediment cores recovered from the headwall area and the adjacent northern outer continental shelf during the 2022 and 2025 R/V Helmer Hanssen expeditions to northern Svalbard. By integrating sedimentological characteristics, stratigraphic relationships, and chronological constraints from both cores, we discuss the timing of the latest retrogressive failure and its potential triggers.

abstracts.title: Ratchet effect of tropical cyclones: Episodic controls on sediment dynamics and depositional evolution of the East China Sea inner shelf
abstracts.text:
Coastal-to-shelf sedimentary systems are shaped by the interplay between persistent background forcing and episodic high-energy disturbances. Although tropical cyclones (TCs) are among the most energetic disturbances affecting continental shelves, their contributions to sediment redistribution and depositional evolution remain poorly understood. The East China Sea (ECS) inner shelf, with a high-resolution archive and 4–5 annual TC impacts, provides an ideal setting to investigate how episodic TC events modify sediment source-to-sink pathways within a complex shelf system influenced by river discharge, monsoon circulation, and tidal processes.

Here, we integrate numerical modeling and observations to investigate the role of TCs in controlling sediment dynamics and depositional evolution on the ECS inner shelf. We reveal a “ratchet effect” of TCs characterized by highly asymmetric sediment dynamics and sedimentary responses. Strong waves and currents during TCs trigger intense nearshore erosion while driving efficient offshore sediment redistribution through downwind transport. The mixing front, migrating seaward under enhanced turbulence, further regulates TC-induced deposition through its boundary effect, constraining the spatial extent of offshore accumulation.

Beyond individual events, simulations of diverse TC trajectories demonstrate that their pathways exert distinct controls on sediment redistribution. Six major TC path clusters were identified from best-track statistics, producing transport patterns ranging from along-shelf redistribution to cross-shelf transport and offshore deposition. The cumulative impacts enhance inner-shelf erosion and contribute to offshore depocenter development between 26°N and 28°N within the ECS muddy belt. Continuous simulations further demonstrate the disproportionate contribution of episodic TCs to cross-shelf sediment transport. Although TCs occupy less than 7% of the time, they contribute more than 60% of seaward sediment flux across the inner shelf.

These findings demonstrate that TCs act as key episodic controls on coastal-to-shelf sediment exchange. Incorporating these high-energy events into source-to-sink frameworks and stratigraphic interpretations is essential for understanding the evolution of depocenters on continental shelves and their sedimentary records.

abstracts.title: Comparison of stratigraphic correlation and AMS 14C ages of sediments from the Bellingshausen Sea continental margin, West Antarctica
abstracts.text: Establishing a robust sediment chronology in the Antarctic continental margin remains challenging because planktonic foraminifera, the primary material for accelerator mass spectrometry(AMS) 14C dating, are often absent, poorly preserved, or affected by old carbon. Previous studies have indirectly assigned interglacial sediments on the Bellingshausen Sea continental rise to Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 5, largely based on tephra stratigraphy. However, recent AMS ¹⁴C dating from foraminifera and acid-insoluble organic matter (AIOM) in core BS17-GC02 indicates significantly younger ages, suggesting that the conventional tephra-based chronology requires reassessment. This study analyzes AMS ¹⁴C ages of planktonic foraminifera, magnetic susceptibility, CaCO₃ concentration, color reflectance, and geochemical proxies from additional sediment cores (BS17-LC03 and BS17-GC04) collected from the Bellingshausen Sea continental margin to investigate these discrepancies. The results show that CaCO₃ peaks and well-preserved foraminifera in the brownish interglacial layers yield calibrated AMS ¹⁴C ages of 32.9–39.1 ka. This conflicts with prior tephra chronology, which implied that deposition occurred during MIS 5, rather than suggesting that these distinctive intervals align with the later MIS 3 interglacial. Anomalously old tephra-derived ages may either result from sedimentary reworking or delayed tephra deposition. This research emphasizes the need for multi-proxy approaches and additional radiocarbon dating to obtain robust age control for Antarctic sedimentary records.

abstracts.title: Last deglacial glacier dynamics and sedimentary responses to hydrographic change in the Hinlopen Strait, Arctic Svalbard
abstracts.text:
The Svalbard Archipelago provides an ideal setting for investigating coupled ocean-cryosphere interactions and associated depositional and environmental responses to past climate variability. The Hinlopen Strait, situated between Spitsbergen and Nordaustlandet, is a major hydrographic passage in northern Svalbard connecting warm, saline Atlantic Water (AW) entering through the Svalbard branch with colder, fresher Arctic Water (ArW). Despite its potential importance for regulating regional water-mass exchange and glacier-ocean interactions, postglacial sedimentary evolution within the strait and adjacent fjords remains poorly constrained. Here, we reconstruct glacier retreat, sediment supply and transport, hydrographic conditions, and glacimarine environmental changes using four ~5 m-long sediment cores recovered along a north-south bathymetric transect during the 4th Joint Korea-Norway Svalbard Cruise aboard RV Helmer Hanssen in 2022. Based on a chronological framework established by AMS 14C dating, a multi-proxy approach combining sedimentological and geochemical indicators constrained changes in depositional processes and hydrographic conditions.

The results indicate that enhanced AW inflow during the Bølling–Allerød interstadial (14.7–12.9 cal kyr BP) coincided with rapid glacial retreat within the Hinlopen Strait, consistent with deglacial records from western and northern Svalbard. The subsequent reduction in AW influence during the Younger Dryas (~12.9–11.7 cal kyr BP) was associated with a marked shift from glacier-proximal deglacial sedimentation toward more distal, open-marine conditions. Following renewed AW inflow, glacier retreat continued during the earliest Holocene (11.7–10.0 cal kyr BP), while the relative contribution of glacier-derived sediment decreased and hydrodynamic redistribution became increasingly prominent. During the early to middle Holocene (~10–4 cal kyr BP), reduced meltwater and glacial sediment input led to lower sedimentation rates, while enhanced current-driven winnowing and lateral sediment redistribution increasingly shaped the depositional environment. By the late Holocene (after ~4 cal kyr BP), increasing ArW influence and renewed proximity of glacier-derived sediment sources drove a progressive increase in glacial influence, initially in the southern part of the strait, with rising sedimentation rates. Nevertheless, persistent open-marine conditions indicate that this renewed glacial influence did not restore the strongly glacier-proximal environment of the earlier deglacial phase.

These findings demonstrate that sedimentation in the Hinlopen Strait reflects a changing balance among glacial sediment supply, meltwater discharge, and current-driven sediment redistribution, modulated by regional hydrographic variability throughout the last deglaciation and Holocene. The strait’s sensitivity to Atlantic-Arctic water-mass exchange and glacier-ocean interactions highlights its potential as a high-resolution sedimentary archive of past glacier–ocean dynamics, hydrographic variability, and sediment-transport processes in northern Svalbard.

abstracts.title: Fair-weather tides and monsoon floods: contrasting controls on morphodynamics and facies architecture in a macrotidal embayment
abstracts.text: Despite recent advances in understanding river-tide interactions in fluvial-tidal transitions, the event-scale effects of river discharge on morphodynamics and facies architecture in macrotidal embayments remain poorly understood. This study examines the contrasting influences of fair-weather tidal processes and short-lived monsoon floods in Gomso Bay, South Korea, using repeated RTK-GPS transect surveys, digital elevation models, short sediment cores, and hydrodynamic observations collected during June-July 2026. DEM differencing between 7 and 16 July documents up to 0.6 m of net aggradation and more than 15 m of lateral cutbank retreat. Heavy rainfall on 8–9 July enhanced ebb dominance, prolonged ebb duration, and generated pronounced turbidity peaks. Rainfall-induced discharge triggered chute cutoff across a bar and subsequent infilling of abandoned channel, rapidly reorganizing the channel-bar system. Under fair-weather conditions, tide-dominated sedimentation produces rhythmic sand-mud lamination and bioturbated deposits in tidal flats and tributary-channel point bars, whereas main-channel bars are characterized by bidirectional ripple cross-laminated and parallel-laminated sand. In contrast, monsoon-influenced bar deposits record episodic erosion and rapid sedimentation, expressed by erosional contacts, mud-pebble layers, climbing-ripple cross-lamination, and structureless sand. Flood-tide-directed climbing ripples formed earlier in the monsoon contrast with ebb-directed climbing ripples deposited following peak rainfall, highlighting changes in depositional conditions during channel-bar reorganization. These observations demonstrate that brief rainfall-induced discharge events can profoundly modify otherwise tide-dominated morphology and sedimentation. Alternation between fair-weather tidal processes and short-lived monsoon floods generates complex facies architecture over remarkably short timescales, with implications for interpreting monsoon-related variability in inclined heterolithic stratification in macrotidal environments.

abstracts.title: Mineralogical and sedimentological signatures of Late Pleistocene ice sheet instability in the Bellingshausen Sea
abstracts.text:
Marine sediment records from the West Antarctic margin provide important archives for reconstructing past ice-sheet dynamics and sediment transport processes. Although the long-term retreat history of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet has been widely investigated, detailed sedimentary evidence for ice-sheet fluctuations in the Bellingshausen Sea during the late Pleistocene glacial interval (MIS 2-4) remains poorly constrained.

Here, we present mineralogical, sedimentological, and geochemical records from sediment cores (BS17-GC04 and BS17-GC15) recovered from the continental rise and shelf of the Bellingshausen Sea, West Antarctica. Our results show down-core variations in terrigenous components, including quartz, illite-rich clay minerals, and smectite compositions, suggesting changes in detrital sediment input from different sources within the MIS 2-4 glacial interval. These variations may reflect episodes of ice-sheet instability rather than a uniform glacial configuration. The combined proxies provide new constraints on late Pleistocene ice-sheet variability in the Bellingshausen Sea.

abstracts.title: Spatiotemporal reorganization of paraglacial spit complexes on a tide-influenced Arctic fjord delta: Dicksonfjorden, Svalbard
abstracts.text:
Rapid Arctic warming is altering terrestrial sediment supply, wave exposure, and relative sea level along deglaciated fjord coasts, yet resulting geomorphic responses remain poorly constrained at annual-to-decadal scales. This study quantifies the 2016-2023 evolution of gravel spit complexes in the fluvial-tidal transition zone at the head of Dicksonfjorden, central Svalbard. Repeat UAV photogrammetry and RTK-GPS surveys conducted in 2016-2019, 2022, and 2023 were used to generate orthomosaics and digital elevation models. DEMs of difference (DoDs), cross-shore profiles, sediment cores, and aerial photographs from 1938 were integrated to reconstruct sediment transport and longer-term coastal reorganization.

The time series reveals a persistent upfjord-downfjord contrast. Relict, breached spits in the inner delta remained nearly stationary, whereas younger downfjord spits underwent rapid upfjord elongation and landward migration. The 2016-2019 record yielded elongation and landward-migration rates of 22 and 4.3 m yr-1, respectively, for the youngest spits (Kim et al., 2022). The extended record demonstrates continued displacement through 2023: spits 3 and 5 shifted 15-18 m landward relative to their 2016 positions, with especially pronounced reworking between 2022 and 2023. Spatially paired seaward erosion and landward deposition show that longshore drift is the dominant transport mechanism, augmented by episodic overwash when energetic waves coincide with high tides. Angular gravel is supplied by retreating alluvial-fan cliffs and meltwater-eroded gullies and is redistributed across muddy tidal-flat substrates.

Historical imagery shows that spits 2-5 were absent in 1938, while the low-tide shoreline has since prograded approximately 500-600 m. Increased post-Little Ice Age sediment delivery, delta progradation, distributary-channel avulsion, and glacial-isostatic uplift have progressively shifted the principal zone of wave shoaling and gravel reworking downfjord, deactivating older spits while enabling new spit formation farther seaward. The expanded observations demonstrate that Arctic fjord-head coasts respond to warming through coupled changes in terrestrial sediment flux, tidal-flat accommodation, and wave exposure, producing sharp spatial contrasts in landform mobility. Paraglacial spit complexes therefore provide sensitive geomorphic indicators of climate-driven coastal reorganization in Arctic fjord systems.

abstracts.title: Source-to-Sink controls on the spatial distribution of a modern mud depocenter and palimpsest sediments on the Northern South China Sea Shelf
abstracts.text:
The Northern South China Sea (NSCS) shelf is supplied by sediment from the proximal Pearl River (PR) and distal sources such as SW Taiwan and Luzon Arc, with dispersal modulated by marine processes (Jia et al., 2023). However, the relative contributions of proximal versus distal sources and terrestrial versus marine-derived organic matter (OM) often remained poorly constrained, particularly across the modern-to-relict transition in the outer NSCS shelf (Wang et al., 2023). Here, we reconstructed the spatial and temporal evolution of sediment dispersal over the last ~70 years using eight sediment cores collected along a 355-km transect following the hypothetical PR dispersal pathway. Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis was applied in spatial and temporal domains. The spatial EOF included granulometry, linear sedimentation rates from 210Pbex, clay mineral assemblages, and the terrestrial fraction (FT) based on δ13CPOM, evaluated across three stratigraphically equivalent time horizons (1954, 2009, and 2020). The temporal EOF assessed the covariability of depth-to-time-converted profiles of P-wave velocity, magnetic susceptibility, color reflectance, FT, and suspended sediment concentration at the Gaoyao gauging station to reconstruct changes from 1954 to 2009.

We identified a modern mud depocenter offshore of the PR mouth delineated by spatial EOF mode 1, composed of polymodal mud, with a maximum LSR (~0.26 cm/yr), consistent with the mid-shelf extension of the Holocene NSCS mud belt (Ge et al., 2014). Mode 2 captures a provenance gradient, with terrestrial-derived OM and kaolinite declining eastward as illite-chlorite and marine-derived OM increase. The depocenter shares the illite-chlorite, marine-OM-enriched signature of the eastern palimpsest rather than the kaolinite- and terrestrially-dominated western palimpsest, indicating that this depocenter is nonetheless supplied predominantly by distal sources. Temporal EOF mode 1 indicates a secular decline in PR sediment supply to the mid-shelf since ~1992, consistent with decreasing sediment load despite stable river discharge (Liu et al., 2018). Mode 2 resolves a multidecadal oscillation, with a strengthened terrestrial influence over the western and central part of the transect (1977-2003), during which marine-derived and distally transported particles were more abundant eastward.

These results define a persistent, three-part spatial framework in the NSCS source-to-sink system: terrestrial-dominated palimpsest sediments occupy the western flank, a modern depocenter supplied primarily by distal and marine-derived material, and marine-influenced palimpsest sediments dominate the east. This suggests a decoupling between sediment provenance and fluvial forcing: discharge trends govern depositional intensity but not depocenter provenance. Resolving this mechanism will require closer examination of sediment resuspension and redistribution.

abstracts.title: Tracing adjacent glacial catchments with single particle smectite composition in surface sediments and gravity cores of the Dotson and Getz A troughs, Amundsen Sea
abstracts.text: The Dotson–Getz Trough in the Amundsen Sea drains a sector of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet that is losing mass rapidly. Three glacial catchments feed the trough, and because their sediment is mixed downstream and their beds lie almost entirely beneath ice, the contribution of each is hard to observe directly. Smectite offers a way around this, since each particle carries the Al, Mg and Fe of the rock from which it weathered and can therefore point to sources that no outcrop exposes. We examined two adjacent tributaries, the Dotson and Getz A troughs, in fifteen surface sediments and two gravity cores, combining the relative content of clay mineral with the elemental composition of single smectite particles. Illite is the principal clay mineral in the Dotson Trough, whereas the Getz A Trough carries substantially more smectite. Dotson smectite particles are Al-rich, in keeping with the granitoid and metamorphic basement exposed in that catchment. Mg-bearing particles are found only in Getz A, indicating a mafic contributor that its granitoid outcrops do not represent. Both cores preserve this contrast. In each core, the open-marine facies cannot be distinguished in elemental composition from the present-day surface of the same trough, and the two subglacial facies remain distinct from each other. Downcore, the Dotson assemblage shifts toward smectite and its compositions narrow onto the Al-rich part of the modern field, while in Getz A smectite decreases but its compositions stay within the modern range. Provenance on this margin can therefore be resolved catchment by catchment. The relative content of clay mineral and single particle elemental composition each separate the two troughs, and the compositions further reveal what each catchment supplied and whether a downcore change reflects a change in supply.
