abstracts.title: Neodymium in modern foraminifera from the southern Philippine Sea: Implications for tracing water masses and continental weathering inputs
abstracts.text: Neodymium isotope compositions (εNd) of planktonic foraminifera are widely used as tracers of deep-water circulation and continental weathering. However, the mechanisms controlling Nd incorporation into foraminiferal tests remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a one-year (November 2017–October 2018) sediment-trap record from the southern Philippine Sea, including Sr-Nd isotope compositions of siliciclastic fractions together with rare earth element (REE), Mn concentrations, and εNd of planktonic foraminifera collected at intermediate (490 m) and deep (4030 m) water depths. The aim is to reconstruct seasonal variations in lithogenic inputs to the southern Philippine Sea and to evaluate their impacts on the foraminiferal εNd signals within the water column. Our results suggest that siliciclastic sediments reflect mixing of volcanic materials from nearby Mindanao and Halmahera Islands and continental detritus from northwestern New Guinea. At 490 m, both stations exhibit pronounced seasonal variability in siliciclastic inputs, driven by seasonal precipitation-induced river discharge and monsoon-related shifts in surface currents. In contrast, seasonal variations at 4030 m correspond to shifts in deep current directions. PAAS-normalized REE patterns of the study foraminifera that characterized by MREE enrichment and negative Ce anomalies, combined with significant positive correlations between Mn and Nd concentrations, collectively indicate that Nd is predominantly hosted in authigenic Mn oxide coatings precipitated on foraminiferal tests during settling through the water column. Higher Mn contents at 4030 m relative to 490 m suggest that foraminifera collected at mid-depth are more sensitive to surface-derived lithogenic inputs. Accordingly, foraminiferal εNd at mid-depth displays seasonal variations closely mirroring those of the siliciclastic fractions, implying rapid Nd exchange (monthly) between smectite-rich particulates and seawater. However, foraminiferal εNd at 4030 m remains comparatively stable and likely reflects continuous Nd absorption from the water column as Mn oxide coatings accumulate on sinking foraminifera tests. These findings provide new constraints on the sources of modern foraminiferal neodymium and the rapid seawater-particle Nd exchange in complex marginal seas, indicating the utility of foraminiferal εNd as a tracer of seasonal lithogenic inputs and water mass mixing in the West Pacific. Our findings also underscore the need for caution when interpreting foraminiferal εNd records from marginal seas characterized by strong land–ocean coupling, particularly in paleocirculation or lithogenic inputs reconstructions.

abstracts.title: Far-field postseismic GNSS constraints on back-arc mantle viscosity beneath the East Sea (Japan Sea) following the 2011 Mw 9.0 Tohoku-Oki earthquake
abstracts.text: The East Sea (Japan Sea) is a broad back-arc basin situated between the 2011 Mw 9.0 Tohoku-Oki earthquake source and the Korean Peninsula. Postseismic deformation recorded by GNSS stations on the Korean Peninsula therefore contains information on viscoelastic relaxation across the intervening back-arc mantle. We investigate this far-field deformation using decadal GNSS time series from 2008 to 2022. Geodetic inversion identifies an early transient component lasting approximately 2 years, followed by longer-lived deformation that persists through 2022. The inferred horizontal displacements constrain three-dimensional spherical viscoelastic models that include the lithosphere–asthenosphere boundary geometry of the Eurasian Plate and a rheologically weak back-arc mantle beneath the East Sea. The back-arc mantle geometry follows low S-wave velocity perturbations reported beneath the basin. The models estimate continental asthenosphere viscosities of 1018–1019 Pa s, whereas the back-arc mantle requires viscosities up to two orders of magnitude lower. The low-viscosity back-arc mantle exerts the strongest control on the early transient deformation, while the continental asthenosphere governs the longer-lived far-field signal. These results demonstrate that GNSS observations located beyond a broad back-arc basin can constrain lateral viscosity variations within the upper mantle. The observed far-field deformation provides geodetic constraints on back-arc mantle rheology.

abstracts.title: Hydroclimatic and sediment physical controls on riverine organic carbon in the Yarlung Tsangpo River
abstracts.text: High-elevation rivers are increasingly recognized as important components of the global carbon cycle. However, the mechanisms controlling dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and sediment organic carbon (SOC), as well as the relationships between these carbon pools, remain poorly constrained. Here, we investigate the spatial and seasonal dynamics of DOC and SOC in the Yarlung Tsangpo River (YTR), originating from the Tibetan Plateau, to elucidate their environmental controls and interactions between dissolved and sediment-associated carbon pools. DOC concentrations in the YTR are consistently low (0.24 ± 0.12 mg L−1) relative to global rivers, but exhibit pronounced spatial and seasonal variability, with elevated values occurring mainly in the midstream reaches and during the wet season. Statistical analyses indicate that DOC dynamics are primarily controlled by hydroclimatic factors, particularly discharge and temperature, reflecting enhanced mobilization of terrestrially derived organic matter during periods of increased hydrological connectivity. In contrast, SOC concentrations (2.90 ± 2.85 g kg−1) are mainly associated with sediment physical properties rather than hydrological forcing. SOC shows significant positive relationships with clay content, silt content, and specific surface area, suggesting an important role of fine-grained sediments in sedimentary organic carbon retention. Water-soluble organic carbon (WSOC) is significantly correlated with SOC but shows no significant relationship with DOC, indicating limited interactions between dissolved and sediment-associated carbon pools at seasonal timescales. Comparison with global river datasets further reveals that both DOC flux and SOC concentration decline with increasing elevation, although DOC exhibits stronger elevational dependence than SOC. These contrasting patterns suggest different controls on dissolved carbon export and sedimentary carbon storage in high-elevation river systems. Collectively, these findings provide new insights into carbon cycling processes in alpine river systems and improve understanding of carbon transport and storage on the Tibetan Plateau under ongoing climate change.

abstracts.title: Evolution of the Western Pacific Warm Pool’s southern margin since 3 Ma: Insights from multi-species foraminiferal vertical profiles and barrier layer dynamics
abstracts.text:
The Western Pacific Warm Pool (WPWP) plays a vital role in global heat and moisture transport, yet its long-term vertical hydrographic evolution remains incompletely constrained over Plio-Pleistocene timescales. Here, we present a 3-million-year (Ma) multi-species planktonic foraminiferal reconstruction from Ocean Drilling Program (ODP) Hole 1115B in the Solomon Sea. By integrating Globigerinoides ruber (0–30 m), Trilobatus sacculifer (30– 60 m), and Neogloboquadrina dutertrei (60–150 m), we trace upper-ocean thermal, salinity, and heat content (OHC) reorganizations.

Our findings reveal a distinct three-stage evolution: (A) 3.0–2.0 Ma: Thermocline cooling initiated during Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (~2.8–2.5 Ma) while mixed layer and barrier layer (BL) temperatures remained stable, initiating an OHC decline. (B) 2.0–1.0 Ma: The BL expanded alongside enhanced salinity stratification. Subsurface connectivity to South Pacific Intermediate Water prompted slight thermocline warming and OHC recovery. (C) 1.0 Ma–Present: Post-Mid-Pleistocene Transition, rapid upper-thermocline cooling outpaced surface cooling, steepening the vertical thermal gradient and severely diminishing OHC.

Cross-site comparisons indicate that high-latitude cooling drove early tropical thermocline shoaling without collapsing the surface BL, highlighting the Solomon Sea's active feedback in global climate dynamics.

abstracts.title: Heterogeneity in ice sheets- vs. monsoon rainfall-induced silicate weathering from high to low latitudes
abstracts.text:
The classical Milankovitch theory proposes that Northern Hemisphere high-latitude summer insolation controls the waxing and waning of ice sheets, thereby exerting a major influence on global climate. Accordingly, many paleoclimate records are characterized by pronounced 100-kyr glacial–interglacial cycles. However, an increasing number of tropical climate records have revealed strong ~23-kyr precession cycles that appear largely independent of high-latitude ice-sheet variability. These observations have raised fundamental questions about the mechanisms governing Earth’s climate variations on orbital timescales.

Previous studies have shown that silicate weathering responds sensitively to variations in both temperature and rainfall. On orbital timescales, high-latitude ice sheets and low-latitude monsoon systems exert distinct climatic influences: the former primarily regulate global temperature variations on glacial–interglacial timescales, whereas the latter strongly modulate tropical hydrological cycles at the precession band. Building on this framework, we integrated silicate-weathering records from multiple marginal-sea sites spanning high, middle, and low latitudes to investigate how weathering processes respond to temperature and rainfall variability and to identify the major controls on orbital-scale climate evolution.

Our results reveal pronounced latitudinal heterogeneity in silicate weathering. At middle latitudes, weathering records exhibit both 100-kyr and 23-kyr periodicities, indicating combined influences of high-latitude ice-sheet dynamics and low-latitude monsoon rainfall. At high latitudes, weathering variability is dominated by glacial– interglacial fluctuations and is more strongly associated with temperature changes linked to ice-sheet dynamics. In contrast, tropical weathering records are characterized primarily by strong 23-kyr precession cycles and respond more sensitively to monsoon-driven rainfall variability. These contrasting responses provide independent evidence in support of the recently proposed “Milankovitch–Kutzbach” hypothesis, suggesting that Earth’s orbital-scale climate variability cannot be explained by high-latitude ice-sheet forcing alone, but instead reflects the combined influences of high-latitude ice sheets and low-latitude monsoon systems. Our findings further highlight the critical role of low-latitude monsoon processes in shaping global climate variability on orbital timescales.

abstracts.title: Holocene dispersal of Chinese river-derived clays to the Korean coast linked to Kuroshio branch variability in the Yellow and East China seas
abstracts.text:
We provide quantitative evidence for the long-distance transport of Chinese-derived fine sediments to the southern coast of Korea during the Holocene. A ~32-m-long sediment core from a semi-enclosed bay was investigated using clay mineralogy, elemental geochemistry, and Sr–Nd isotopic compositions to trace changes in sediment provenance. The results indicate that Chinese river-derived material formed a major component of the clay-sized fraction, particularly during ~6.3–2 ka, when its contribution averaged about 70% based on clay mineral mixing and Al–Mg regression models. Temporal variations in Chinese sediment contribution occurred in several distinct stages, with major changes near ~6.3, ~5, ~4.3–3, and ~2 ka. These shifts appear to reflect changes in regional circulation within the Yellow and East China Seas associated with Kuroshio-derived currents. Enhanced Huanghe-derived clay input around ~5 ka may indicate a stronger influence of the Jeju Warm Current, whereas its marked decline after ~2 ka coincided with the transition from marine- to freshwater-dominated depositional conditions. These results demonstrate that sediment accumulation along the southern Korean coast was influenced not only by nearby Korean rivers but also by cross-shelf transport of sediments derived from Chinese rivers.

abstracts.title: Paleoceanographic changes reconstructed by biomarker analysis of the sediment core from the Gulf of Alaska in the northern North Pacific over the last 10 million years
abstracts.text:
Late Miocene cooling (LMC; ca. 7.5~5.5 Ma) marks the first major global cooling in the cool climatic regime since the late Miocene. Globally distributed ice rafted debris records, including that from Alaska (Lagoe et al., 1993), suggests large scale glacial development during the LMC. After an interval of warm climate represented by the Pliocene climatic optimum (PCO; ca. 4.4~4.0 Ma) during the early Pliocene, global climate faced a significant cooling, known as the Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (NHG; ca. 3.2 Ma~). At the Gulf of Alaska (GOA), the development of Alaskan alpine glaciers started after 4.2 Ma, which enhanced sedimentation at the GOA. Modern marine ecological system in GOA shows blooms composed mainly of diatoms are caused by enhanced nutrient input via glacial meltwater as well as coastal upwelling in warm seasons. In the present study, we analyzed biomarkers in sediment core samples from the GOA to reconstruct the variations in paleoenvironments and primary productions in the sea surface layers since the late Miocene (ca. ～11.6 Ma) in the northeastern North Pacific.

We used the sediment cores recovered at the distal Surveyor Fan in the GOA (Site U1417; 56° 57.5'N, 147°6.5'W) by IODP Expedition 341. Freeze-dried sediments were extracted by solvents and then separated into fractions by silica-gel column These fractions were analyzed by GC-MS and GC-FID.

We identified various algal biomarkers including long-chain alkenones (haptophyte), long-chain alkyl diols (diatom and eustigmatophyte), and steroids such as dinosterol (dinoflagellate), brassicasterol (haptophyte and diatom), ostreasterol (diatom), and 22-dehydrocholesterol (diatom). Sea surface temperatures (SSTs) estimated by alkenone unsaturation indices (UK37 and UK’37) and long-chain diol index (LDI) varied in synchronous with global cooling since the late Miocene as previously reported foraminiferal δ18O records and also showed remarkable increase/decrease during the warming/cooling events such as the LMC, PCO and NHG, LMC being the most significant with ~8℃ drop in SST. Concentrations and mass accumulation rates (MARs) of the algal biomarkers show that marine paleo-productivity frequently varied over the past 10 Ma. Highest TOC MAR occurred during ~7 Ma to 6.5 Ma with highest haptophyte and pennate diatom productivity, then diatom productivity increased alongside the LMC progression, although haptophyte productivity decreased. Productivity of both pennates and centrics also spiked after 2.7 Ma. The results suggest the cold and mixed ocean created by the Neogene cooling events had strong impact on diatom productivity and possibly significant CO2 removal at the GOA.

abstracts.title: Overburden characterization for offshore CO2 storage: seismic stratigraphy and key monitoring targets, offshore Korea
abstracts.text: Ensuring long-term containment integrity in offshore geological CO2 storage requires rigorous evaluation of fluid migration pathways and geological risk features discontinuities within the overburden, extending from the primary caprock to the seafloor. Here, we characterize the seismic stratigraphy and shallow risk features (e.g., faults and shallow gas) of two prospective Korean storage sites: the Gunsan East Subbasin and the southwestern Ulleung Basin. Integrating newly acquired 2D multichannel seismic and high-resolution sub-bottom profiler data, we mapped fault upward continuation and acoustic anomalies associated with fluid accumulation. In the Gunsan East Subbasin, observed fault tips are confined to deeper strata and terminate far beneath the modern seafloor, with continuous overlying strata confirming the absence of upward propagation. Furthermore, while elevated sweetness values occur along stratigraphic boundaries, their poor spatial correlation with vertical faults or seismic chimneys renders their interpretation as fluid migration ambiguous. In contrast, in the southwestern Ulleung Basin, high-resolution data successfully resolved the upper tips of crestal faults extending close to the modern seafloor, which were not clearly resolved on legacy 3D volumes; structural correlation indicates that these shallow faults are decoupled from the deeper reservoir and primary caprock. Importantly, prominently developed seismic chimneys and acoustic anomalies characterized by high-amplitude, reversed-polarity reflections are clearly identified across the overburden, marking high-priority targets for focused baseline monitoring. These site-specific overburden characteristics establish essential boundary conditions for optimizing offshore monitoring networks, designing time-lapse seismic surveys, and parameterizing dynamic leakage simulations for future offshore CO2 storage projects in Korea.

abstracts.title: Asian sedimentary continuum
abstracts.text: Asian continental margins connect the world’s highest plateau (Tibetan Plateau) with the largest and deepest ocean (west Pacific), where develop the most dynamic and diverse source-to-sink systems and foster the densely populated deltas on the Earth planet. A major frontier in international Earth system science is to conduct integrated "mountaintop-to-ocean" research that combines terrestrial and marine perspectives, spans multiple scales and Earth spheres, and employs interdisciplinary approaches, aiming to study material cycling and carbon sequestration effects. It is also a critical initiative for addressing global climate change and achieving sustainable marine environmental development. We propose the "Asian Sedimentary Continuum" research initiative, which aims to elucidate the fluxes of terrestrial material generation and exchange across the land-sea continuum—from the Tibetan Plateau to Asian continental margins and the deep oceans—through typical river "source-to-sink systems." This research will uncover key mechanisms through which continental weathering and seafloor processes regulate multi-scale carbon cycling and climate change. It will also investigate the environmental effects of critical element cycling across land and sea in a rapidly changing Earth system, as well as the adaptability and resilience of ecosystems. Keywords: Asia, continental margin, sedimentary continuum, source-to-sink process, Tibetan Plateau

abstracts.title: Upper ocean thermo-haline variability of the Indonesian Throughflow during the Plio-Pleistocene based on IODP Site U1482
abstracts.text:
The Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) is the only low-latitude connection between the Pacific and Indian Oceans, and the heat and salt it exports, more than half via the Timor Passage, make it an important control on eastern Indian Ocean hydrography (Gordon, 2005; Sprintall et al., 2009). Because the archipelago's sills are shallow, its strength, and hence the heat and salt it delivers, is sensitive to sea level and climate change (Cane and Molnar, 2001). The Plio-Pleistocene transition (3.5–1.5 Ma) spans the mid-Piacenzian warm period, the intensification of Northern Hemisphere glaciation at ~2.7 Ma and the strengthening of the Walker circulation (Ravelo et al., 2004), so the outflow is likely to have changed across this interval. Its thermal and haline structure, however, has yet to be reconstructed systematically. The first and last appearances of Globigerinoidesella fistulosa in the Indo-Pacific, at 3.33 and 1.88 Ma, fall close to these boundaries, and we also aim to understand how environmental variability influenced its ecological response.

Here, we reconstructed upper water column conditions at IODP Site U1482 (15°03'S, 120°26'E, 1464 m) in the Timor Sea, within the ITF outflow. We used Mg/Ca and ice-volume corrected δ¹⁸Osw of depth-specific planktonic foraminifera picked from the 150–350 µm fraction of 282 samples. Water column variability was resolved from the surface-dwelling Globigerinoides ruber, upper thermocline Neogloboquadrina dutertrei and lower thermocline Globorotalia tumida. The residual δ¹⁸Osw was interpreted as a salinity signal (Mohtadi et al., 2010).

Our reconstructions give a mean temperature of 27.2 ± 1.0 °C at the surface and 19.9 ± 1.0 °C in the lower thermocline, with the gradient between the two staying near 7.3 °C throughout. This indicates a largely unchanged vertical structure. Within the age-constrained interval, sea surface temperature increased by 0.9 °C and the lower thermocline by 0.7 °C after 2.0 Ma, accompanied by a 0.4–0.5 ‰ rise in δ¹⁸Osw, about one salinity unit. Over the same interval the benthic δ¹⁸O became 0.2 ‰ heavier, yet surface temperature showed no coherence with it (r = 0.04), so the warming was not owing to glacial–interglacial forcing.

Our records therefore show that the upper water column warmed and salinified without a change in its vertical gradient, pointing to a change in the exported water properties rather than local forcing. During the early Pleistocene the Throughflow exported warm, saline water to the eastern Indian Ocean through the cooling recorded by the benthic isotopes.

abstracts.title: Machine-learning mapping of surface sediment organic carbon across the South China Sea
abstracts.text: Marine sedimentary organic carbon is an important component of regional carbon inventories, yet its basin-scale distribution remains poorly resolved in low-latitude marginal seas because observations are uneven and depositional environments differ markedly among shelves, slopes, and deep-sea basins. We integrated 3,382 surface-sediment total organic carbon (TOC) observations with seven groups of environmental predictors in a machine-learning framework to map TOC across the South China Sea at 0.25° resolution and estimate its stock in the upper 10 cm. The basin-wide Extra Trees model achieved a median fold-wise R² of 0.62 and an RMSE of 0.21% under geomorphically stratified fivefold cross-validation. Predicted TOC ranged from 0.03% to 2.02% and averaged 0.63 ± 0.26%. Mean TOC was lowest on the shelf (0.51%), highest on the slope (0.83%), and intermediate in the deep-sea basin (0.74%). High-TOC areas did not follow a simple nearshore-offshore decline; instead, they formed multiple enrichment centers in subaqueous deltaic and shelf mud depocenters, localized slope zones, and the central deep-sea basin. Predictor importance and partial dependence responses indicated contrasting associations among geomorphic units. Shelf TOC was mainly associated with grain-size sorting and shallow-water hydrodynamics; slope TOC with particulate organic matter supply, hydrodynamic redistribution, and water-mass structure; and deep-basin TOC with marine-derived organic matter supply, fine-particle settling, and depositional preservation. The upper 10 cm was estimated to contain 1.94 Pg C (95% uncertainty interval: 1.21-2.83 Pg C), with 84% stored on the shelf and slope. This machine-learning map provides a spatially explicit basis for comparing organic carbon accumulation across geomorphic units and a framework for thematic mapping of sedimentary organic carbon in Asian marginal seas.

abstracts.title: Reservoir regulation has brought a classic river-dominated delta under human control
abstracts.text: Damming of wild rivers has trapped vast quantities of sediment that would otherwise nourish deltas, causing severe sediment deficits and accelerating delta erosion worldwide. The Yellow River Delta, once prograding seaward at ~10 km2/yr, began retreating at -5.6 km2/yr following completion of the Xiaolangdi Reservoir. Implementation of the Water and Sediment Regulation Scheme (WSRS)―a reservoir flushing program―fundamentally reversed this trend. By mobilizing trapped sediment and enhancing downstream channel scouring, the WSRS increased sediment delivery to the sea from 17.6 Mt/yr before its initiation to 178.5 Mt/yr during operation years. This renewed sediment flux restored delta growth, producing subaerial expansion of 6-7 km2/yr and significant subaqueous deposition near the estuary. These results demonstrate that the Yellow River Delta has entered a new phase of evolution under active human management and highlight that sediment trapped behind dams can become a potentially important source for restoring sediment-starved deltas worldwide.

abstracts.title: Refinement of late Pliocene to Pleistocene calcareous nannofossil biostratigraphy of IODP Expedition 363 Site U1487 (Manus Basin, West Pacific Ocean) (Online presentation)
abstracts.text: The western equatorial Pacific plays an important role in the global climate system and preserves valuable sedimentary records of past changes in tropical ocean circulation, climate variability, and marine productivity. International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Expedition 363 Site U1487, located in the Manus Basin approximately 190 km west-southwest of Manus Island, recovered a continuous uppermost Pliocene to Recent succession composed primarily of foraminifer- and nannofossil-rich sediments with varying amounts of clay and volcanic ash. Shipboard investigations established the initial biostratigraphic framework for the site, but the relatively broad sampling intervals limited the precise placement of several microfossil bioevents. This study provides higher-resolution biostratigraphic constraints for the uppermost Pliocene–Pleistocene interval of Hole U1487A using calcareous nannofossils. The assemblages are generally moderately to well preserved and are dominated by placoliths, helicosphaerids and discoasters. The stratigraphic positions of eleven calcareous nannofossil bioevents, comprising six primary and five secondary biohorizons, were refined. The former includes five zonal-boundary markers represented by the top occurrences (T) of Discoaster surculus (NN16/NN17), D. occurrence (B) of Emiliania huxleyi (NN20/NN21). However, B E. huxleyi was not considered a chronological point in the present study because its stratigraphic position could not be reliably resolved from the T. P. lacunosa datum at the available sampling resolution. The top occurrences of Gephyrocapsa sp. >5.5 μm and Calcidiscus macintyrei provided additional chronological control points that improved age–depth resolution within Calcareous Nannofossil Zone NN19/Subzone CN13b. Four additional biohorizons were recognized but were not incorporated as numerical control points in the age–depth model because of low abundance, sporadic occurrence, and stratigraphic positions inconsistent with their expected biochronology. These include the base occurrence of Gephyrocapsa spp. 4–5.5 μm, the top acme of Gephyrocapsa caribbeanica, and the top occurrences of Helicosphaera sellii and Discoaster provides a stronger biostratigraphic framework for future paleoceanographic and paleoclimatic reconstructions in the western equatorial Pacific.

abstracts.title: Influence of gas chimney connectivity and permeability on CO2 migration in offshore geological storage
abstracts.text:
Offshore geological CO2 storage requires assessment of geological structures that can influence vertical fluid migration beyond reservoir-scale plume evolution. Gas chimneys and seafloor pockmarks are widely recognized as indicators of past fluid migration in marine sedimentary basins, making their distribution and connectivity important for storage-site characterization and containment assessment. However, the leakage potential associated with gas chimneys depends on hydraulic connection to the storage reservoir and on permeability contrasts between the chimney and surrounding formations.

The study evaluates gas chimneys as potential migration pathways for injected CO2 using an idealized offshore geological model. Two-phase CO2–brine flow simulations are performed for scenarios with different chimney–reservoir connectivity and hydraulic properties. The simulations track reservoir-scale plume evolution, vertical CO2 migration through the chimney, and transfer into overlying strata. Leakage behavior is quantified using CO2 flux and cumulative migrated mass across selected stratigraphic boundaries.

The model design separates the effect of chimney geometry from the effects of hydraulic connectivity and permeability contrast. Two end-member configurations are considered: an overburden chimney hydraulically isolated from the storage interval and a vertically connected high-permeability chimney extending upward from the reservoir. Additional permeability scenarios are used to evaluate how changes in chimney transmissivity modify the onset and magnitude of upward migration.

The numerical framework provides a basis for identifying conditions under which gas chimneys can act as CO2 migration pathways in offshore storage systems. The comparison also supports evaluation of chimney structures detected in seismic and marine geophysical data by linking mapped geological features with their potential hydraulic significance. Such information can contribute to site screening, leakage-risk assessment, and selection of monitoring targets where gas chimneys or associated pockmarks are present above prospective offshore storage reservoirs.

abstracts.title: Long-term depositional changes linked to redox heterogeneity and microbial zonation in carbonate-rich sediments of KC–7 Seamount, western Pacific
abstracts.text: KC–7 Seamount, located above the carbonate compensation depth (CCD) in the western Pacific, preserves a ~4.3 Myr sediment record dominated by calcareous nannofossils and foraminifera, with East Asian aeolian material as the main terrigenous component. Although seamount summits differ from abyssal plains in particle supply and organic matter preservation, the links among long-term depositional processes, sediment properties, redox structure, and microbial communities remain poorly constrained. Here, we integrated sediment physical properties, pore-water geochemistry, TOC, polarized light microscopy, and 16S rRNA gene-based microbial data to examine how long-term depositional changes shape redox structure and microbial zonation. Dry bulk density rose from ~0.6 g cm⁻³ near the surface to ~0.9 g cm⁻³ in the middle interval (140–468 cm), then dropped to ~0.7 g cm⁻³ below ~470 cm, whereas porosity showed the opposite pattern, decreasing from ~66% near the surface to ~47% in the middle interval and increasing again to ~62% below. The middle interval also recorded lower Eh values (367–380 mV), pointing to restricted pore-water exchange and localized low-redox conditions. TOC, however, remained stable at 0.7–0.9 wt% with no downcore trend, and pore-water SO₄²⁻ averaged 26.7 mM with no depletion at depth, which rules out organic matter enrichment or strong reducing diagenesis as drivers of this pattern. Microscopic examination showed that nannofossil-dominated ooze persisted through the middle and lower intervals, but below ~468 cm the same ooze contained a higher proportion of foraminiferal components. This textural shift likely improved pore-water circulation and oxygen supply in the lower interval. Microbial zonation closely corresponded to these physical and textural changes. Aerobic taxa such as Methylophaga and Marinobacter dominated the upper interval, while the middle interval supported a mix of aerobic, facultatively anaerobic, and anaerobic taxa, including Clostridium, reflecting its restricted oxygen supply. Aerobic taxa again prevailed below ~468 cm, coinciding with the increase in foraminiferal content and porosity. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that depositional inheritance and sediment fabric exert a first-order control on subseafloor redox structure and microbial zonation, even where pore-water conditions remain broadly oxic.

abstracts.title: A centennial perspective on recent phytoplankton community change along the Asian continental margin: From the Arctic to tropics
abstracts.text: Coastal margins are hotspots of organic carbon burial, where climate warming and intensified anthropogenic activities have driven pronounced yet regionally heterogeneous environmental changes over the past century. Whether and how these heterogeneous changes alter the environmental controls governing phytoplankton (e.g., light, temperature, and nutrient supply) and, in turn, affect phytoplankton productivity dynamics across marginal seas from the Arctic to the tropics, however, remains largely unexplored. Here, we reconstructed multi-decadal variations in phytoplankton productivity and community structure using sedimentary biomarkers in three contrasting marginal seas spanning distinct gradients of climate and human influence, namely the East Siberian Sea (ESS), the Bohai Sea, and the Gulf of Thailand (GoT). By integrating biomarker records with environmental observations in a structural equation modelling framework, we quantitatively assessed the regional trajectories of phytoplankton change and identified their dominant environmental controls. Our results reveal pronounced regional differences in both the direction of phytoplankton change and the mechanisms driving these changes. Diatom contribution inferred from molecular biomarkers exhibited contrasting trajectories across the Arctic, tropical, and temperate coastal systems, increasing in the ESS in association with climate-driven sea-ice loss, but declining in the GoT under intensified terrestrial sediment input and coastal erosion. In the temperate Bohai Sea, the relative diatom contribution was comparatively lower and further decreased, primarily in response to anthropogenically induced nutrient imbalance. Together, these records reveal a latitudinal shift in the dominant controls on phytoplankton community evolution, from climate-driven forcing in the Arctic to increasingly important anthropogenic and terrestrial influences in temperate and tropical coastal systems. These findings underscore the need to incorporate regionally and latitudinally distinct environmental forcings into projections of future phytoplankton dynamics and coastal carbon cycling under continuing climate change and human pressure.

abstracts.title: Temporal and spatial coherence between physical processes and seafloor sediment records of the source-to-sink mud belt system on the inner shelf of the East China Sea
abstracts.text: This abstract integrates major findings of three studies on the different aspects of the source-to-sink nature of the sediment dispersal system of the Changjiang (Yangtze) River (CJR) in the inner shelf of the East China Sea (ECS)(Fig. 1). The river plume delivered CJR sourced sediment to the ECS whose southward transport is further facilitated by the monsoon driven Zhi-Min Coastal Current (ZMCC) along the coast. The CJR buoyant plume created a mid-depth interface to prevent suspended sediment from being entrained into the upper water column. The buoyant plume also created a vertical front that prevents suspended sediment from being dispersed seaward. These two boundaries form the major mechanism for sediment retention on the mud belt (Liu et al., 2018). Tidal flows were the most important forcing that transported suspended sediment and water masses. The influences of diurnal to spring-neap tidal cycles are clearly seen in the grain-size distribution patterns and laminations of captured particles in the sediment trap located at St. B2 (Fig. 1). CJR buoyant plume, ZMCC, Kuroshio Branch Current were the major water masses that carried terrestrial- and marine-sourced particles to St. B2. The most important effect of the physical processes on the trapped sediment is the hydrodynamic sorting that separated the clay from silt and sand. Geochemical signals were carried by clay, and coarser grain-sizes contributed to the mass flux. The covariability of water-column process-response variables and down-trap particle characteristics complement each other and point to the close coupling between the physical processes and geochemical signatures of suspended particles in the CJR dispersal system (Liu et al., 2021). The CJR was the dominant river source, accounting for 43% of the covariability in mud belt sediment characteristics. The influence of dam construction in both the Changjiang and Minjiang river basins became evident around 2002. Damming altered grain-size distributions and clay mineral assemblages, leading to temporal shifts in sediment endmember compositions across the shelf. Taiwan-sourced greenish sediments and reddish sediments from the Chinese mainland collectively influenced approximately 22 % of the mud belt’s sediment characteristics, highlighting a dual-source system. The integrated stratigraphic and statistical approach offers a robust framework for identifying, interpreting, and accounting for anthropogenic overprints in continental shelf systems (Yang et al., 2025).

abstracts.title: Paleoceanographic change in the Magellan Seamounts of the western Pacific Ocean since the early Pliocene
abstracts.text:
Here, we report depositional ages and stable oxygen and carbon isotope data of benthic foraminifera in the western Pacific Ocean since ~4.5 Ma, in order to clarify long-term paleoceanographic changes. Cores PC311 and WP-GPC-230202 were taken from the top (17°0.559ʹN, 152°1.907ʹE; 1,370 m water depth) of a seamount in the Magellan Seamounts (western Pacific Ocean). Planktonic foraminifera and calcareous nannofossil biostratigraphy along with magnetostratigraphy in core WP-GPC-230202 indicate continuous sedimentation record since ~4.5 Ma. Despite the greater depth of carbonate-free ocean floor in the open oceanic basin, these cores consist of calcareous sediment throughout the core due to its shallower depth on the top of seamount. Thus, these cores provide us great opportunity to understand the long-term palaeoceanographic transition between the surface and deep oceans in more detail.

The sedimentation rates show decline at ~2 Ma in both cores (2.4 Ma: Khim et al., 2025; 1.9 Ma: Takata et al., 2026). The core sites are located near the boundary between the North Equatorial Current and the more oligotrophic North Pacific Gyre, making biological productivity sensitive to variation in oceanographic conditions. The southward movement of the mean position of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) may result in the decrease of primary production, shifting the equatorial wind-driven mixing zone away from the core sites, as suggested by Wang et al. (2023). Because these cores primarily consist of biogenic carbonates, the decreasing sedimentation rate at ~2 Ma may be explained by the southward displacement of the mean ITCZ position, migrating from the equatorial wind-driven mixing zone, which is characterized by high primary and carbonate productions.

Stable carbon isotope data of benthic foraminifera has been used to infer deep-water circulation. It has been suggested that deep-water formed in the high-latitude North Pacific during the early Pliocene (e.g., Le Houedec et al., 2016; Ford et al., 2022). We examined stable carbon and oxygen isotope ratios of benthic foraminifera (Cibicidoies mundulus; >150 µm) in ~180 samples of our core spanning last ~4.5 Myrs. Our results indicated higher carbon isotope values during the early Pliocene. It would provide important constraint to improve our knowledge of the deep-water circulation in the bathyal depth of the western Pacific Ocean. We will discuss the spatiotemporal distribution of benthic foraminiferal δ13C in the western Pacific Ocean during the early Pliocene.

abstracts.title: Climate-driven shifts in the carbon sequestration of reactive iron minerals in the Arctic shelf
abstracts.text: The organic carbon (OC) stored in the Arctic permafrost accounts for almost half of the global soil OC res-ervoir, with reactive iron oxides (FeR) playing a crucial role in sequestrating and stabilizing the labile perma-frost OC. Under global warming and Arctic amplification in recent decades, the thawing of Arctic permafrost, increased river runoff, and enhanced coastal erosion have not only accelerated the release and transition of permafrost OC in the land-ocean continuum, but also likely altered the flux of FeR-associated OC (OC-FeR), thereby affecting the burial of permafrost OC in the marginal seas and its feedback to climate warming. Therefore, reconstructing the burial records of OC-FeR and the environmental response mechanisms in the Arctic is essential for accurately assessing the role of mineral protection in the carbon neutrality in a natural setting. This study investigated the burial of OC-FeR in sediments from the East Siberian Arctic Shelf over the last decades. It was found that an average of 19.82% of OC is bound to FeR, and this association occurs during terrestrial transport and marine deposition prior to burial. Comparing to the coastal erosion-affected region, the burial of OC-FeR in estuarine exhibits temporally-distinct responses to permafrost thawing dy-namics in the watershed. By integrating permafrost environmental parameters in the Lena River watershed, such as permafrost temperature, moisture, active layer thickness, and precipitation, this study uncovered the response of OC-FeR burial to the terrestrial permafrost-climate dynamics. Specifically, during the pre-2000s, the progressive decline in OC-FeR coincided with watershed-scale soil moisture redistribution driven by gradual active-layer deepening, which preferentially retained OC-FeR in permafrost, attenuating its land-to-ocean fluxes. Since 2000s, although abrupt thaw has rapidly mobilized OC, ∼19% of sedimentary OC remained stabilized as OC-FeR, thus partially decoupling abrupt thaw from immediate permafrost car-bon-climate feedbacks. Therefore, this mineralogical buffering mechanism can attenuate the net climate im-pact of accelerating abrupt thaw across the Northern Hemisphere cryosphere.

abstracts.title: Holocene to Anthropocene organic carbon burial mechanisms in the Yangtze Estuary: Impacts of natural and anthropogenic drivers
abstracts.text:
Coastal mega-deltas serve critical carbon sinks regulating global atmospheric CO2, yet their organic carbon (OC) sequestration capacity has been drastically reshaped by natural Holocene climate shifts and human disturbances in the Anthropocene. Two core research systems are established based on recent sediment geochemical investigations in the Yangtze Delta and Hangzhou Bay. Integrated sedimentary records, porewater geochemistry and radionuclide chronologies are adopted to systematically contrast OC burial drivers, transformation pathways and carbon source variations under natural climate, dam interception and coastal engineering disturbances.

Over the mid-Holocene to pre-dam Anthropocene, the Yangtze Delta OC evolution experienced three distinct phases. From 8 ka to 2 ka, weakened East Asian Summer Monsoon reduced terrestrial OC input, forming a stable slow-progradation stage with average OC burial rate of 0.79 Mt yr-1 dominated by climate and sea-level controls. Since 2 ka, intensified human land cultivation and watershed erosion boosted river sediment discharge, lifting OC burial by 78% (1.40–1.44 Mt yr-1) and shifting dominant control from natural climate to anthropogenic activities. After the Three Gorges Dam impoundment in 2003, sharp sediment depletion triggered widespread subaqueous delta erosion; OC burial rate declined by 59%, and the delta transformed from a net carbon sink to an OC source exporting ~0.81 Mt yr-1 terrestrial carbon to the Zhejiang-Fujian mud belt. Coastal artificial island construction further altered storm-driven carbon cycles: post-reclamation typhoons triggered large-scale submarine landslides, generating thick storm deposits with nine-fold instantaneous OC accumulation, while severe pre-depositional erosion and enhanced post-burial organic matter remineralization caused far greater net carbon loss than temporary burial gain. Contrast analysis reveals natural Holocene carbon cycling is regulated by monsoon intensity and relative sea level, maintaining stable long-term carbon preservation. Anthropogenic disturbances exert two-tier destructive effects: upstream dams cut sediment and terrestrial OC supply to collapse delta carbon sink capacity; offshore reclamation reshapes seabed topography, amplifying storm erosion and organic mineralization to accelerate estuarine carbon turnover. This study clarifies divergent carbon sequestration mechanisms between Holocene natural evolution and Anthropogenic human interference, providing theoretical support for delta carbon sink restoration and coastal ecological carbon management.

abstracts.title: DSDP 296 re-drilling: to recover continuous carbonate ooze for the last 20 Myrs on the Kyushu-Palau Ridge in the western North Pacific
abstracts.text: We aim to re-drill the Site DSDP 296 drilled on the northern Kyushu–Palau Ridge in 1973 (29°20.41′N, 133°31.52′E; 2,920 m water depth). The core samples were retrieved using a rotary core barrel, recovery rates were low (60%), leaving its utility as a paleoclimate archive uncertain. However, our previous study (Matsui et al., 2020) based on biostratigraphy (calcareous nannofossil, planktic foraminifera, and radiolarians) and chemostratigraphy (δ18O and Sr isotopes) revealed that the sedimentary sequence is continuous for the last 20 Myrs with sedimentation rates between 0.5 and 4 cm per kiloyears (Fig. 1), covering both the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum (16.9–14.7 Ma) and the subsequent Middle Miocene Climatic Transition (14.7–13.0 Ma). Nonetheless, it is unable to establish magnetostratigraphy and to discuss orbital-scale paleoceanographic changes due to the rotation and low recovery of the sediment core samples. Site 296 is located at the northern limit of the carbonate ooze in the North Pacific, with relatively abundant foraminifera. In addition, deposited tephra layers are promising key beds, recording volcanic eruption history in the western North Pacific margin. We are planning to submit an IODP3 proposal to redrill Site DSDP 296 to retrieve a truly continuous sedimentary sequence from the early Miocene to establish a reference paleoceanographic site in the western North Pacific.

abstracts.title: Status of the geological investigations in the Huatung Basin and future scientific ocean drilling perspectives
abstracts.text:
The western Pacific is among the most tectonically complex regions on Earth, marked by a highly fragmented lithosphere and the formation of numerous marginal seas and subduction zones. Despite extensive geological investigations, its tectonic evolution remains poorly understood, representing a major unresolved problem in global plate tectonics. Recent geochronological studies of rock samples suggest that the Huatung Basin, located east of Taiwan in the western Pacific, may preserve Early Cretaceous oceanic crust. If confirmed, this ancient crust would provide critical constraints on the Mesozoic–Cenozoic tectonic evolution of the western Pacific.

Interpretations of diverse geophysical datasets indicate that the Huatung Basin is underlain by normal to relatively thin oceanic crust, with an estimated thickness of approximately 5–7 km. Geochemical studies of available basement rock samples reveal transitional characteristics between mid-ocean-ridge basalt (MORB) and ocean-island basalt (OIB), together with a pronounced affinity to Indian Ocean-type depleted mantle. The Gagua Ridge, which forms the eastern boundary of the Huatung Basin, records Early Cretaceous arc-related magmatic activity and has been proposed as a rare example of failed subduction initiation preserved in the geological record. However, the lack of scientific drilling data severely limits our knowledge of the basin. In particular, the non-uniqueness of geophysical interpretations, the scarcity of available rock samples, and their limited representativeness have introduced considerable uncertainty into interpretations of the basin’s formation and evolution.

Here, we review the major advances in research on the formation age, oceanic crustal structure, rock geochemistry, seismic stratigraphy, and tectonic origin of the Huatung Basin. We further summarize the major unresolved questions and discuss potential targets, objectives, and strategies for future scientific ocean drilling. We propose that future drilling should target (1) key magnetic anomalies in the abyssal plain of the southern Huatung Basin, where basement deformation is relatively weak and a relatively complete sedimentary succession may be preserved, and (2) the Gagua Ridge, which has been interpreted as a potential record of failed subduction initiation. Recovery of in situ samples from the complete sedimentary succession and basement igneous rocks would allow us to test the proposed Late Mesozoic age of the basin, constrain the composition, nature, and origin of its oceanic crust, and ultimately provide critical evidence for reconstructing the Mesozoic–Cenozoic tectonic evolution of the western Pacific.

abstracts.title: Sustained deep-sea carbon flux by zooplankton fecal pellets under multiscale climate forcing in the South China Sea
abstracts.text: The efficiency of the biological carbon pump depends on the vertical transfer of particulate organic carbon, with zooplankton fecal pellets playing an important role. However, the mechanisms maintaining deep fecal pellet fluxes across multiple timescales of climate variability remain poorly constrained. Here, we present a high-resolution, four-year (2021–2025) record derived from dual-depth (500 and 1,970 m) sediment traps in the northern South China Sea to elucidate these dynamics. By establishing a fecal pellet carbon (FPC)-specific Martin attenuation coefficient (bFPC = 0.37) , we separate physical particle transport from mesopelagic biological processing. We show that FPC fluxes respond to climate forcing across multiple timescales. Pulsed export is triggered by mesoscale eddy activity and typhoon-induced mixing, seasonal variability is driven by monsoon forcing and stratification changes, and interannual variability tracks the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), suggesting ENSO-driven modulation of regional nutrient supply and carbon export. Contrary to the conventional view of exponential attenuation, our mass-balance analysis shows that only 29.6% of the FPC flux at 1,970 m is derived from direct settling of upper-ocean material. Instead, mesopelagic egestion and repackaging account for 60.9% of the deep FPC flux, while lateral advection contributes the remaining 9.5%. This “biological pump within the pump” mechanism explains the widespread observation of deep FPC enrichment across the basin. We conclude that the persistence of deep carbon export under climate variability is largely supported by mesopelagic biological processing. Ignoring this active repackaging underestimates long-term carbon sequestration potential in a warming ocean.

abstracts.title: Exploring the history of slip-to-the-trench and element cycling in a hadal trench basin through drilling of trench-fill sequence at the central Japan Trench: IODP3 Exp. 503 “Hadal Trench Tsunamigenic Slip History – Buried in the Trench”
abstracts.text:
Hadal trenches are among the least explored environments on Earth, despite their association with the largest and most devastating earthquakes. Hadal trenches act as terminal sinks for sediment and carbon transported by gravity flows in the active subduction margin. The sedimentary sequence of the trench-fill represents geological archive to reconstruct long-term earthquake behavior, including rare slip-to-the-trench events that generate large tsunamis. The basins also host extreme subseafloor ecosystems and play an important role in global carbon cycle.

IODP3 Expedition 503 drilled a trench-fill basin in the central Japan Trench at Site C0028 using the D/V seafloor, recovering the first continuous record of the full trench-fill sequence. Initial results confirm that drilling successfully penetrated the full trench-fill and its base. The drill cores were divided into five lithostratigraphic units, revealing an upward progression from volcaniclastic-rich sediments to mixed siliciclastic sediments and uppermost biosiliceous sediments, reflecting basin initiation, growth, and progressive migration toward the trench axis. Event deposits are exceptionally well preserved except for the lowest unit. Numerous thick turbidites, which are correlated between holes and seismic reflectors, provide a robust framework for paleoseismological interpretation. Tephro- and magneto-stratigraphy offers a high potential for establishing high-resolution age model even under hadal environments below the CCD. The first-order age model indicated that as the basin approached the trench axis, the sedimentation rate increased sharply at ~100 ka, and the basin was buried by thick, fine-grained event deposits. Such dynamic changes in sedimentation also influenced the burial of carbon.

These initial findings indicate that hadal trench basins well preserve long, continuous records of tsunamigenic earthquake behavior and associated biogeochemical processes, providing new perspectives on earthquake recurrence, subduction-zone hazards, and carbon and element cycling along the subduction zone margins.

abstracts.title: Distribution of terrestrial plant-derived terpenoids in North Pacific surface sediments: Insights into terrigenous material transport and paleoenvironments
abstracts.text:
Terrestrial plant-derived terpenoids (TPTs) possess diverse chemical structures depending on plant taxonomy and can constrain their sources more specifically than other biomarkers such as long-chain n-alkanes derived from higher plant waxes. Therefore, they are considered potential powerful biomarkers for evaluating the transport processes of terrestrial material into the ocean, as well as its sources and hinterland vegetation. In deep-sea sediments, bioterpenoids containing functional groups synthesized by modern plants are predominantly detected; however, it has become clear that geoterpenoids such as terpene hydrocarbons that have undergone diagenesis and maturation are also present in trace yet significant amounts. For example, retene, a diagenetic product of abietic acid produced by living conifers, is widely detected in deep-sea sediments (Sawada and Kobayashi, 2025). Such diagenetic terpenoids do not originate directly from modern vegetation; instead, their primary sources are presumed to be highly mature sedimentary rocks that have undergone diagenesis in the hinterland, as well as soils heavily influenced by these rocks. Furthermore, arid and desert regions in inland China are considered likely candidate hinterlands, suggesting that terpene hydrocarbons in marine sediments, such as those in the Pacific Ocean, are delivered from these areas as atmospherically transported dust. Matured TPT hydrocarbons are also generated through combustion processes such as wildfires. These combustion-derived molecules are likewise believed to be transported to the ocean primarily via airborne soot. Consequently, terpene hydrocarbons record information distinct from that of vegetation-derived bioterpenoids, providing insights into atmospheric transport and wildfires. However, studies investigating such terpene hydrocarbons in modern marine sediments remain extremely limited.

However, several concerns have been raised regarding these hydrocarbons: 1) Anthropogenic gases and particulate matter originating from urban areas rather than natural environments may contribute to their presence, and 2) The possibility of terpenoid inputs derived from marine bacteria cannot be entirely ruled out. Addressing these issues is essential to enhance the applicability and reliability of TPT hydrocarbons as geochemical proxies. To resolve these concerns, our research group has conducted extensive studies focusing on TPTs in surface sediments, sediment cores, and IODP drilling cores collected from the Pacific Ocean. Our findings confirmed that these potential confounding factors exert a negligible influence on the vast majority of deep-sea sediment samples. In this presentation, we compare the compound distributions of TPT hydrocarbons primarily in North Pacific sediments to discuss their sources and transport processes, as well as their utility as proxies for terrestrial material transport and paleoenvironmental reconstructions.

abstracts.title: E-ODP initiative: Advancing global ocean drilling data integration and AI-driven scientific discovery
abstracts.text:
The international ocean drilling programs (Deep Sea Drilling Program, Ocean Drilling Program, Integrated Ocean Drilling Program, and International Ocean Discovery Program) have drilled more than 4200 holes and recovered about 500 km long cores worldwide over the past nearly six decades. This sustained global effort has driven a series of significant scientific discoveries that have fundamentally redefined our understanding of the Earth system. The resulting data legacy, encompassing over 200 types across disciplines such as lithostratigraphy, sedimentology, paleontology, geochemistry, and geophysics, can continue to provide critical insights into our planet's evolution and future prediction. While some recent studies have successfully developed specialized databases and yielded high-impact results, the scientific potential of the ocean drilling data legacy remains largely fragmented and heterogeneous formats. Rapid advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) now provide the technical capabilities required to facilitate large-scale data integration and multidisciplinary synthesis for future ocean drilling studies.

In view of these developments, the Electronic Ocean Drilling Program (E-ODP) has been initiated to advance global ocean drilling data integration, thereby fostering AI-driven scientific discovery (AI for Science). The first international E-ODP workshop was organized by Deep Ocean Drilling Program (DODP) and Tongji University during 9–11 September 2026 at Shanghai, aiming to convene experts in ocean drilling and data science to share recent scientific discoveries, assess existing multi-disciplinary databases, and establish a strategic roadmap for AI-supported ocean drilling research. About 180 participants in fields of core records, databases, and AI research from 24 countries attended the workshop. Follow-up collaboration actions to realize the E-ODP initiative were discussed. They include: (1) establishing the E-ODP framework: DODP and relevant partners will collaboratively develop the E-ODP infrastructure, formalize partnerships through signed agreements, and define a joint operational support model; (2) formulating governance structure: two dedicated implementation bodies (management working group and scientific working group) to be established; (3) implementing core operational pillars: database, shared platform, and AI for Science research; all must strictly adhere to the FAIR principles. This presentation will introduce future roadmap and partner collaboration of the E-ODP initiative in detail.

abstracts.title: Monsoon and Coriolis force driven multi-provenance evolution of the Sunda Shelf since the mid-Holocene
abstracts.text: Shelf in marginal seas act as critical links among the lithosphere and hydrosphere, and its provenance evolution and dynamic mechanisms are essential for understanding the interactions within the Earth system. In this study, core sediments from the central Sunda Shelf were selected as study material. Sr-Nd isotopes of the fluvial sediments from surrounding lands and islands were used for qualitative provenance identification. Combined with an isotopic mixing model and riverine sediment flux, we quantitatively reconstructed the provenance evolutionary history of the core since the mid-Holocene. The results reveal that the Mekong River is the dominant sediment source for the major part of the Sunda Shelf, while rivers across Thailand constitute secondary sources. Furthermore, this study indicates that sediment inputs from northern rivers and remobilized fine-grained particles derived from shelf also exert influences on sediment composition across the shelf. Provenance variations are predominantly governed by the East Asian monsoon. Since the mid-Holocene, sea level has remained stable; the weakened summer monsoon and intensified winter monsoon have strengthened the counterclockwise circulation of the SCS, especially the persistent western boundary current. This hydrodynamic system transports fine-grained sediments derived from the Red River, Beibuwan Gulf and the shelf off the Indochina Peninsula to the Sunda Shelf over long distances, forming a complex multi-source sedimentary pattern. This study complements the quantitative records of multiple sediment sources on the Sunda Shelf, improves the theory of long-distance sediment transport driven by monsoons in marginal seas, and provides new insights into Earth system processes of low-latitude continental shelves.

abstracts.title: Towards reconstruction of million-year-scale Kuroshio variability: Insights from sedimentary records of the northwestern Pacific
abstracts.text: The Kuroshio Current is a major western boundary current of the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre and plays a critical role in regulating climate variability in East Asia. Paleoceanographic reconstructions of Kuroshio variability have primarily relied on marine sediment cores recovered south of the Japanese archipelago. However, most studies are limited to the last glacial cycle because recovery of older sediments is often impeded by thick tephra deposits, such as the widespread Aira-Tanzawa (AT) tephra east of Kyushu, which restrict the penetration of conventional piston corers. Furthermore, robust reconstructions of Kuroshio variability require well-preserved sediments containing abundant fossil foraminifera to both establish high-resolution chronologies and apply paleoceanographic proxies. To investigate longer-term variability, alkenone-derived sea-surface temperatures were analyzed from Core MD01-2422 and ODP Hole 1176A off the Nankai margin of Shikoku, Japan. These records indicate that sea-surface temperatures during the Last Interglacial (MIS 5e) were approximately 2°C higher than during the Holocene (Yamamoto, 2004), whereas temperatures during the Last Glacial Period and MIS 6 were broadly comparable. Similar MIS 5e warming has also been reported from the East China Sea (Lee et al., 2021) and Paleo-Tokyo Bay (Kajita et al., 2022), suggesting that exceptionally warm Kuroshio conditions were widespread across the northwestern Pacific during this super-interglacial interval. Despite extending back to approximately 300 ka, sedimentary records from MD01-2422 and ODP Hole 1176A are affected by slumping and stratigraphic disturbance in their deeper sections. Similar sediment deformation occurs at ODP Sites 1175 and 1178 in the Nankai margin (Moore et al., 2001). In contrast, continuous pelagic sequences recovered at ODP Sites 1173 and 1174 in the Shikoku Basin are characterized by low sedimentation rates and poor preservation of fossil foraminifera (Moore et al., 2001). Consequently, existing records from the Nankai Trough region are inadequate to investigate relationships between Kuroshio variability and East Asian climate change on million-year timescales. These results highlight the need for new continuous sedimentary archives from the northwestern Pacific. In particular, the northern Kyushu-Palau Ridge represents a promising target for future drilling to reconstruct the long-term evolution of the Kuroshio Current and its role in regional oceanographic and climatic change.

abstracts.title: Li isotopic constraints on terrestrial weathering signal transport in the Changjiang-East China Sea continuum
abstracts.text: Owing to the pronounced isotope fractionation associated with silicate alteration, lithium (Li) isotopes are increasingly used to reconstruct past continental weathering. Their sedimentary record, however, is shaped not only by weathering within drainage basins but also by processes operating during sediment transfer. As particles move downstream, hydrodynamic sorting and differential transport progressively reorganize their mineralogical and geochemical composition, potentially even modifying provenance and weathering signals in marginal-sea environments. To examine how terrestrial signal evolves during source-to-sink transfer, surface sediments collected from the Yangtze River–estuary–East China Sea shelf continuum are analysed for major and trace elements, Li isotopic compositions, and mineral assemblages. Results show that sedimentary δ7Li values within the catchment are closely linked to the abundance of secondary minerals contributed by different sub-basins and are thus provenance-dependent. When sediment passing through the estuary, differential transport (e.g., kaolinite flocculation and settling) modify sediment chemical compositions. The Li isotopic mass balance model indicates that the proportion of weathering products in bulk sediments decrease while shale components increase. After examining through subsequent leaching, we confirm that the variation in sedimentary δ7Li values can be attributed to physical processes rather than chemical alteration (e.g., reverse weathering). This study provides a source-to-sink perspective on how continental weathering signals are transferred, modified, and ultimately preserved in marginal-sea sediments. These modern-process constraints are critical for improving the application of sedimentary Li isotopes as a proxy for reconstructing continental weathering through geological time.

abstracts.title: Revised composite splice stratigraphy of IODP Site U1445 in the Bay of Bengal
abstracts.text:
The Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) is a major component of the global climate system, yet its long-term variability and influence on climate forcing remain unconstrained due to the lack of records. Existing reconstructions extending beyond the Late Pleistocene have primarily relied on sediment archives from the Arabian Sea, which mainly reflect monsoon wind intensity rather than monsoon precipitation, river discharge, and their influence on marine productivity. In contrast, the Bay of Bengal (BoB), a key region integrating ISM variability in discharge and sediment transport from the Ganges, Brahmaputra, Meghna, and Mahanadi River systems, offering insights into paleomonsoon evolution and its impact on regional climate and marine productivity. Therefore, this study investigates sediments recovered from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U1445, located on the upper continental rise of the Mahanadi Basin in the northwestern BoB.

Site U1445 contains a continuous sedimentary sequence extending back to the late Miocene and is dominated by hemipelagic sediments with significant biogenic components. However, the construction of the stratigraphic splice with a robust composite depth scale and chronological framework is complicated by stratigraphic inconsistencies due to significant core disturbances which make it difficult to utilize bulk physical property data such as Natural Gamma Radiation (NGR), Gamma Ray Attenuation (GRA) bulk density, and Reflectance Spectroscopy and Colorimetry (RSC). In order to solve these difficulties, the stratigraphy was refined through the development of an improved stratigraphic splice using photo RGB datasets from Holes U1445A and U1445C. Then, composite ln(R/G) profile was compared with high resolution logging data of Formation Microscanner (FMS) to examine the continuity of the stratigraphic splice.

The resulting splice will provide the stratigraphic framework for subsequent analyses of foraminiferal stable isotopes (δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C), grain-size distributions, and biomarkers to investigate sedimentation processes and long-term ISM-driven changes in marine productivity. The age model will be further refined by an orbitally tuned foraminiferal δ¹⁸O stratigraphy. A reassessed orbitally constrained chronology will place these marine records into a reliable framework, enabling them to reveal the changes in regional and global paleoclimate. Ultimately, this integrated multiproxy approach aims to enhance our understanding of long-term ISM variability and the interactions between continental processes and the marine environment in the BoB.

abstracts.title: Multi-proxy reconstruction of environmental responses to marine transgression in Hangzhou Bay since MIS 6
abstracts.text: The occurrence of marine deposits during MIS 3 in eastern China remains controversial in the Hangzhou Bay (HZB) region due to limited availability of continuous sedimentary records with reliable chronological constraints. Here we present a multi-proxy investigation of the 145.52 m-long ZH02 sediment core recovered from the Zhejiang coastal plain. An improved chronological framework spanning approximately ~189 ka (MIS 6–MIS 1) was established by integrating AMS radiocarbon dating for the upper section with lithostratigraphic interpretation, spectral analysis, and stratigraphic age modelling for the deeper sequence, providing a robust framework for reconstructing long-term environmental evolution. A total of 57 pollen and spore taxa were identified, accompanied by diagnostic planktonic and benthic foraminifera and ostracod assemblages, indicating recurrent alternations between continental and shallow-marine depositional environments. Based on lithological characteristics, microfossil assemblages, and chronological constraints, the sediment sequence is divided into three environmental phases: Zone A (145.52–79.02 m; ~189.9–102.85ka), Zone B (79.02–27.8 m; ~102.85–36.51 ka), and Zone C (27.8–0.50 m; 36.51–1.63 ka). Three major transgressive events are identified in HZB: a relatively weak Jiangyin transgression during MIS 5 (~123-84 ka), the most pronounced Gehu transgression during MIS 3 (~42 ka), and the Zhejiang transgression during MIS 1 (~8.5 ka). Among these, the Gehu transgression is the most pronounced, characterized by continuous occurrence of marine microfossils, reduced terrestrial pollen input, and fine-grained sediments, indicating sustained marine inundation. In contrast, the Jiangyin and Zhejiang transgressions are relatively weaker, reflecting strong fluvial influence, tidal reworking, and estuarine dynamics that modulated the sedimentary response to sea-level rise. These results reveal complex transgressive–regressive dynamics in the HZB coastal system, driven by interactions among regional sea-level change, sediment supply, tectonic subsidence, geomorphological setting, and climatic variability.

abstracts.title: Distinguishing grain-size signals of eolian and laterally transported hemipelagic sediments in the East Sea (Japan Sea)
abstracts.text:
In marginal seas, eolian dust records can be obscured by hemipelagic sediments supplied through lateral transport. We investigated two sediment cores from contrasting depositional settings in the East Sea (Japan Sea) to distinguish eolian signals from those of laterally transported hemipelagic sediments. Core 05-P21 was recovered at 1,721 m water depth from an elevated site on the Korea Plateau, where previous studies demonstrated that eolian sedimentation dominates the detrital fraction. Core 24MAP-P02 was recovered at 1,960 m water depth from the central Ulleung Basin, approximately 224 km south-southwest of 05-P21, where reworked shelf and upper-slope sediments can be supplied intermittently by downslope transport.

We compared mean grain size (Mz) records from the two cores since marine isotope stage (MIS) 5e. Turbidite intervals and tephra layers identified in 24MAP-P02 were excluded from the grain-size record. Both cores have their finest Mz values of approximately 3 μm during interglacial MIS 1 and MIS 5e. During colder intervals, 05-P21 shows moderate coarsening, whereas 24MAP-P02 exhibits frequent and pronounced coarsening, with Mz values exceeding 16 μm particularly during MIS 2-3. End-member (EM) analysis of 24MAP-P02 grain-size distributions distinguished three components. EM1 and EM2 have mean sizes of approximately 3.2 and 8.8 μm, respectively, resembling the fine and coarse eolian end members previously identified in 05-P21. They represent dust transported by the upper-level westerlies and low-level northwesterly winter monsoon winds, respectively. The coarser EM3, with a mean size of approximately 16.7 μm, represents reworked hemipelagic sediments supplied by lateral transport.

To reconstruct the eolian grain-size signal at 24MAP-P02, EM3 was removed by rescaling the proportions of EM1 and EM2 to sum to 100%. The modeled eolian Mz at 24MAP-P02 is similar to that at 05-P21 during MIS 1 and MIS 5e, when fine EM1 dominates at both sites. During colder intervals, the relative contribution of coarse EM2 increases at both sites, but more strongly at northern 05-P21. Removing EM3 thus converts the apparent southward coarsening of the bulk sediments into southward fining of the eolian fraction. These preliminary results indicate that the meridional difference in eolian grain size primarily reflects a southward decrease in the relative contribution of coarse dust transported by the winter monsoon, rather than changes in the characteristic grain sizes of the eolian end members.

abstracts.title: Synchronous sediment provenance shifts in the southern South China Sea across the glacial-Holocene transition
abstracts.text: The Sunda Shelf, the largest tropical continental shelf on Earth, was extensively exposed during glacial lowstands, potentially altering sediment provenance and silicate weathering in the southern South China Sea (SCS). However, whether provenance changes were synchronous across the southern SCS slope and how sea-level oscillations controlled them remain debated. Here we present Sr–Nd isotopic and U-series comminution-age records from two sediment cores: core 18252-3 and core 17964-3, both retrieved from the southern SCS slope. Sr–Nd isotopes from both cores show synchronous provenance shifts. During the Last Glacial period (Unit 1, ~28– 40 ka), low sea level exposed the Sunda Shelf; sediments were dominated by the Mekong River. During the deglacial–Holocene (Units 2–3, ~28 ka to present), sea level rose and the Mekong River mouth retreated; contributions from northern South China Rivers (SCRs: Red River and Pearl River) increased, especially in the Holocene. Uranium comminution ages from both cores increase during the glacial period and decrease in the Holocene, indicating longer sediment storage and reworking of old shelf sediments during lowstands, versus rapid delivery of fresh fluvial sediments during highstands. We attribute these synchronous changes to sea-level forcing: glacial lowstand exposed the Sunda Shelf, delivering the adjacent Mekong sediments to the slope; postglacial sea-level rise submerged the shelf and the intensified South China Sea western boundary current (SCSwbc) established a hydrodynamic barrier that curtailed Mekong sediment dispersal while facilitating along-slope transport of South China River sediments. These findings demonstrate that sea-level change is the first-order control on sediment provenance at this continental slope site, with important implications for paleoenvironmental reconstructions and sediment routing models in the southern SCS.

abstracts.title: Near-bottom sediment dynamics in the Swatch of No Ground (SoNG) Canyon in the Bay of Bengal, northern Indian Ocean
abstracts.text: The shelf-incised canyon ‘Swatch of No Ground (SoNG)’ connects the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna river delta (Earth’s largest and most populated delta) with the Bengal Fan (Earth’s largest deep-marine sedimentary system) and provides an efficient route for the rapid transfer of terrigenous material to the deep sea. While sedimentological studies have documented depositional patterns and long-term sediment budget estimates, physical processes controlling sediment transport within the SoNG have not been directly monitored. This study presents an 18-day mooring record of current velocity, acoustic backscatter intensity and settling particles from March 2024, combined with shipboard measurements and surface sediment analyses, capturing near-bed sediment dynamics in the SoNG during the dry season. Two distinct processes modulating suspended sediment concentrations at the canyon bottom are identified: (1) Nonlinear Internal Waves (NLIWs), prevalent during spring tides but also occurring during neap tides, which enhance turbulent mixing and lift particles from the bottom boundary layer; (2) Lateral transport of a high-turbidity plume, associated with enhanced downward vertical velocity and settling fluxes reaching six times the pre-event values. During the plume event, the proportion of terrestrially derived organic carbon increased. It is hypothesized to be triggered by tide-driven sediment gravity flows. These first-time observations demonstrate that the dry season is a period of sediment resuspension, temporary storage, and stepwise redistribution of fine-grained sediments and organic carbon. Repeated NLIWs and plume events modulate the fate of terrestrially derived materials from the wet season, directly influencing annual sediment accumulation and carbon cycling in the Bay of Bengal.
