abstracts.text: Potassium (K) is a major cation in seawater, but its budget remains not fully constrained. Marine clay authigenesis is assumed to exert a substantial control on seawater chemistry and Earth's climate. Nevertheless, the global importance of K-rich authigenic clays for the marine K budget remains poorly quantified. Here, we investigated particulate K/Al ratios and porewater geochemical compositions along the Changjiang (Yangtze) River–East China Sea transect to elucidate the role of authigenic K uptake in the marine K budget. Our results show that marine particulates exhibit substantially higher K/Al ratios (0.31 ± 0.04) than riverine endmember materials (0.25 ± 0.02). Coupled with downcore decreases in porewater K concentrations and increasing green grain abundance toward the shelf, we propose that systematic variations in particulate K/Al ratios are driven by active authigenic K uptake from porewater and seawater. The preliminary estimate yields a global K uptake flux of 81 ± 62 Tg/yr when extrapolated to all river-dominated ocean margins, a magnitude comparable to the global riverine dissolved K input. Meanwhile, porewater geochemical profiles exhibit distinct seasonal variability, indicating rapid rates of authigenic clay formation/transformation. Collectively, these findings highlight the pivotal role of authigenic mineral formation in modulating seawater and marine sediment geochemistry.

abstracts.title: Morphodynamics and stratigraphic architecture of tidal point bars and abandoned channel fills in macrotidal Gomso Bay, Korea
affiliations: School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
E&P Portfolio and A&D Department, Korea National Oil Corporation, Ulsan, Korea
abstracts.text: The stratigraphic architecture of point bars and abandoned channel fills is well documented in fluvial meanders, but remains poorly understood in tidal channels, particularly where episodic runoff interacts with strong tidal forcing. Here, we reconstruct the stratigraphic architecture of a meandering tidal channel in macrotidal Gomso Bay, west coast of Korea, using long-term morphodynamic and hydrodynamic observations combined with densely spaced short cores. Channel migration was controlled by both tidal currents and seasonally enhanced, rainfall-induced runoff. Bend-apex trajectories show that migration occurred mainly through downstream elongation and rotation, with subordinate downstream translation where the migrating channel encountered resistant muddy cutbanks. During the summer rainy season, enhanced runoff strengthened ebb currents and promoted chute cutoff of a tight meander bend, followed by rapid abandonment of the former channel. The point-bar architecture reflects pronounced tidal-current asymmetry. Mutually evasive flood and ebb currents, together with overall ebb dominance, produced fining toward the bend apex and subordinate flood-directed ripples within predominantly ebbward-dipping inclined heterolithic stratification (IHS). Time-velocity asymmetry and pronounced peak-velocity asymmetry contributed to the development of planform morphology at the tight bend and partitioned the point bar into a sand-dominated lower part and a mud-dominated upper part. Within the lower point bar, seasonal variations in runoff produced alternations between sandier rainy-season deposits and muddier fair-weather deposits. Abandoned-channel fills record two distinct stages of abandonment. Early-stage fills comprise IHS of rippled sand and irregularly interlaminated sand and mud, recording continued point-bar migration while substantial through-flow persisted after chute cutoff. Late-stage fills are muddier and dominated by rhythmically interlaminated sand and mud, recording rapid aggradation, locally reaching 20 cm per month, after complete flow disconnection. Their architecture was further modified by proximity to the active channel, rill-channel activity, and tidal-current asymmetry. These results demonstrate that seasonal and episodic runoff can exert a first-order control on channel migration, cutoff, abandonment, and their resulting stratigraphic expression even in a macrotidal environment with otherwise limited fluvial influence.

abstracts.title: Muddy tidal rhythmites in a channelized open-coast macrotidal flat: Implications for paleoelevation reconstruction and IHS architecture
affiliations: School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
Marine Natural Disaster Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
Division for Public Infrastructure Assessment, Korea Environment Institute, Sejong, Korea
abstracts.text: Tidal rhythmites are widely regarded as one of the most reliable indicators of tidal sedimentation and are most commonly documented in protected environments, such as the upper intertidal zones of confined estuarine channels. In contrast, examples from open-coast tidal flats, where wave activity seasonally modifies sediment dynamics and preservation potential, remain relatively rare. This study documents muddy tidal rhythmites preserved within point bars of tributary channels in the lower intertidal zone of the Yeochari macrotidal flat along the western coast of Korea. The rhythmites record at least four months of nearly continuous tidal sedimentation and form inclined heterolithic stratification (IHS) associated with tributary-channel point bars migrating at rates of up to 5 m per month. The rhythmites display a clear hierarchy of tidal cyclicity, including diurnal inequality, neap– spring cycles, and perigean–apogean modulation. Their muddy facies contrasts sharply with the ripple cross-laminated and upper-flow-regime parallel-laminated sandy facies that characterize point-bar deposits of the adjacent main tidal channel. This facies contrast reflects differences in channel scale, hydrodynamic exposure, and sedimentation pattern between the main and tributary channels. Although the open-coast tidal flat is influenced by strong tidal currents and seasonally intensified wave activity, the relatively narrow and sheltered tributary channels provided favorable conditions for the development and preservation of muddy tidal rhythmites. Rhythmite formation was likely enhanced during summer periods of reduced wave activity and rainfall-induced channel migration, which promoted rapid point-bar accretion and preservation of tidal lamination. The coexistence of sand-dominated and mud-dominated point-bar deposits within a single meander-bend system highlights the complexity and compartmentalization of stratigraphic architecture in open-coast tidal flats. These findings demonstrate that muddy tidal rhythmites can form locally within lower intertidal tributary channels of wave-influenced tidal flats and suggest that caution is warranted when using tidal rhythmites as straightforward indicators of paleoelevation or protected depositional settings.

abstracts.title: From overwash-driven rollover to alongshore dispersal: Chenier evolution under changing boundary conditions in Gomso Bay, Korea
affiliations: School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
abstracts.text: Cheniers are coarse-grained ridges on muddy coastal plains that record interactions among sediment supply, waves, tides, storms, and sea-level change. Yet the controls on where cheniers form, how their migration mode changes landward, and how they respond to natural and anthropogenic boundary changes remain poorly constrained in macrotidal settings. We investigated an upper-intertidal chenier in Gomso Bay, west coast of Korea, using repeated topographic surveys, satellite imagery, and trench observations from 2009 to 2014, supplemented by longer-term geomorphic records, including DEMs of cheniers from 2022 and 2026. The chenier migrated landward at an average rate of approximately 1.7 m/month, with rates exceeding 7 m/month during storm periods. Migration was strongly controlled by storm-tide coincidence: storms during neap tides produced little displacement, whereas storms coinciding with spring or perigean spring high tides caused seaward-side erosion, crest lowering, overwash, and rapid landward accretion. Repeated crest buildup and overwash generated cyclic morphologic changes recorded internally by alternating washover-sheet and washover-delta deposits. As the chenier reached higher elevations, cross-shore overwash became less frequent and alongshore transport became increasingly important, producing ridge elongation and spit-like extension. Historical observations show that chenier formation was spatially selective: only two prominent cheniers developed in the study sector since the 1980s and later merged, whereas numerous adjacent swash bars failed to form persistent ridges. This suggests that chenier development requires an upper-intertidal accommodation zone where landward-moving coarse sediment can accumulate. Reclamation may reduce this space and promote sediment bypass. Recent accelerated migration is further interpreted as a storm-mediated response amplified by relative sea-level rise. These results show that chenier evolution depends on changing wave access, accommodation space, and sediment-transport pathways, with implications for shoreline management and for benthic habitats repeatedly affected by erosion, burial, and substrate change.

abstracts.title: Geological evolution and coastal geomorphology of St. Martin’s Island, Bangladesh
affiliations: Geological Survey of Bangladesh, Dhaka-1000, Bangladesh
abstracts.text:
St. Martin’s Island is located in the southeastern coastal region of Bangladesh, which is the only offshore coralline island and represents an important geological and geomorphological element of the Bengal Basin. The island occurs within the Folded Flank of the Bengal Foredeep and is associated with the Chittagong-Cox’s Bazar tectonic zone. This study investigates the geological framework, structural characteristics, stratigraphy, coastal geomorphology, sedimentary processes, coral development, and geo-environmental conditions of the island to reconstruct its geological and coastal evolution.

There are eighteen surficial geological and geomorphological units are identified formed through marine, marine-aeolian, and fluvio-marine processes. Structurally, the island is characterized by an asymmetrical, doubly plunging anticline with a NNW-SSE-oriented axis (Fig.1). The geological succession comprises Upper to Middle Miocene Tipam Formation, Pleistocene St. Martin’s Limestone, and Holocene unconsolidated deposits. The Tipam Formation consists mainly of shale, silty shale, fossiliferous sandstone, and conglomerate, whereas the St. Martin’s Limestone includes shelly limestone, coquina, and coralline limestone. Elevated coquina and limestone deposits provide evidence of relative uplift and past sea-level fluctuations.

The present coastal morphology comprises beaches, beach-dune complexes, lagoonal deposits, tidal plains, intertidal flats, active and abandoned tidal channels, depressions, tidal marshes, and mangrove areas. Beach sediments are predominantly medium to fine grained, well sorted, and quartz rich sand, with subordinate heavy minerals. Their distribution reflects the combined effects of wave action, tidal currents, longshore sediment transport, aeolian activity, and sediment deposition. The western coast is comparatively more embayed due to stronger tidal and wave erosion, whereas the eastern coast is relatively less embayed. The southern coast locally forms cliffed shorelines, while rocky intertidal platforms occur around much of the island. Coral colonies and limestone exposures occur particularly along the eastern, southern, and southwestern coasts. The geological record indicates repeated interactions among tectonic uplift, marine transgression and regression, coral growth, sea-level fluctuations, and coastal sedimentation, which collectively shaped the present island morphology. The water temperature around the island ranges from 27-29°C, dissolved oxygen from 3.5-5.5 mg/L, pH from 8.1-8.5, and average salinity is approximately 33‰. Sediment analyses revealed variable concentrations of trace and rare earth elements, including Cr, Zr, La, Ce, Pb, Th, and U.

So, the geological and geomorphological evolution of St. Martin’s Island reflects the combined influence of tectonic uplift, sea-level change, carbonate production, marine sedimentation, wave and tidal erosion, longshore transport, and aeolian processes. The integrated geological framework provides a basis for understanding the island’s coastal evolution and its present geo-environmental conditions.

abstracts.title: Atypical northward spit growth on a macrotidal beach against prevailing northwesterly winds – implications for sediment compartment and beach management
affiliations: Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Chonnam National University
abstracts.text: Spits are depositional coastal landforms that develop through longshore sediment transport, growing progressively in the direction of dominant flow when sediment supply is sufficient. Located on the macrotidal west coast of Korea (eastern Yellow Sea), Jeungdo island is characterized by tidal ranges exceeding 4 m and extensive tidal flats. The spit at Ujeon Beach on this island exhibits anomalous northward growth of approximately 750 m over the past 50 years, despite the southward-directed Korea Coastal Current (KCC) along the western Korean Peninsula and prevailing northwesterly winds. This study investigates the mechanisms responsible for this paradoxical northward spit development. Repeated cross-shore beach profiling surveys were conducted along 8 transects at approximately 3-month intervals from March 2025. Surface sediment samples were collected at 101 and 60 stations during winter and summer, respectively, with a grid extending from the beach to the subtidal zone. Acoustic Doppler velocimeters (ADV) were deployed simultaneously at the southern and central parts of the beach over three observation periods, and suspended sediment concentrations (SSC) were additionally measured in January 2026 to quantify sediment fluxes. The subtidal zone is composed of fine-grained muddy sediments, effectively excluding offshore sand supply to the beach. Grain size analysis revealed a fining trend in mean grain sizes from south to north, suggesting that beach and coastal dune sands at the southern serve as the primary source of spit sands. Under calm conditions, tidal forcing dominated with southward longshore flow, consistent with the macrotidal setting, whereas northward currents developed consistently during strong winds regardless of wind direction. During winter storms with maximum wind speeds of 12.3 m/s, the northward longshore current reached a mean velocity of 0.28 m/s and a maximum of 1.02 m/s. SSC at the northern station exceeded that at the southern station by more than threefold during storm events. Cumulative sediment flux records showed a clear reversal from southward to northward transport coinciding with strong wind conditions. These results suggest that another nearshore circulation cell forms during storm events, operating separately from the offshore southward KCC-driven flow. Sediment eroded from the southern beach is transported northward by this storm-driven circulation, thereby leading to the anomalous spit growth. These findings provide new insight into nearshore sediment transport dynamics in the Yellow Sea tidal coast, with implications for coastal management and shoreline change prediction.

abstracts.title: How do ebb-dominated elongate sand bars migrate upslope across multi-timescales? A case study from the upper mudflat of the semi-enclosed Hampyeong Bay, SW Korea
affiliations: Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Korea
abstracts.text: Numerous but narrow sandy beaches and spit bars are distributed along the macrotidal shores of the semi-enclosed Hampyeong Bay on the southwestern coast of Korea, which experiences a tidal range of 5.24 m. Unlike typical tidal flats, this area exhibits a shoreward-coarsening grain-size pattern, driven by the presence and migration of various sand bars in the upper intertidal zone situated above the mean sea level. A particularly notable feature is the ebb-oriented, elongate sand bars that have migrated upslope on the upper mudflat over the past 50 years; these downcurrent-oriented bars contrast with the long-term landward migration direction of the bar systems. In this context, this study aims to elucidate the migration processes and drivers responsible for the upslope migration of these ebb-oriented sand bars on a macrotidal mudflat. To achieve this, drone-based 3D mapping and VRS-GPS profiling were repeatedly conducted. Trenching across the sand bars was performed to identify migration directions through internal sedimentary structures, and historical aerial photographs were analyzed to assess long-term migration patterns. Additionally, ADVs measurements were conducted to quantify current velocities and directions. The sand bar is approximately 1.5 km in length and 20–60 m in width, extending from the mean sea level to above the mean high water springs, with its elevation gradually increasing from south to north. The southern profile is strongly asymmetrical, whereas the northern profile displays a relatively symmetrical form. Ebb-oriented bedforms, such as 2D and 3D dunes, are well-developed on the bar surface. Since the 1960s, the bar has migrated approximately 60 m landward, with the northern section showing a larger migration distance of about 90 m. The most significant migration occurred between 1986 and 2010, with migration distances increasing from south to north. Topographic surveys indicate seasonal cyclic patterns of migration: seaward migration from March to July 2025, followed by landward migration from July 2025 to January 2026, and a seaward return by March 2026. Interestingly, the ebb-oriented bar forms remained unchanged throughout these periods. The ADVs data indicated that during the summer season, tidal currents were consistently ebb-dominated. In contrast, during the winter season under normal conditions, tidal currents remained ebb-dominated; however, during strong wind events exceeding 8 m/s, wave action substantially attenuated the influence of tidal currents, resulting in a markedly weakened tidal signal. Trench sections reveal that the bar section near the mean sea level exhibits ebb-dominated cross-bedding with intervening parallel laminations formed by winter waves. In contrast, the section near the mean high water level shows flood-oriented structures at the base, overlain by parallel laminations and ebb-oriented cross-bedding. These findings suggest that while the seaward-oriented bar forms are generally maintained by tidal currents, the bars migrate upslope via wave action during strong wind events. However, wave-induced features, except for the parallel laminations, rarely survive within the sedimentary record of the sand bars. This study calls attention to the landward migration of ebb-dominated sand bars in a modern environment, which can often mislead the reconstruction of paleoflow directions in ancient tidal deposits.

abstracts.title: Sediment partitioning in an engineered macrotidal estuary: four decades of contrasting erosion and accretion in the Geum River estuary, west coast of Korea, reconstructed from archived bathymetric surveys (1982–2025)
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology
abstracts.text:
Human intervention in macrotidal estuaries reorganises sediment dynamics over decadal scales, yet the resulting morphodynamic trajectories are rarely quantified beyond a few survey epochs because historical bathymetric records survive only as non-georeferenced engineering drawings. Here we reconstruct four decades of seabed change in the Geum River estuary, west coast of Korea (mean spring tidal range ~6 m), a system successively modified by an estuarine barrage, coastal reclamation and navigational dredging.

Sounding annotations in 37 archived CAD survey charts (1982–2025) were converted into 3.2 × 10⁵ georeferenced depth points, interpolated onto a common 100 m grid through triangulated irregular networks with constrained data areas, and differenced (Wheaton et al., 2010). The limit of detection (LoD) was derived empirically from surveys repeated within the same year (σ = 0.42 m before 2013, 0.18 m thereafter), giving pairwise LoD values of 0.25–0.59 m (Brasington et al., 2000). Two fixed comparison windows, each restricted to the area surveyed in every epoch it contains, were analysed.

The outer approach channel (34.6 km²) lost 63.4 × 10⁶ m³ between 1989 and 2019 (mean −1.83 m), with deepening concentrated along the navigation axis. The inner estuary between the harbour and the barrage (19.2 km²) gained 45.9 × 10⁶ m³ between 1982 and 2019 (mean +2.39 m), accreting on the northern channel bank and on the tidal flats fronting the barrage while only the thalweg deepened; 59 % of this gain occurred between 1991 and 2002. Since 2013 both windows have been close to balance (+2.9 and +0.4 × 10⁶ m³).

The two windows indicate that the estuary has been partitioned rather than uniformly disturbed. The dredged seaward channel has remained in a persistently deepening state, whereas the reach landward of the harbour has acted as a long-term sink, accreting on the channel margins and on the flats fronting the barrage; metre-scale accumulation and comparable erosion thus coexist within a single estuary, the transition broadly coinciding with the reach occupied by harbour and barrage works. Read in this way, archived engineering surveys become a sedimentological record of how sustained human activity redistributes estuarine sediment rather than simply adding to or removing it. Extending the approach to other engineered estuaries, and combining it with concurrent tidal-current measurements, would allow the trapping and export terms of the sediment budget to be estimated directly and give dredging, disposal and coastal spatial planning an observational basis.

abstracts.title: Asymmetric barrier-island morphodynamics driven by regulated fluvial sediment supply and wave forcing
affiliations: School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
Division for Public Infrastructures Assessment, Korea Environment Institute, Sejong, Korea
Marine Natural Disaster Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Busan, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
abstracts.text: Barrier-island morphology reflects the combined effects of marine forcing, fluvial sediment supply, and antecedent topography, yet their interactions remain poorly understood in regulated estuaries. We investigated the recent morphodynamics of Doyodeung, a barrier island in the Nakdong River Estuary, Korea, using repeated digital elevation models and RTK-GPS transect profiles collected between 2022 and 2026, satellite imagery, and empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis. Doyodeung exhibits a distinct seasonal morphodynamic cycle, with winter retreat and overwash contrasting with summer stabilization and accretion. A strong typhoon in August 2022 generated extensive overwash and pronounced morphological changes, whereas subsequent years experienced relatively limited large-scale adjustment in the absence of comparable storm events. EOF analysis captures this seasonal and event-scale variability, particularly the recurring contrast between winter erosion/overwash and summer accretion. Repeated RTK-GPS profiles further show these seasonal changes as systematic cross-shore adjustments, including winter erosion, local lowering, and landward sediment redistribution associated with overwash, followed by summer accretion and partial profile recovery. Satellite imagery reveals a longer-term transition from a relatively narrow barrier of near-uniform width during the 2010s to an increasingly asymmetric morphology characterized by progressive widening of the western sector and narrowing of the eastern sector, with little net landward migration since the early 2020s. We attribute this asymmetry, at least in part, to spatially uneven sediment delivery associated with regulated Nakdong River Discharge. The western inlet receives substantially greater river discharge than the eastern inlet and is associated with a larger ebb-tidal delta and greater sediment accumulation. Subsequent wave- and tide-driven reworking likely redistributes part of this sediment toward western Doyodeung, promoting progressive barrier widening. This widening appears to have reduced overwash susceptibility along former western overwash pathways, while overwash has become increasingly concentrated within lower and narrower sectors farther east. These observations indicate that regulated fluvial sediment delivery can influence not only barrier geometry but also the spatial distribution of overwash vulnerability. Doyodeung therefore represents a barrier system in which variation in extreme-wave forcing and human-modified estuarine sediment delivery jointly regulate seasonal morphodynamics, alongshore sediment redistribution, barrier asymmetry, and the shifting spatial pattern of overwash.

abstracts.title: Impact of artificial disturbance and episodic weather events on the morphologic and sedimentologic changes in the sheltered macrotidal flats (Shinsi tidal flats, Korea)
affiliations: Environmental Assessment Group, Korea Environment Institute, Sejong 30147, Republic of Korea
Marine natural disaster research department, Korea institute of ocean science & technology, Busan, Republic of Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul 08826, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: The morphodynamics of tidal flats reflects the interaction of various factors such as tides, seasonal wave activity and precipitation. The influence of dike construction and meteorological event further complicate the geomorphology and sedimentary processes by disturbing physical processes on the tidal flats. Distinguishing the anthropogenic effects from the natural factors on the tidal flat morphodynamics is fundamental in estimating the adverse effects of man-made impacts. However, it remains a challenge due to latent constraints in quantifying spatiotemporal variability of the tidal flats. A six-yearlong field survey using unmanned aviation vehicle (UAV)-assisted photogrammetry, sedimentological and hydrodynamic data were seasonally conducted on the Shinsi tidal flats near the Saemangeum dike, west coast of Korea, to evaluate the relative significance between natural and anthropogenic influence on the morphologic changes of the tidal flats. The Shinsi tidal flats exhibited non-seasonal sedimentation patterns and experienced overall erosion due to changes in relative dominance between tide, wave, and rainfall-induced runoff discharge. Despite the protected location from offshore waves, the Saemangeum dike contributed to the sustained erosion by reflecting offshore waves toward the tidal flats during winter to spring. The local embankments complicated the spatiotemporal sedimentation trend by protecting tidal flats from offshore waves or accelerating erosion with shoaling waves. The rapid elongation of tidal channels and incipient rill channels during summer implies the effect of heavy rainfall, strengthened by the impermeable condition of catchment area and watershed morphology. During the study period, the tidal flats became steepened with net sediment export in the lower intertidal zone, suggesting a reduced sediment supply presumably caused by dike construction. The Shinsi tidal flats showcase how human disturbance dampens the seasonality in the tide-flat morphodynamics and sedimentation under a strongly seasonal wave climate.

abstracts.title: Chute cutoff and abandoned channel infilling create localized blue carbon hotspots in an unvegetated macrotidal flat
affiliations: School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea
abstracts.text: Unvegetated macrotidal flats are increasingly recognized as potential blue carbon reservoirs, but their capacity to retain organic carbon depends on both rapid burial and subsequent preservation. This study investigates how tidal channel morphodynamics control the formation of localized depositional settings with contrasting blue carbon potential in the semi-enclosed Dokgotri tidal flat, Garolim Bay, Korea. Multi-temporal UAV-derived digital elevation models (DEMs) from 2022 to 2026 were used to quantify channel mobility and erosion-deposition patterns and were integrated with precipitation and tidal-elevation data. Sediment cores were collected from contrasting geomorphic settings and analyzed for sedimentary facies and total organic carbon (TOC). Sequential DEMs of Difference (DoDs) were used to identify depositional intervals preserved at each core site. Low-tide rainfall events were associated with enhanced channel mobility, including lateral migration, chute cutoffs, stream piracy, and channel abandonment. Active channels experienced repeated erosion and deposition and therefore had low preservation potential. In contrast, chute cutoffs and flow diversion created localized accommodation space in which abandoned channels rapidly infilled with fine-grained sediment. Although these fills occupied only about 2-3% of the total mapped area, they accounted for 8.7% of total depositional volume, indicating efficient localized sediment trapping. Core results show that high short-term carbon accumulation is controlled not by TOC alone, but by the combined effects of sedimentary carbon density and rapid vertical accretion. However, this accumulation contributes to long-term carbon burial only where subsequent reworking is limited. Abandoned channel fills therefore represent localized blue carbon hotspots, whereas active channels and adjacent tidal flats have lower potential for persistent carbon burial because of continued reworking or limited accretion.

abstracts.title: The influence of tidal channel migration on intertidal dune evolution and surface sedimentary facies in macrotidal environments
affiliations: Marine Natural Disaster Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Sciences & Technology, Busan, Republic of Korea
Environmental Resources Assessment Division, Korea Environment Institute, Sejong, Republic of Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
Research Institute of Oceanography, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text:
Intertidal dunes are ubiquitous bedforms developed on sand bars and channel point bars in tidal flats. This study investigates the spatiotemporal morphological and sedimentological responses of intertidal dunes to meandering channel migration and discusses the major controls on dune evolution and point-bar sedimentary facies development. Long-term field observations were conducted from 2011 to 2018 at the macrotidal Yeochari tidal flat, northern Gyeonggi Bay, west coast of Korea.

The intertidal channel in the lower intertidal zone migrated laterally, particularly during summer, with sinuosity increasing from 1.01 to 1.14 and the width-to-depth ratio decreasing from 154.35 to 48.74 during the study period. Intertidal dune fields consisting mainly of simple dunes (0.3–0.7 m in height and 4–10 m in wavelength) developed on the channel point bar and exhibited contrasting evolutionary patterns between the upstream and downstream parts of the point bar. Until spring 2016, the dune fields expanded with point-bar accretion. After summer 2016, however, the dune field on the upstream part of the point bar, adjacent to a newly developed ebb barb, disappeared and was replaced by a rippled sand flat. In contrast, the dune field farther downstream from the ebb barb continued to expand, accompanied by the southward migration of compound dunes, suggesting a downstream shift in the bedload convergence zone. Between March 2016 and October 2017, sediments on the ebb barb became finer (0.31 to 1.68 phi), whereas those farther from the channel axis and adjacent to the subtidal channel became coarser (0.96 to 0.53 phi).

The disappearance of the upstream dune field likely reflects a reduced supply of coarse sand from the upstream channel, combined with enhanced seaward sediment export under ebb-dominant tidal asymmetry. These results demonstrate that channel migration reorganizes sediment pathways across a point bar, producing spatially contrasting dune evolution and sedimentary facies in macrotidal environments.

abstracts.title: Effects of particle size on the erosion and resuspension of glass particles
affiliations: Department of Oceanography, Chonnam National University, Republic of Korea
School of Marine Sciences, Sun Yat-Sen University and Southern Marine Science and Engineering Guangdong Laboratory (Zhuhai) Zhuhai, China
abstracts.text: Coastal environments are continuously exposed to anthropogenic debris such as plastics, metals, and glass. Compared to plastics and metals, glass is more prone to fragmentation into fine microparticles. These fine glass particles can reduce sediment permeability, potentially inducing hypoxia, and cause physical and biochemical damage to benthic organisms when ingested. In this study, laboratory erosion experiments were conducted to evaluate the size-dependent erosion behavior of glass particles in comparison with natural subtidal sediments. Three size-fractionated glass particle samples (6.18, 23.2, and 293 μm) were prepared alongside natural subtidal sediment samples (7.99 and 181 μm) collected from water depths of approximately 45 m and 105 m. Using a Gust Erosion Microcosm System (GEMS), seven stepwise-increasing shear stress levels ranging from 0.01 to 0.6 Pa (applied for 20 min per step) were imposed to determine critical erosion parameters, including critical shear stress (tce), erosion rate (E), and erosion coefficient (M) based on suspended sediment concentration. The results showed that the tce of fine glass particles (6.18 μm) was 0.18 Pa, lower than that of natural sediment of comparable size (7.99 μm, 0.28 Pa). Despite their similar grain sizes, the maximum eroded mass of the glass particles (753 mg l-1) substantially exceeded that of natural sediment (1.53 mg l-1), indicating that fine glass particles possess weak cohesion and are readily susceptible to resuspension and transport in marine environments. For coarse particles, the 293 μm glass exhibited a tce of 0.29 Pa compared to 0.03 Pa for the 181 μm natural sediment. However, once erosion was initiated, substantial erosion (up to 297 mg l-1) of the glass particles occurred relative to the natural sediment (up to 8 mg l-1), demonstrating that coarse glass particles are resistant to initial motion but prone to severe mass loss under higher flow conditions. Furthermore, the M decreased with increasing erosion depth only in the 293 μm glass, exhibiting a depth-dependent behavior comparable to that of the 7.99 μm natural sediment. In conclusion, unlike natural sediments that exhibit high resistance to erosion in fine grain sizes due to cohesion, glass particles showed an increase in erosion resistance with increasing grain size due to their weak cohesion.

abstracts.title: Long-term coastal dune dynamics following typhoon erosion along the west coast of Korea: Insights for nature-based solutions
affiliations: Department of Geography Education, Catholic Kwandong University, Gangneung-si, Gangwon-do, Republic of Korea
Department of Sustainable Environment, Graduate School, Catholic Kwandong University, Republic of Korea
Independent Researcher
abstracts.text:
As global sea levels rise due to climate change, coastal erosion has progressively intensified. In response, Nature-based Solutions (NbS) have gained increasing prominence, with growing emphasis on the establishment and management of coastal dunes along sandy coastlines (Jordan & Fröhle, 2022). Conventionally, afforestation using arboreal species such as black pine (Pinus thunbergii) or the implementation of gray infrastructure has been used to stabilize coastal dune zones against erosion (Kim et al., 2014). However, empirical studies evaluating the long-term impacts of these interventions on coastal dune resilience remain remarkably scarce. This study investigates dune recovery mechanisms by analyzing decade-long, high-resolution topographic and vegetation monitoring data from two contrasting coastal dunes on the West Coast of South Korea, which differ fundamentally in their management regimes and vegetation structures. The study sites experienced severe dune erosion triggered by Typhoon Kompasu in 2010 (Choi et al., 2012).

The results demonstrate that post-typhoon dune recovery is fundamentally governed by initial post-erosion foredune morphology and vegetation structure (Fig.1). The dune system featuring a wide herbaceous vegetation zone achieved self-recovery as native pioneer herbs (e.g., Leymus mollis, Carex kobomugi) trapped sand, promoted embryo dune development, and maintained uninterrupted beach–dune sediment connectivity. Conversely, the dune characterized by a narrow herbaceous zone and a dense black pine forest underwent persistent shoreline retreat following storm disturbance, eventually necessitating the installation of artificial gray infrastructure. However, these artificial structures compromised dynamic coastal flexibility and ecological integrity, ultimately diminishing geomorphic resilience.

Consequently, effective coastal dune management must shift away from rigid hard engineering and tree afforestation, prioritizing gentle foredune slopes and native herbaceous-to-bare-sand land cover. Sustaining dynamic beach–dune interactions, including aeolian sand transport, is essential to effective Nature-based Solutions (NbS) for coastal dunes.

abstracts.title: Different depositional systems under comparable highstand conditions: Holocene and MIS 5 mud successions on the southeastern continental shelf of Korea
affiliations: Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM)
Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM)
Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM)
abstracts.text:
The southeastern shelf of Korea, adjacent to the Korea Strait sill, is a current-dominated margin where highstand systems tracts are classically expected to be thin, condensed, or absent because of persistent sediment starvation. Core 19ESDP-104, however, preserves two chronologically distinct highstand mud successions: a Holocene mud (0–2 m; OSL 7.4–9.6 ka) and an MIS 5 mud (17–18.5 m; OSL 123 ± 7 and 136 ± 7 ka) (Yoon et al., 2023), offering a rare opportunity to test whether a shared interglacial conditions predicts a shared depositional system.

We combine sedimentological description, high-resolution XRF core-scanning geochemistry, and grain-size data to compare these two intervals directly. Despite occupying comparable highstand positions, the two mud facies differ fundamentally in structure and sediment-supply dynamics. The Holocene mud is structureless to weakly mottled and pervasively bioturbated, reflecting a quiescent, predominantly biohomogenized depositional regime with an oxic bottom-water signature marked by the retention or enrichment of reactive Fe phases under comparatively oxic conditions, without a proportional increase in pyrite-bound Fe.

The MIS 5 mud, in contrast, preserves wavy to parallel primary lamination formed under anoxic, current-influenced conditions, with decline in Ca/Ti and elevated Br/Al indicating enhanced organic matter and carbonate supply, and coupled K/Al–Rb/Sr variability together with pronounced sediment fining, suggesting episodically intensified chemical weathering and fine-sediment delivery, plausibly linked to a strengthened East Asian summer monsoon during the MIS 5 (particularly MIS 5e) highstand (An, 2000).

The anomalous preservation of this MIS 5 highstand mud, atypical for current-dominated shelf margins, reflects a combination of locally enhanced current-driven sediment supply (Shan et al., 2025), anoxia-suppressed bioturbation, and protective burial beneath coarser deposits during the subsequent MIS 4–2 sea-level fall. These results demonstrate that eustatic highstand position alone does not determine the continental shelf depositional system, and that local current pathways, sediment-source dynamics, and climate boundary conditions exert an equally important control.

abstracts.title: Millennial-scale climate variability and East Asian monsoon dynamics during MIS 3 revealed by eolian sedimentary records from Hainan Island, China
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Tropical Oceanography, South China Sea Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Guangzhou
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China
China
abstracts.text: The eolian sequence at Kenway Garden (KWS) on Hainan Island, located in the low-latitude land-sea transition zone, provides crucial insights into climatic variations during Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3) and their driving mechanisms. This underrepresented archive uniquely captures the coupling of high- and low-latitude processes, beyond what mid-to-high latitude terrestrial or marine records can provide. This study addresses a fundamental question: How did this sensitive region respond during MIS 3 to the apparent divergence between the intensified summer monsoon recorded in mid-to-high latitude terrestrial archives and the strengthened winter monsoon documented in low-latitude marine archives? The KWS section comprises a 6.6 m thick continuous sedimentary sequence. The KWS3 interval (target of this study), 110 cm thick, spans ca. 28.3–55.8 ka (MIS 3), based on a Bayesian age–depth model integrating three AMS-¹⁴C and fifteen OSL ages. High-resolution grain size and mineralogical analyses of the KWS3 interval reveal a composite response pattern. Three lithostratigraphic units (KWS3c, KWS3b, KWS3a) alternated: fine-grained segments (KWS3c and KWS3a) reflected warm, humid conditions associated with enhanced summer monsoons, while coarse-grained segments (KWS3b) indicated cold, dry periods dominated by winter monsoons. These millennial-scale oscillations precisely correlate with Greenland ice core and Hulu cave stalagmite records, fully capturing Heinrich events and Dansgaard-Oeschger cycles, highlighting strong mid-to-high latitude teleconnections. Orbital-scale Northern Hemisphere summer insolation drives summer monsoon intensity, while millennial-scale variability is amplified by sea-level changes exposing continental shelves—which supply sediments to winter monsoons. KWS records indicate that the East Asian monsoon exhibited a coupled winter-summer response pattern during MIS 3—rather than simple anti-phase— modulated by high-latitude ice volume, Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) perturbations, and rapid sea-level fluctuations. These findings challenge conventional monsoon paradigms, highlighting the critical role of low-latitude coastal regions in global climate dynamics research. Keywords: MIS3, climate fluctuation, maritime-terrestrial interface, Hainan Island, eolian sedimentary

abstracts.title: Reassessing continental sediment fluxes at a marginal sea gateway: Quantitative provenance of the Korea Strait Shelf Mud (KSSM)

abstracts.text: The Korea Strait Shelf Mud (KSSM) is a major fine-grained sedimentary deposit formed in a gateway region linking the northern East China Sea and the East/Japan Sea. The KSSM serves as an important depocenter for terrigenous materials supplied from surrounding continental sources and redistributed through the Korea Strait. However, the provenance of KSSM sediments remains controversial, with previous studies suggesting predominant contributions from either Chinese rivers or the Nakdong River (ND) in South Korea. This study re-evaluated the provenance of KSSM sediments based on the grain size, rare earth element (REE), and major element compositions of 114 surface sediment samples. To reduce grain-size effects, provenance analysis was restricted to fine-grained sediments with mean grain size (Mz) ≥ 5.6 ϕ (n = 91). The upper continental crust-normalized light-to-heavy REE ratio LREEN/HREEN of these fine-grained sediments was inconsistent with a single ND source and instead fell within the compositional ranges of Changjiang (CJ) and Huanghe (HH) river sediments. The Fe2O3/Al2O3 ratios exhibited intermediate values that could not be explained by any single endmember composition. A three-endmember mass-balance mixing model integrating the LREEN/HREEN and Fe2O3/Al2O3 ratios yielded average contributions of 50% from CJ, 36% from HH, and 14% from ND. These results indicate that fine-grained KSSM sediments are predominantly derived from Chinese river sources, with a relatively minor contribution from ND. The two geochemical proxies provided complementary constraints on the provenance system: REE fractionation primarily constrained the relative contribution of ND versus combined Chinese river sources, whereas Fe2O3/Al2O3 ratio constrained CJ versus the combined HH and ND components. Unlike previous approaches that treated Chinese river-derived sediments as a single source or applied two-endmember models, this study separately resolved the CJ and HH contributions and revealed a substantial HH component. The results highlight the Korea Strait as a key mixing and redistribution gateway for fine-grained sediments from multiple continental sources and provide new constraints on sediment transport and material connectivity between the northern East China Sea and Eest/Japan Sea.

abstracts.title: Operational sequential digestion of sedimentary biogenic silica and its application to BSi–TOC distributions in the Korea Strait shelf mud (KSSM)
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, Korea
Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, Korea
Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, Korea
Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources, Daejeon, Korea
Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, Korea
Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, Korea
abstracts.text:
Biogenic silica (BSi) in marine sediments reflects biological production and export, potentially influenced by detrital dilution, dissolution, and post-depositional preservation. BSi quantification in mud-rich shelf sediments is complicated by lithogenic silica (LSi) co-extraction, surface coatings, and BSi pools with contrasting alkaline extractabilities. We evaluated these biases using <32 μm fractions of the northern East China Sea surface sediments. Samples underwent sequential digestion with 0.2 M Na2CO3, 0.5 M NaOH, and 4.0 M NaOH after diluted H2O2 and HCl pretreatments. In unpretreated samples, the two NaOH-extractable fractions were 2.5 and 5.8 times the initial Na2CO3-extractable fraction, indicating that single-step weak-alkaline extraction primarily captures rapidly extractable Si. BSi fractions of 0.1N pretreated samples were comparable to those in unpretreated samples, without detectable XRD peak pattern changes. Conversely, 1.0 N HCl, especially with heating, markedly increased the apparent Na2CO3-extractable fraction and attenuated chlorite-related peaks, indicating enhanced alkaline extractability of acid-sensitive LSi. These results support a conservative protocol combining diluted H2O2, room-temperature 0.1 N HCl, and weak-to-harsh sequential alkaline digestion.

We applied this framework to five box cores along estuary-proximal to estuary-distal settings in the southern distal sector of the Korea Strait Shelf Mud (KSSM). We compared Na2CO3-extractable labile BSi (lBSi) with total organic carbon (TOC), organic-matter source proxies, grain size, and excess 210Pb-derived sedimentation rates. Sediments were uniformly fine-grained (94.0 ± 1.6% mud; 6.8 ± 0.2 F), while sedimentation rates decreased from 4.4 to 0.9 mm yr-1 with distance from the Nakdong River estuary. Conversely, lBSi increased by approximately 46%, from 2.8 ± 0.2 to 4.1 ± 0.7 wt%, and was inversely related to sedimentation rate (r = −0.94, p = 0.017). A dry-bulk-density-normalized apparent lBSi accumulation index decreased distally, consistent with detrital dilution as a first-order influence on the lBSi content gradient. Bulk TOC averaged 1.3 ± 0.1 wt% without a clear trend, whereas δ13Corg and TOC/TN molar ratios varied systematically. TOC/TN-based marine TOC (TOCmarine) decreased distally, revealing organic-matter source variation masked by bulk TOC. Thus, higher distal lBSi/TOCmarine ratios do not necessarily indicate greater diatom dominance, but likely reflect contrasting effects of dilution, organic-matter supply, degradation, and retention. Operational BSi fractionation provides a constrained basis for interpreting BSi–organic carbon coupling, although the fractions are not source-specific and post-depositional processes were not independently evaluated. Future mineralogical and biogeochemical analyses of diagenesis are therefore needed to test the inferred relationships.

abstracts.title: Preliminary Geochemical analysis result of Sediment Cores from the South Sea
affiliations: Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources
abstracts.text: Glacial-interglacial cycles during the Quaternary were accompanied by substantial sea-level fluctuations, leading to changes in depositional environments, sediment provenance, and local biogeochemical cycle. In order to understand environmental changes resulting from sea level fluctuation, various geological data should be integrated; however, previous studies only mainly focused on sedimentological aspects of these environmental changes. In this study, organic carbon contents and stable isotope compositions were analyzed to further investigate variations in provenance and depositional environments. Two sediment cores, 24SSDP-101C and 24SSDP-102B, recovered from South Sea near the Jeju Island were analyzed. In core 101C, carbon and nitrogen contents appeared to be largely controlled by grain-size variations, and δ15N values also covaried with grain size. In addition, δ13C values became more negative below approximately 80 m depth. These observations suggest that changes in depositional conditions associated with sea-level fluctuations may have influenced the organic geochemical signatures in this interval. In core 102B, grain-size effects were less pronounced than in core 101C. The 55 m interval is tentatively interpreted as the Pliocene-Pleistocene boundary, although no clear geochemical change is apparent across this inferred boundary. Future work will combine precise age constraints with major and trace element analyses to investigate depositional environments and sediment provenance changes during glacial-interglacial cycles and across the Pliocene-Pleistocene transition.

abstracts.title: Preliminary multiproxy analysis of sediment provenance and depositional processes in the East China Sea coastal mud area
affiliations: Institute of Earth Sciences, National Taiwan Ocean University, Taiwan *Presenting author
abstracts.text: The East China Sea inner shelf receives substantial terrestrial sediment from surrounding river systems and preserves high-resolution records of source-to-sink processes and hydroclimatic variability. This study presents preliminary multiproxy analyses of sediment cores W12-2, ST1, and ST3 from the Min–Zhe Coastal Mud Area. The three cores provide age-constrained sedimentary records spanning approximately the last 1.2–1.4 kyr. Age control is based on accelerator mass spectrometry radiocarbon dating, and chronological uncertainties are evaluated using COPRA. We integrate minimally destructive visible–near-infrared (VIS–NIR; 350–2500 nm) reflectance spectroscopy with handheld X-ray fluorescence (XRF) geochemistry and particle-size analysis. Spectrally inferred variations in illite, kaolinite, smectite, and epidote are examined together with XRF-derived elemental ratios, particularly Zr/Rb, and particle-size distributions. Clay-mineral assemblages are evaluated as potential indicators of sediment provenance and transport pathways, while particle-size data are used to assess hydrodynamic sorting and the extent to which variations in Zr/Rb may be influenced by sediment texture. Down-core profiles from each core are evaluated individually and then compared to examine mineralogical, geochemical, and sedimentological patterns across the study area. Relationships among spectral mineral indicators, elemental ratios, and particle-size parameters are explored in terms of sediment provenance, terrigenous input, hydrodynamic sorting, and local depositional processes. The resulting profiles provide a basis for identifying intervals that warrant further chronological and mineralogical investigation. This preliminary assessment evaluates the applicability of a rapid multiproxy approach to marine sediment cores in the East China Sea coastal mud system. Applying the same analytical approach to additional cores across the East China Sea could provide a broader spatial basis for evaluating sediment provenance, transport pathways, depositional processes, and hydroclimatic variability.

abstracts.title: Reconstructing late Holocene tropical cyclone activity from grain-size records in the Hupo Basin, East Sea (Sea of Japan)
affiliations: Chungnam National University, Department of Earth, Environmental & Space Sciences, Daejeon 34134, Korea, Republic of Korea
Chungnam National University, Department of Marine Environmental Science, Daejeon 34134, Korea, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text:
Previous Late Holocene paleotempestological studies have focused mainly on southern Japan and the South China Sea, leaving tropical cyclone (TC) activity at the northern margin of the major storm tracks poorly constrained. This study reconstructs paleo-TC activity using grain-size fractions sensitive to extreme events in the Hupo Basin, located on the eastern continental margin of Korea. Limited coarse-sediment supply and generally low-energy depositional conditions make the basin favorable for preserving storm-reworked layers.

The mean grain-size records of two piston cores, P1 and P3, collected at water depths of 160 and 200 m, respectively, show overall fining-upward trends since 8 ka, punctuated by episodic increases in mean grain size to approximately 20 μm, particularly after 3 ka. For P1, the proportion of the coarsest grain-size fraction (>100 μm), which corresponds to sandy sediment derived from the Hupo Bank, was selected as the TC proxy. For P3, the fine-grained background mode was removed, and the modal grain size of residual fraction (40–80 μm) was used as the proxy. Extreme-event layers were identified using a statistical threshold defined as the background mean plus two standard deviations.

Several statistically defined event layers were identified in both cores, whereas others occurred in only one. Events detected in both cores may represent relatively intense TCs with broader spatial impacts, while events confined to one core may reflect weaker or more localized TCs. The resulting TC event chronology is currently being compared with existing Late Holocene TC records from southern Japan and the South China Sea to evaluate regional TC activities. These records provide a new basis for reconstructing Late Holocene TC variability at the northern margin of western North Pacific storm tracks and for evaluating its relationship with regional and global climate forcing.

abstracts.title: Mid-Holocene environmental change and its impact on human settlement in the eastern Jianghuai region of coastal China: Mineralogical and geochemical evidence
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Estuarine and Coastal Research, East China Normal University, Shanghai 200241, China
State Key Laboratory of Estuarine and Coastal Research, East China Normal University, Shanghai 200241, China
State Key Laboratory of Estuarine and Coastal Research, East China Normal University, Shanghai 200241, China
abstracts.text: Holocene environmental changes in the eastern Jianghuai region of coastal China were driven by climate variability, sea-level fluctuations, and the evolution of the palaeo-Huai River Delta, making the region a key nexus for Neolithic cultural interactions between societies in the lower basins of Yangtze and Yellow rivers. Unravelling how environmental dynamics shaped human activities here provides valuable insights into past human– environment interactions and their broader implications. In this study, we conducted detailed mineralogical and geochemical analyses of mid-Holocene sediments from a profile situated in the palaeo-Huai River Delta, to reconstruct past environmental changes. Elevated Sr/Ba ratios, together with authigenic gypsum and pyrite, indicate brackish water intrusion between 7400 and 6700 cal. yr before present (BP), consistent with the event of accelerated global sea-level rise. A subsequent long-term drying trend from 6700 to 3000 cal. yr BP is reflected in declining Clay/Quartz ratios and TOC contents, as well as enriching δ13Corg, while the recovery in Clay/Quartz ratios indicates climatic amelioration during 6000–4400 cal. yr BP. These environmental shifts shaped human settlement patterns and cultural development, with population growth closely linked to warmer and more humid conditions. In addition, landscape features including the palaeo-Huai River Delta and chenier ridges likely further promoted human settlements. Our findings highlight the combined influence of climate and landscape on demographic evolution in the coastal lowlands.

abstracts.title: Pyrites formed by seawater–rock interaction in altered oceanic crust drive both oceanic sulfur cycling and atmospheric oxygen levels
affiliations: South China Sea Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
abstracts.text: The oceanic sulfur cycle is intimately coupled with the cycling of organic matter and oxygen at Earth's surface. However, the dominant pathway of Phanerozoic sulfur cycle—whether via pyrite or evaporite burial—and its impact on atmospheric oxygen remain debated. This uncertainty stems largely from divergent estimates of pyrite burial flux (Fpy = 2.40 vs. 31.5 × 10¹¹ mol yr⁻¹), which arise from the exclusion of seawater–rock interaction (SRI)-derived pyrites in sedimentary inventories and the underestimation of evaporite burial flux. To address these gaps, we performed in-situ sulfur isotopic analysis on SRI-derived pyrites from Hole U1502B in the South China Sea and calculated their burial flux (FSRI-PY) using a newly developed equation that avoids reliance on evaporite flux data. The studied pyrites show positive δ³⁴S values (1.93–5.96‰), elevated contents of fluid-mobile elements (Pb: 5810–8870 ppm; Mo: 8260–10240 ppm), and high concentrations of temperature-sensitive elements (Co up to 1761 ppm; Cu up to 798 ppm), indicative of a hydrothermal origin. Based on our isotopic data combined with compiled global data for SRI-derived pyrites, FSRI-PY is estimated at 7.23–14.9 × 10¹¹ mol yr⁻¹—a range comparable to the sedimentary pyrite burial flux—underscoring the significant role of SRI in the Phanerozoic sulfur cycle. When both sedimentary and SRI-derived pyrites are considered, the total Fpy (1.40–2.91 × 10¹² mol yr⁻¹) and pyrite burial fraction (ƒpy = 47–97%) indicate that pyrite burial was the dominant pathway, actively modulating atmospheric oxygen levels. Furthermore, the abrupt increases in both Fpy and atmospheric O₂ during the Phanerozoic are potentially linked to supercontinent assembly.

abstracts.title: Sedimentological characteristics of flood- and earthquake-related turbidites in slope basin sediment off Shikoku, Japan (site C9037, Exp. 913): Insights from visual core description and grain size analysis
affiliations: Kuroshio Science Program, Graduate School of Integrated Arts and Sciences, Kochi University
Marine Core Research Institute, Kochi University
Department of Agriculture and Marine Science, Graduate School of Integrated Arts and Sciences, Kochi University
abstracts.text:
Deep-sea turbidite successions serve as continuous archives of past extreme events, including earthquakes and floods. Accurate discrimination of triggers of individual turbidites is fundamental not only for reconstructing paleoseismic and paleoclimatic histories, but also for assessing geohazard risks and recurrence intervals (Goldfinger, 2011).

The Nankai Trough, located along a convergent plate margin, is a well-known seismogenic zone where turbidite successions have been widely utilized to investigate past megathrust earthquake records (e.g., Ashi et al., 2014). However, a recent investigation at Site C9037 by D/V Chikyu in an intraslope basin on the landward slope of the Nankai Trough off Kochi (Japan) suggested frequent occurrences of plant-fragment-bearing turbidites (Ikehara, unpublished data). In this region, where terrestrial sediment input is considered significant, the turbidite succession likely includes not only earthquake-triggered deposits but also flood-induced turbidites (Vandekerkhove et al., 2020; Zavala et al., 2012). Accurately distinguishing turbidites based on their triggering mechanisms not only improves the fidelity of event histories but also enhances our understanding of event magnitude and frequency. This study aims to characterize and classify turbidites based on sedimentological characteristics and evaluate potential indicators for distinguishing flood- and earthquake-related deposits at site C9037.

The sediment core analyzed in this study, C9037A, was obtained offshore Shikoku at a water depth of approximately 3000 m. We conducted visual core description (VCD) and laser diffraction grain-size analysis on over 400 discrete samples, focusing on sedimentary structures, terrestrial plant fragments, and vertical grain-size variations. Grain-size parameters were calculated following Folk and Ward (1957).

Three preliminary turbidite types were identified. Type 1 shows the presence of plant-fragment lamination and fluctuating grain-size patterns (i.e., repetitive coarsening- and fining-upward patterns) in both VCD and grain-size profiles. The grain-size patterns represent waxing-waning of prolonged sediment supply, which, combined with the presence of plant-fragment lamination, indicates flood-derived turbidite (Mulder et al., 2001; Zavala et al., 2012) It is predominantly composed of silt and has a bed thickness 45 cm. Type 2 contains terrestrial plant-fragment laminae but shows normal grading suggesting reworked ssediment from shallower environment, potentially associated with earthquake-triggered remobilization. It is predominantly composed of fine sand, with an average and maximum bed thickness of 47.5 and of 93 cm. Type 3 shows normal grading, lacks terrestrial plant-fragment laminae, and is interpreted as an earthquake-related turbidite. It is predominantly composed of fine sand, with an average bed thickness of 27.9 cm and a maximum thickness of 159 cm.

The classification remains preliminary because the boundaries between turbiditic mud and hemipelagic sediments have not yet been constrained. Microstructural analysis and age dating will be conducted to refine depositional boundaries, establish event chronology, and correlate the deposits with known earthquake and flood events.

abstracts.title: The transport process of turbidity currents and their impacts on deep-sea environments
affiliations: Frontiers Science Center for Deep Ocean Multispheres and Earth System, and Key Laboratory of Marine Chemistry Theory and Technology, Ministry of Education and College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, 266100, China
abstracts.text:
Turbidity currents transport massive volumes of terrigenous sediments into the deep ocean, exerting a pivotal role in deep-sea material transport and circulation, geomorphic evolution, and environmental change. Recent studies have identified a high-density bottom-driven turbidity current system composed of a near-bed high-concentration layer and an overlying turbulent entrainment cloud layer. Complex dynamic material exchange takes place across the seabed, high-concentration layer, and cloud layer, giving rise to vertical heterogeneities in flow velocity and flow regime. In addition, latest in-situ observations have documented pulsed sediment transport with alternating high- and low-concentration intervals within turbidity currents — a feature that departs from the classical fully turbulent model for conventional turbidity currents.

This study employs an integrated methodology combining physical model experiments, numerical simulation, and theoretical calculation. It aims to elucidate the correlations between the intrinsic properties (concentration, grain size) and behavioral characteristics (flow velocity, flow regime) of different turbidity current types, quantify the governing factors controlling the velocity and flow regime of high-density bottom-driven turbidity currents, decipher the spatiotemporal evolution pattern of concentration–grain size–velocity during turbidity current propagation, and explore the deep-sea environmental impacts induced by sediment-laden turbidity transport.

The research outcomes will not only enrich and refine the theoretical framework of dynamic sedimentary processes for turbidity currents and lay a solid foundation for an in-depth understanding of turbidity current–seabed interaction mechanisms, but also provide dynamic theoretical support for turbidity current hazard mitigation and deep-sea resource exploitation.

abstracts.title: Zooplankton fecal pellet characteristics and their potential implications for sinking behavior and carbon export in the southern South China Sea
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
abstracts.text: Zooplankton fecal pellets play an important role component in the biological pump process as rapidly sinking particles that drive the vertical transport of particulate organic carbon from the surface area to the deep ocean depth. However, the contribution of different fecal pellet morphotypes to carbon export and their seasonal variability remain poorly resolved. In this study, we report the morphology characterisation of zooplankton fecal pellets from 13 samplings of a sediment trap that was deployed at 500 m depth on the TJ-SB mooring for the period of July 2024 to July 2025 in the southern South China Sea. We performed light microscopy analysis to classify their morphological characteristics and estimate fecal pellet numerical and fecal pellet carbon fluxes. This preliminary study demonstrated that fecal pellets can visually classified into ellipsoidal, cylindrical, and spherical types. Zooplankton fecal pellet fluxes displayed a distinct seasonal pattern, with an average numerical flux of 3.89 x 104 pellets m-2 d-1 and an average carbon flux 0.47 mg C m-2 d-1. Among the three morphotypes, ellipsoidal pellets showed the highest average numerical and carbon fluxes (3.14 x 104 pellets m-2 d-1 and 0.40 mg C m-2 d-1 respectively), followed by spherical pellets (0.66 x 104 pellets m-2 d-1 and 0.03 mg C m-2 d-1 respectively), whereas cylindrical pellets had the lowest numerical fluxes (0.09 x 104 pellets m-2 d-1), with an average carbon fluxes (0.04 mg C m-2 d-1). Both numerical and carbon fluxes showed a pronounced seasonal peak from January to March 2025, with the highest fluxes in January and lowest in June 2025. We consider may be associated with the influence of the Asian winter monsoon. These findings highlight the importance of upper-ocean processes on fecal pellet dynamics and vertical carbon transport in the mesopelagic zone.

abstracts.title: Frequent and large-volume event deposition in the bottom of Challenger Deep: Insights from OC 14C-ages and elemental anomalies
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
Department of Biology, HADAL & Nordcee, University of Southern Denmark, 5230 Odense M, Denmark
abstracts.text:
Hadal trenches act as depocenters for sediments and organic carbon, yet the frequency and geochemical fingerprints of event deposition in the deepest trench environments remain poorly constrained because robust chronological markers are scarce. Here, we investigate a ~4.6-m-long sediment core recovered from the bottom of Challenger Deep, Mariana Trench, using bulk organic-carbon (OC) 14C ages together with total organic carbon and nitrogen contents (TOC and TN), stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes, grain-size data, and major- and trace-element compositions.

The core displays a highly irregular OC 14C age-depth relationship, with multiple anomalously old ages and pronounced age reversals rather than a simple down-core increase. These radiocarbon anomalies recur at several depth intervals and broadly coincide with marked enrichments of transition metals, particularly Ni and Co, while U shows synchronous depletion. Ni, Co, and several other redox-sensitive or particle-reactive elements exhibit repeated, quasi-cyclic down-core excursions, defining a clear rhythmic geochemical structure throughout much of the core. In contrast, TOC, TN, δ13CTOC, and δ15NTN show comparatively modest variations and do not alone account for the magnitude of the radiocarbon and trace-metal anomalies.

We interpret these coupled signals as repeated inputs of remobilized, pre-aged sediments and organic matter to Challenger Deep by event-driven sediment transport, most plausibly gravity flows sourced from the trench slopes and potentially triggered by tectonic disturbance. The correspondence between anomalously old OC event deposits where conventional sedimentological or chronological markers are limited. The rhythmic recurrence of these anomalies further suggests that event deposition has been frequent and has contributed substantially to sediment accumulation at the trench bottom.

To our knowledge, this study provides the first combined use of bulk OC 14C anomalies and transition-metal signatures to identify recurrent event deposition in the Mariana Trench, offering a new approach for reconstructing sediment remobilization and carbon transfer in hadal environments.

abstracts.title: Submarine landslide distribution and slope instability in the Ulleung Basin, East Sea
affiliations: Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources (KIGAM), Daejeon, Republic of Korea
Institute of Marine Sciences (ICM), Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), Barcelona, Spain
abstracts.text:
The Ulleung Basin in the East Sea is characterized by widespread submarine landslides along its southern and western slopes. This study investigates their distribution and geological characteristics using high-resolution bathymetric data and extensive seismic profiles, including airgun, sparker, and sub-bottom profiler data.

A GIS-based database was constructed to systematically map submarine landslide features. A total of 82 scarps and 74 associated deposits were identified. Major headscarps are mainly distributed along relatively steep slopes, and overlapping deposits indicate repeated episodes of slope failure and sediment remobilization. In particular, two large scar-like features, approximately 25 km and 13 km long, were identified on the upper western slope at water depths of about 130–560 m, suggesting potentially unstable slope sectors.

Comparison of seismic stratigraphy with sediment physical properties shows a marked decrease in shear strength near a stratigraphic boundary corresponding to the basal surface of previous landslides. This weak layer may have acted as a preferential glide plane. These results indicate that submarine landslides in the Ulleung Basin are closely related to slope morphology, stratigraphic architecture, and variations in sediment mechanical properties, providing important information for assessing submarine geohazards in the East Sea. Keywords: submarine landslide; Ulleung Basin; East Sea; seismic profile; slope instability; marine geohazard

abstracts.title: Transport of particulate organic carbon along the eastern margin of the Tsushima Warm Current
affiliations: The University of Tokyo
Kitami Institute of Technology.
Fukui Prefectural University.
Japan Fisheries Research and Education Agency
abstracts.text:
The vertical transport of sinking particles from the surface to the interior of the ocean is an important factor that controls the transport of materials on relatively short time scales, ranging from a few days to several tens of days. The authors have been studying the flux of sinking particles (mass of particles that settle by gravity per unit time and area) in the Japan Sea over 20 years, but there are few observations in the Tsushima Warm Current (TWC) regions. In this study, we summarize the seasonal variations of particulate organic carbon (POC) flux based on the time-series sediment trap experiment at the eastern margin of the TWC (Sta. FATO: (38 °43’ N, 137° 48’ E, trap depth 890m). In addition, by incorporating geochemical indicators that characterize particles in this region, we discuss the processes of POC supply to and transport within the basin.

The total mass flux measured in this study ranged from 198 to 564 mg m-2 d-1, and two maximums were observed in the winter (January to February) and spring (March to April). About 60% of the sinking particles in winter are composed of aluminosilicates. Biogenic silicates and organic matter particles dominate in spring, and the high opal flux and the corresponding increase in organic matter particle flux are presumed to be the factors for the increase in the total mass flux during this period.

POC flux ranged from 19 to 67 mg m⁻² d⁻¹. The fluxes exceeding 60 mg m⁻² d⁻¹ were observed between March and April, a level higher than that found in other areas. Flux levels remained in the range of 20–30 mg m⁻² d⁻¹ during other periods, including winter. The δ¹³C values of POC ranged from approximately -25.0 to -20.5‰, showing higher values in spring and lower values in summer. The δ¹³C value was -23.3‰, indicating that marine-derived POC was the primary component even during winter, when biological production was low.

Based on the above and the analysis results of various geochemical indicators, it was concluded that while the supply of POC via gravitational settling starting in spring was the primary process at FATO, marine-derived POC was also horizontally transported from the shelf region to the interior of the ocean basin during winter, a period of low biological production.

abstracts.title: Organic carbon stocks of the surficial sediments in the territorial waters of Korea
affiliations: Marine Research Institute, Pusan National University, Korea
Division of Glacial and Earth Sciences, Korea Polar Research Institute, Korea
Department of Oceanography, Pusan National University, Korea
BK21 School of Earth Environmental Systems, Pusan National University, Korea
Department of Marine Science & Convergence Engineering, Hanyang University, Korea
abstracts.text: Shallow marine environments, including the continental shelf, are important in the global carbon cycle in which organic carbon is transported from land, produced within the ocean, and buried in sediments. The territorial waters of Korea (Republic of Korea) encompass predominantly shallow continental shelves. This study examined the organic carbon distribution of surficial sediments in the territorial waters of Korea to approximate the carbon stocks in the surficial sediments of the seafloor at a national scale. For the estimation, the reported data (mean grain size (MGS), total organic carbon (TOC) content, and dry bulk density) around the Korean Peninsula were documented and organized to evaluate the potential for carbon sequestration in the territorial waters of Korea. The distribution of the MGS and the TOC content in surficial sediments varied regionally according to the depositional processes, but they exhibited the typical characteristics of marine sediments whose TOC content increased as the MGS decreased. Among the four zones (A, B, C, and D) in the territorial waters of Korea, the estimated total carbon stock was highest (2.27 × 106 Mg C) in zone A and lowest (1.04 × 106 Mg C) in zone C, despite zone C having the highest carbon stock per unit area (1.64 Mg C/ha). However, for a precise assessment of long-term carbon stock and sequestration rates, more comprehensive and robust data along with representative sedimentation rates and the vertical profiles of the TOC content are essential at a national scale.

abstracts.title: Interannual variability in particulate organic carbon and its isotopic characteristics in the Western Indian Ocean
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, 49111, South Korea
abstracts.text: Particulate organic carbon (POC), produced by marine primary producers through the uptake of atmospheric CO₂, is a key component of the biological carbon pump and is closely associated with the vertical transport of carbon in the ocean. The Seychelles–Chagos Thermocline Ridge (SCTR), located in the tropical western Indian Ocean, is characterized by open-ocean upwelling and relatively high biological productivity, making it an important region for understanding Indian Ocean biogeochemistry and carbon cycling. However, studies on the distribution and characteristics of POC in this region remain limited. To investigate spatial patterns and temporal changes in POC and its sources, we measured POC concentrations and stable carbon isotopic compositions (δ¹³C) along 65°E from 5°N to 20°S during 2023-2025. POC concentrations varied from 12.8 to 57.8 μg L⁻¹ and were generally higher within the SCTR, while δ¹³C values ranged from –20.0‰ to –25.0‰. During 2023, strong upwelling in the SCTR core was associated with enriched δ¹³C values and lower C/N ratios, indicating enhanced biological productivity and a greater contribution of fresh marine organic matter. In contrast, the weaker upwelling years (2024 and 2025) were characterized by lighter δ¹³C signatures and slightly higher C/N ratios, suggesting reduced productivity and a greater contribution of degraded organic matter. These results indicate that variations in upwelling intensity control source and characteristics of POC in the tropical Western Indian Ocean.

abstracts.title: Turbidity current overspills dominated the transfer of terrestrial particulate organic carbon in deep-canyon levees
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
