Frontier Science Center for Deep Ocean Multisphere and Earth System, Key Laboratory of Marine Chemistry and Technology, Ministry of Education, Ocean University of China, Qingdao 266100, China
abstracts.text: The transport and sequestration of particulate organic carbon (POC) in the deep ocean strongly modulate atmospheric CO₂ concentrations. Previous studies have highlighted turbidity currents as the primary mechanism delivering sediments and POC to the deep sea via submarine canyons. Nevertheless, the sources, transport pathways, and controlling mechanisms of POC delivery and deposition under turbidity and non-turbidity current conditions in canyon systems remain poorly constrained. Here, we report one year of time-series observations (6 May 2017–27 April 2018) of POC fluxes, POC composition, current velocity and hydrography from a mooring array deployed at 2120 m on the flat western levee of the middle Gaoping Canyon, deep South China Sea. Our results reveal that mass fluxes of total suspended sediment and POC at 2090 m are 1–3 orders of magnitude greater than those at 500 m, demonstrating lateral transport of sediment-bound POC below 500 m. The Δ¹⁴C and δ¹³C values of POC at both depths generally fall along mixing lines between marine and Gaoping River POC, showing that lateral transport of riverine POC contributing to the lower Δ¹⁴C relative to marine POC in the sunlit zone. Concurrent elevated fluxes of suspended sediment and POC at 2090 m and increased sediment concentrations, paired with weak currents (< 30 cm/s) at 1667–2091 m during summer and early autumn, were ascribed to the occurrence of three turbidity current overspills triggered by heavy rainfall and typhoons. These events transported large volumes of terrestrial POC and sediment from the Gaoping River to our study site. In other seasons, sediment and POC fluxes at 2090 m were ~5–30 times lower than summer/early-autumn values but still ~5–200 times higher than fluxes at 500 m. Minor rises in suspended sediment concentration under low current speeds suggest down-canyon transport of intermediate and bottom nepheloid layers onto adjacent levees. At 500 m, high POC fluxes in late autumn and early winter and low fluxes at other times are controlled by primary production and mesoscale eddies. Overall, turbidity current overspills account for ~76% of the annual sinking POC flux, emphasizing their dominant role in transferring terrestrial and coastal POC to the deep ocean through submarine canyons.

abstracts.title: Trends in elemental variations in sediments off Shodoshima Island, Harima Nada, Seto Inland Sea, Japan: a possible recovery from heavy metal contamination in recent decades
affiliations: Kuroshio Science Program, Kochi University
Marine Core Research Institute, Kochi University
Seto Inland Sea Regional Research Center, Kagawa University
Japan Coast Guard Academy
abstracts.text:
The Seto Inland Sea, Japan's largest semi-enclosed sea, received heavy metal loading during the post-war economic miracle, and the element supply has generally declined following the discharge regulations implemented after the late 1970s as documented in sediment records (Hoshika et al., 1991). In Harima Nada, the eastern part of the Seto Inland Sea, however, the spatial pattern of heavy metal concentrations in sediments is variable, with some locations showing an increase in the 1990s (Komai et al., 1998). This study examines the characteristics of heavy metal variation using three sediment cores (up to 40 cm long) collected off Shodoshima Island, in the western part of Harima Nada.

Sediment characterization was conducted using visual core description, X-ray CT imaging, and X-ray fluorescence core scanning (ITRAX). We also applied osmium (Os)-staining combined with scanning electron microscopy–energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) mapping (Arai et al., 2019) to visualize the spatial association between organic matter and heavy metals.

The sediments are primarily composed of olive-gray silt with diatom and a brown oxidized layer at the top. ITRAX data indicate that the relative concentrations of heavy metals (e.g., Cu, Zn, Cr, and Ni) peak in the deeper part of the cores and show an overall decreasing trend toward the surface. SEM-EDS elemental mapping reveals that Cr, Cu, Ni, and Zn consistently coincide with osmium-stained organic particles. Additionally, iron- and manganese-enriched micrometer-scale microparticles are distinctive in the oxidized surface layer.

The overall decrease in heavy metals captured by ITRAX represents a decline in anthropogenic heavy metal loading. The SEM-EDS results provide a mechanistic complement to the bulk ITRAX trend: the consistent co-localization of heavy metals with Os-stained organic particles demonstrates that sedimentary organic matter acts as a host for these metals, rather than the metals being incorporated into the mineral matrix. The presence of Fe- and Mn-enriched microparticles has, to our knowledge, previously been reported only from open-ocean, deep-sea oxic sediments (Uramoto et al., 2019). Such observations of discrete microparticles in shallow sediments are noteworthy and likely represent a redox-driven authigenic phase forming under the currently oxic near-surface conditions. Taken together, the tightening of regulations on anthropogenic discharge appears to be driving environmental recovery in the Seto Inland Sea, as reflected in the ITRAX data. The occurrence of Fe-Mn microparticles in the surface sediments may further reflect this recovery, or instead records a redox process operating independently of the contamination trend.

abstracts.title: Evolution of current circulation in the Malacca Strait since the middle Holocene
affiliations: Key Laboratory of Marine Geology and Metallogeny, First Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural Resources, Qingdao 266061, China
Laboratory for Marine Geology, Qingdao Marine Science and Technology Center, Qingdao 266237, China
Faculty of Science and Technology, National University of Malaysia, Selangor 43600, Malaysia
abstracts.text: The current circulation of the Malacca Strait (MS) plays a critical role in the transportation of materials and energy within the Indo-Pacific region. However, the evolution of the currents, especially the northwestward current, has not been comprehensively understood. Based on a high-resolution chronology, grain size and Sr-Nd isotope analysis of the Core M41collected from the MS, it investigates the currents circulation evolution in the MS since 7.4 ka, explores the northwestward currents evolution during NE monsoon periods and SW monsoon period, respectively. The results reveal that the sediments of core M41 have been consistently supplied by the Sunda Shelf and the eastern shelf of the Andaman Sea since 7.4 ka, while the current circulation in the strait show asynchronous evolution. Since 7.4 ka, the SW monsoon currents display a progressively weakening trend, which is consistent with the variations in the ISM. However, the northwestward currents during the SW monsoon period have been strengthening overall since 7.4 ka. Because of the enhanced EASM and weakened ISM intensify sea level gradients between the two ends of the MS, which further strengthens the northwestward currents. In contrast, the evolution of northwestward currents during the NE monsoon period have displayed three stages since 7.4 ka, as following: a weak current during 7.4-5.5 ka, substantially strengthened current during 5.5-3.5 ka, and notably weakening current since 3.5 ka. The enhanced EAWM winds facilitated a higher sea level gradient and strengthened the northwestward currents during 5.5-3.5 ka. Whereas the notably weakened currents during 6.5- 5.5 ka and 3.5-1.7 ka might have been due to El Niño events, which could have reduced sea levels in the southeast of the MS and thus lowered water pressure gradients. Our results demonstrate that the sea level gradient plays a primary role in regulating the strength of the northwestward currents, whereas the monsoon climate and ENSO activities are indirectly related to the current intensity by influencing the sea levels at the two ends of the strait.

abstracts.title: Taxonomic control improves the Mg–temperature proxy in crustose coralline algae: Evidence from the Korean mid-latitude coast
affiliations: Library of Marine Samples, Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Geoje 53201, Korea
Sea Power Reinforcement⋅Security Research Department, Marine Domain Research Division Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Busan 49111, Korea
abstracts.text: Crustose coralline algae (CCA) are important geochemical archives of past seawater conditions because their high-magnesium (Mg) calcite skeletons can preserve temperature-dependent variations in Mg incorporation. However, skeletal Mg signals may also vary among taxa, complicating their application as quantitative temperature proxies. This study evaluates the Mg–temperature relationship in CCA from the mid-latitude Korean coast, with particular emphasis on growth-season temperature and taxonomic effects. Twenty-two CCA specimens were collected from ten coastal sites extending from the northern East Sea to Jeju Island and analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). Long-term sea surface temperature (SST) records from nearby monitoring stations were used to compare Mg-derived temperatures with annual and growth-season (May–October) SSTs. All specimens were predominantly composed of Mg-calcite. Relative to pure calcite, the (104) diffraction peak shifted by 0.29–0.46° toward higher 2θ values, indicating increased substitution of Ca²⁺ by Mg²⁺ within the calcite lattice. The (104) peak position was strongly correlated with lattice parameters and unit-cell volume, demonstrating that skeletal Mg incorporation is systematically reflected in the crystal structure. XRD-derived Mg contents ranged from 8.9 to 14.5 mol%, corresponding to estimated temperatures of 18.4–24.8°C. These Mg-derived temperatures were generally closer to growth-season SSTs than to annual mean SSTs, suggesting that skeletal Mg preferentially records thermal conditions during periods of active growth and calcification. Although Mg contents broadly reflected regional thermal conditions, considerable variability remained when multiple CCA taxa were considered together. In contrast, restricting the comparison to the genus Lithophyllum reduced compositional variability and produced a more pronounced relationship between skeletal Mg content and latitude. Comparison with previously published data further indicates that taxonomic mixing may account for part of the scatter observed in global CCA Mg datasets. These results demonstrate that CCA Mg-calcite provides a useful archive of growth-season thermal conditions and highlight taxonomic identity as an important control on Mg-based temperature reconstructions. Taxonomically constrained calibration may therefore improve the reliability of CCA Mg–temperature proxies, particularly in mid-latitude coastal environments where calibration data remain limited.

abstracts.title: Precession-driven upper-ocean heat redistribution in the tropical Indian Ocean: Evidence from thermocline variability in the western Indian Ocean
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, Shanghai, 200092
State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, Shanghai, 200092
Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University, Taipei, 106
abstracts.text: The tropical Indian Ocean is a key component of the Indo-Pacific climate system, yet whether orbital forcing produced basin-scale upper-ocean heat redistribution comparable to that in the Pacific, and what controlled western Indian Ocean subsurface heat accumulation, remain poorly understood. Here, we present paired Mg/Ca and stable-isotope records of the surface-dwelling Globigerinoides ruber and thermocline-dwelling thermocline water temperature (TWT) over the past ~500 kyr. Both SST and TWT exhibit pronounced precession-paced variability, warming synchronously during precession minima, whereas upper-ocean stratification and export productivity peak during precession maxima. Comparison with eastern equatorial Indian Ocean records reveals an orbitally paced IOD-like mean state characterized by coherent east-west thermocline reorganization. In contrast, the western Indian Ocean leads the western Pacific warm pool in subsurface temperature variability, arguing against direct Indonesian Throughflow heat transport as the primary heat source. Instead, the close correspondence between TWT and the meridional SST gradient across the southern Indian Ocean is consistent with enhanced subtropical ventilation supplying additional heat to the tropical thermocline during precession minima. Our results demonstrate that precessional forcing reorganized upper-ocean heat storage across the tropical Indian Ocean and highlight southern subtropical ventilation as a potentially important contributor to western Indian Ocean thermocline heat accumulation, with implications for long-term Indo-Pacific ocean-atmosphere interactions.

abstracts.title: A diatom-dominated plankton community under prolonged Pliocene warming in the South China Sea
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China
abstracts.text: The Pliocene warmth provides a valuable, yet under-exploited, testbed for ecological forecasts under sustained high-CO2 conditions. Here we integrate lipid biomarkers, bulk and compound-specific nitrogen isotope, and export productivity (EP) proxies from sediments in the South China Sea to reconstruct plankton community dynamics from 5.3 to 1.8 Ma. Our alkenone-derived sea surface temperature (SST) and sea water δ18O records indicate elevated SSTs and salinities, particularly during the 4.5–3.8 Ma warm climax. During this Pliocene warm climax, prokaryotic primary producers (including diazotrophs) declined, likely due to weakened stratification and the alleviation of nitrate limitation in surface waters. Concurrently, steroid biomarkers suggest diatoms-dominated phytoplankton community and zooplankton grazers were suppressed, resulting in peak EP. Post-3.6 Ma cooling reversed this configuration: grazer abundance increased, diatoms declined, and EP weakened. In contrast, Holocene sediment data exhibit even higher EP, but under conditions of abundant grazers and reduced diatoms— representing an inverted food-web structure compared to the Pliocene. We propose that Pliocene warming switched the biological pump from grazer mediated “packaging” mode to a “grazer-bypass” mode, enhancing direct diatom aggregate sinking. Therefore, Earth-system models that ignore temperature-sensitive grazer mortality and nutrient dynamics will misrepresent future carbon flux projections for the western tropical Pacific.

abstracts.title: Integrated chronostratigraphy of Magellan seamount KC-7 in the western Pacific Ocean for late Neogene paleoceanographic studies
affiliations: Department of Oceanography, Pusan National University, Korea
Ocean Resources Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Korea
Estuary Research Center, Shimane University, Japan
Graduate School of Human and Environmental Studies, Kyoto University, Japan
Institute of Geosciences, Christian-Albrechts-University, of Kiel, Germany
Faculty of Dinosaur Paleontology, Fukui Prefectural University, Japan
abstracts.text: Integrated chronostratigraphy of core WPGPC230202, which was taken from the summit of seamount KC-7 located in the Magellan Seamounts of the western Pacific Ocean, was established using planktonic foraminifera biostratigraphy, calcareous nannofossil biostratigraphy, and magnetostratigraphy. Planktonic foraminiferal biostratigraphy clearly shows 17 biohorizons from Pliocene Zones PL1 to Pleistocene Subzone PT1b. Calcareous nannofossils yielded 12 biostratigraphic index taxa, revealing 15 biohorizons from Plio-Pleistocene Zones CNPL2 to CNPL11. In addition, 6 paleomagnetic reversal events were recorded, which correlate continuously to the geomagnetic polarity time scale, ranging from the Brunhes (C1n) to the upper Gilbert (C3n.1n). As a result, the integrated chronostratigraphy provided an age of ~4.3 Ma, which can be applied to regional stratigraphic correlations and to better understand Late Neogene paleoceanographic changes in the study area. The age-depth model of core WPGPC230202 shows the distinct decrease of sedimentation rates from ~0.19 to ~0.07 cm/kyr at ~2.4 Ma, which corresponds to the Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (NHG). Core WPGPC230202 primarily consists of biogenic carbonate ooze (foraminifera and nannofossils) and due to the shallow water depth at the core site limiting the effect of dissolution, the sedimentation rate is mainly dependent on the degree of paleoproductivity. The NHG is characterized by the gradual global cooling and change in the deep-water circulation patterns. During the NHG, surface water cooling and reduced formation of the North Pacific Deep Water may degrade carbonate productivity in the subtropical ocean including the study area, similar to what is recorded in the subarctic North Pacific.

abstracts.title: Orbital-scale variability of coarse fraction in the western tropical Pacific sediment during the Plio-Pleistocene periods
affiliations: Kanazawa University, Kakuma-machi, Kanazawa, Japan
National Museum of Nature and Science, Amakubo 4-1-1, Tsukuba, Japan
abstracts.text:
Coarse fraction of deep-sea sediments (>63 micron/bulk sediment) has been used as a proxy for bottom water carbonate chemistry as it closely relates to fragmentation of foraminiferal shell, caused by carbonate dissolution. Since the coarse fraction data can be obtained during the washing process for extraction of foraminifera from the sediment, it is easy and simple but important data for paleoenvironmental studies. The coarse fraction is also influenced by primary productivity in surface ocean. When the primary productivity was enhanced, fine fraction was elevated due to higher concentration of calcareous nannofossil in the sediment. Therefore, it is important to understand which factors primarily influence the coarse fraction.

Previous studies showed that the variability of coarse fraction in the tropical Pacific sediments had ~100 kyr eccentricity cycle, suggesting the orbital control on the global carbon cycle. However, little is known about its relationship to orbital parameters with higher frequencies, i.e., precession and obliquity. To better understand the influences of the orbital parameters on the global carbon cycle and its relationship with the major climatic transition, e.g., the Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (NHG) or Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT), high-resolution records of the coarse fraction spanning longer time intervals are required.

Here, we have constructed 4 Myr-long oxygen isotope stratigraphy for International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U1488 and investigated high-resolution coarse fraction with an approximately 2-kyr spacing. Both benthic and planktic foraminiferal d18O show clear glacial-interglacial cycles for the last 4 Myr, providing a robust age constraint. The coarse fraction varies between 6 and 45 wt%, and the result shows clear periodicities that related to Milankovitch cycles, including 19 and 23 kyr precession, 41 kyr obliquity, and 100 and 400 kyr eccentricity. Their relative strength and phase relationship with orbital parameters changed across the mid-Pleistocene transition (MPT). Obliquity signal is more dominate before MPT, whereas precession and eccentricity are more dominate after MPT. The relationship between coarse fraction and precession parameter changed from negative to positive correlation across the MPT. These results imply that the mechanism of orbital control over the global carbon cycle varies with the Earth’s climatic condition.

abstracts.title: Surface-subsurface temperature contrasts over the past 400 kyr in the northern Okinawa Trough
affiliations: National Korea Maritime and Ocean University, Busan, South Korea
National Korea Maritime and Ocean University, Busan, South Korea
Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan
abstracts.text:
Changes in surface–subsurface temperature contrasts in the northern Okinawa Trough over the late Pleistocene were examined using multiple temperature proxies. A TEX86H record was generated from sediment samples from IODP Site U1429 (31°37.04′N, 128°59.85′E; 732 m water depth). The record spans approximately 400 kyr with an average temporal spacing of 2 kyr. TEX86H values were converted to temperatures using the calibration of Kim et al. (2012) for depth-integrated temperatures over 0–200 m. These temperatures were compared with existing alkenone- and planktonic foraminiferal Mg/Ca-derived temperature records from the same core (Lee et al., 2021). The alkenone and Mg/Ca records are interpreted to mainly reflect annual mean and summer surface temperatures, respectively, whereas TEX86H is interpreted to reflect subsurface temperatures. TEX86H-derived temperatures ranged from approximately 13 to 20°C, showed glacial–interglacial variability, and were consistently lower than both surface-temperature records at the compared ages.

All three temperature records showed broad glacial–interglacial changes, but their behavior within glacial stages differed. During MIS 8 and 6, cooling in the TEX86H and alkenone records was more pronounced than in the Mg/Ca record. In MIS 6, the TEX86H and alkenone records both reached low temperatures near 160 ka. The relationships among the records also differed across glacial terminations. Around Termination IV, both surface-temperature records rose while TEX86H-derived temperatures initially decreased. Around Termination II, alkenone-derived temperatures rose while TEX86H-derived temperatures remained low; the initial rise in Mg/Ca-derived temperatures was smaller than that in the alkenone record. In both cases, the alkenone–TEX86H difference widened and then narrowed as TEX86H-derived temperatures rose. During Termination I, all three records warmed without a comparable widening of that difference. Under this interpretation, these differences suggest that surface– subsurface temperature contrasts changed through time. The different seasonal sensitivities of the alkenone and Mg/Ca records must also be considered when interpreting those contrasts.

abstracts.title: Seawater osmium isotope variations in the Okinawa Trough: Implications for climate-driven weathering over the past 20 kyr
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Busan 49111, Republic of Korea
Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Qingdao 266071, China
abstracts.text: We reconstruct a high-resolution record of seawater osmium (Os) isotope compositions (187Os/188Os) in the Okinawa Trough (OT) over the past 20 kyr. The record closely tracks climate variability on both glacial– interglacial and millennial timescales, with lower 187Os/188Os ratios during cold periods and higher ratios during warm intervals. This pattern likely reflects changes in the global seawater Os isotope composition associated with variations in continental weathering and riverine runoff, with regional oceanographic influences superimposed on this global signal. Notably, the deglacial increase in 187Os/188Os was likely driven by enhanced continental Os flux and increased release of radiogenic Os during intensified weathering, especially during the Bølling–Allerød warming. Excursions toward less radiogenic values during the last glacial period and other cold events (i.e., the Younger Dryas and the 4.2-ka cooling) are attributed to increased inflow of relatively unradiogenic North Pacific Intermediate Water, together with reduced continental Os inputs under colder climatic conditions. In the Holocene, additional inputs of unradiogenic hydrothermal Os associated with enhanced Kuroshio Current inflow may have further lowered seawater 187Os/188Os ratios in the OT. Our study highlights the utility of Os isotopes as an independent tracer for reconstructing changes in continental weathering and ocean circulation associated with climate variability, particularly in dynamic marginal basins such as the OT. Further details are provided in Lim et al. (2026) [Palaeogeogr. Palaeoclimtol. Palaeoecol., 689, 113676]. The samples for this study were provided by the Library of Marine Samples, Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology (KIOST).

abstracts.title: Library of marine samples (LIMS): A national hub for marine sample curation and collaboratory research
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Busan 49111, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Marine samples collected through research cruises require substantial time, cost, and effort, and therefore represent valuable scientific assets for future research. The Library of Marine Samples (LIMS), established by the Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST), provides infrastructure for the long-term preservation, curation, and shared use of marine samples collected from Korean and global oceans. LIMS currently manages more than 100,000 geological, biological, and environmental samples, including approximately 25,000 geological samples such as sediment cores, surface sediments, and rocks. These archived samples are available for scientific research and have contributed to a wide range of findings in marine geology, geochemistry, paleoenvironmental reconstruction, and related fields. LIMS also provides analytical facilities, including an XRF core scanner, optical microscopes, and a field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM), together with an integrated sample management and search system. Through the preservation and reuse of valuable marine materials, LIMS supports collaborative research and provides opportunities to generate new scientific outcomes from archived samples. With its extensive geological collections and research infrastructure, LIMS serves as an important platform for marine geological research and collaboration in Korea.

abstracts.title: Wettability-controlled capillary back-pressure stabilizes supercritical CO₂ during injection into depleted gas reservoir
affiliations: Interdisciplinary Program in Earth Environmental System Science & Engineering
Department of Geophysics, Kangwon National University, Chunchoen, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Depleted gas reservoirs are attractive targets for CO2 storage, yet injecting supercritical CO2 into their low-pressure environment triggers Joule-Thomson cooling as the pressure drops, which can convert CO2 back to a less dense gas that reduces storage capacity and can drive phase change and hydrate formation during early injection. The role of pore-surface wettability in this coupled thermal and phase behavior remains poorly quantified. This study resolves the pore-scale mechanism through three-dimensional thermal multiphase lattice Boltzmann simulations of CO2 injection through a nozzle and perforation tunnel into a water-coated sandstone matrix, spanning eighteen contact angles and five initial pressures approaching the critical pressure. The repulsive interaction between CO2 and the water-coated silica surface raises the pressure within the tunnel and prevents CO2 from wetting the pore throats, hence snap-off isolates CO2 into ganglia within the wider pore bodies (Wang et al., 2024). This trapping increases the capillary pressure, secures CO2 against leakage, and enhances the potential for residual trapping. The mechanism holds regardless of the initial pressure, but as the initial pressure approaches the critical pressure, the amplified thermodynamic sensitivity recovers the local pressure and temperature and sustains the supercritical state. The perforation tunnel and the pore space respond to wettability in opposite directions, and near the nozzle the Joule-Thomson cooling forms a solid phase that shrinks as the initial pressure rises and the surface becomes more water-wet, which lowers the risk of hydrate and solid formation. Our results establish wettability and near-critical initial pressure as coupled controls and provide quantitative thresholds for designing CO2 injection into depleted gas reservoirs.

abstracts.title: Effects of grain-size evolution on mantle exhumation during continental rifting: Implications for thermodynamic H2 generation potential
affiliations: Interdisciplinary Program in Earth Environmental System Science & Engineering, Kangwon National University, Republic of Korea
Department of Geophysics, Kangwon National University, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text:
Serpentinization of ultramafic mantle rocks, a major abiotic mechanism of natural H2 generation, requires water supply and suitable pressure–temperature (P–T) conditions. During continental rifting, deep faults can provide pathways for water circulation, while mantle exhumation changes the amount of mantle entering P–T conditions favorable for serpentinization. The balance between grain-size reduction and growth modifies mantle rheology through grain-size-dependent creep, affecting strain localization and mantle exhumation. Previous studies have separately examined the effects of grain-size evolution on lithospheric weakening and mantle exhumation, and serpentinization-related H2 generation at magma-poor rifted margins. The effects of grain-size-dependent changes in mantle exhumation on P–T conditions favorable for serpentinization and thermodynamic H2 generation potential remain insufficiently quantified.

We evaluate the effects of the balance between grain-size reduction and growth on mantle exhumation, P–T conditions favorable for serpentinization, and thermodynamic H2 generation potential during continental rifting. We simulate continental rifting using a two-dimensional ASPECT–FastScape thermomechanical model with grain-size evolution and a composite rheology combining dislocation creep and grain-size-dependent diffusion creep. Lagrangian particles track mantle exhumation and P–T paths. Equilibrium H2 yield derived from the P–T paths quantifies thermodynamic H2 generation potential. Reduction-dominated models developed smaller grain sizes, lower effective viscosities, and stronger strain localization in the mantle beneath the rift center. Grain-size-dependent rheological weakening enhanced mantle exhumation, and exhumed mantle followed lower-pressure P–T paths. More exhumed mantle reached P–T conditions favorable for serpentinization in reduction-dominated models, where thermodynamic H2 generation potential was higher. Grain-size-dependent rheological evolution can therefore modify thermodynamic H2 generation potential during continental rifting through changes in mantle exhumation.

abstracts.title: Molecular fingerprinting traces anthropogenic and natural sources of organic compounds in core sediments from Arctic fjord
affiliations: Chungnam National University
Korea Polar Research Institute
abstracts.text: Arctic fjords are sensitive depositional environments where naturally derived organic matter and anthropogenic contaminants accumulate together, enabling reconstruction of temporal changes in organic matter sources and environmental conditions from sedimentary records. In this study, core sediments (0–30 cm) were collected in 2023 aboard the R/V Helmer Hanssen from the inner (HH23-1053) and outer (HH23-1045) basin sites of Kongsfjorden, southeastern Svalbard. We determined the concentrations and compositions of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and n-alkanes, together with compound-specific carbon and hydrogen stable isotope ratios (δ13C and δ2H) of individual n-alkanes. Samples were processed by accelerated solvent extraction, silica gel column chromatography, and high-performance thin-layer chromatography purification, and compound-specific isotope ratios were analyzed using GC-IRMS. In both sites, sedimentary PAHs were dominated by phenanthrene. In the inner site, this composition indicates strong inputs from fossil fuel combustion and mining activities, whereas in the outer site, the dominance of phenanthrene is likely attributable to the geomorphological characteristics of the fjord, which govern particle transport and deposition. The concentrations and relative compositions of PAHs and n-alkanes varied with depth in both cores, reflecting differences in source contributions and depositional history between the two sites. Compound-specific isotope analysis revealed that isotopic variations of the n-alkanes were more pronounced for hydrogen than for carbon. In the inner site, the hydrogen isotopic ratios shifted toward more enriched values in recent decades, suggesting a recent change in organic matter sources or environmental processes. In the outer site, by contrast, this enrichment was observed only for the long-chain homologues (C25–C30), indicating that the two sites recorded distinct source or environmental signals. Down-core, isotopic variability was substantially greater below approximately 10 cm depth, a pattern that was particularly evident in the odd-numbered n-alkanes. Toward the sediment surface, both cores displayed a consistent trend of isotopic enrichment. Overall, these results demonstrate that compound-specific carbon and hydrogen isotopic indicators, combined with PAH and n-alkane distributions, provide a powerful means of resolving the sources of sedimentary organic compounds and their temporal changes in Arctic fjord environments. The contrasting isotopic signals between the inner and outer sites highlight the influence of both local anthropogenic inputs and fjord geomorphology on organic matter accumulation in Kongsfjorden.

abstracts.title: Evaluating GDGT-based temperature proxies in Kongsfjorden Trough, Svalbard
affiliations: Division of Glacier and Earth Sciences, Korea Polar Research Institute, 26 Songdomirae-ro, Yeonsu-gu, Incheon 21990, Republic of Korea
Department of Earth Surface and Seabed, Geological Survey of Norway, 7491 Trondheim, Norway
iC3: Centre for ice, Cryosphere, Carbon and Climate, Department of Geosciences, UiT The Arctic University of Norway, 9037 Tromsø Norway
Department of Environmental Science for Sustainability, IE University, Cardenal Zúñiga 12, 40003 Segovia, Spain
Marine AI Convergence Center, Inha University, Incheon 22212, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Reconstructing past ocean temperatures is essential for understanding Arctic climate evolution, particularly in regions experiencing rapid environmental change beyond modern analogs. Hydroxylated isoprenoidal glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraether (OH-isoGDGT)-based proxies have emerged as promising tools for high-latitude temperature reconstructions, yet their environmental controls remain insufficiently constrained. Here, we evaluate multiple OH-isoGDGT-based temperature indices (%OH, OHC, RI-OH, RI-OH′, and TEX!" using sediment core CAGE19-3-KH17-GPC01 from the Kongsfjorden Trough, western Svalbard, spanning the last 14 kyr. By comparing proxy records with sedimentological and environmental datasets, we assess the influence of temperature, terrestrial organic matter input, and hydrographic variability on OH-isoGDGT distributions. Temperature is identified as the dominant control, although secondary influences from terrestrial input and water-column structure are evident for several of the evaluated indices. Among the examined proxies, RI-OH′ most consistently tracks depth-integrated temperatures (0–200 m), exhibiting lower sensitivity to non-thermal influences than the other indices. The RI-OH′ record indicates progressive upper-water-column warming during the last deglaciation and early Holocene, reaching a maximum between 8 and 7 cal kyr BP, followed by a long-term cooling trend through the middle and late Holocene. These results demonstrate the potential of RI-OH′ as a robust 0-200 m temperature proxy in Arctic glacimarine settings and provide new constraints on the application of OH-isoGDGT-based proxies in high-latitude fjord–shelf systems.

abstracts.title: Sedimentary organic carbon dynamics off Kongsfjord, Svalbard over the past 14,000 years
affiliations: Division of Glacier and Earth Sciences, Korea Polar Research Institute, 26 Songdomirae-ro, Yeonsu-gu, Incheon 21990, Republic of Korea
Department of Earth Surface and Seabed, Geological Survey of Norway, 7491 Trondheim, Norway
iC3: Centre for ice, Cryosphere, Carbon and Climate, Department of Geosciences, UiT The Arctic University of Norway, 9037 Tromsø Norway
Marine AI Convergence Center, Inha University, Incheon 22212, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Arctic fjords are dynamic interfaces where glacial retreat, terrestrial erosion, sediment discharge, sea-ice variability, and oceanographic exchange regulate the sources and burial of organic carbon (OC). Here, we reconstruct changes in OC sources and depositional processes in Kongsfjorden, Svalbard, over the last approximately 14,000 years. Bulk geochemical parameters were integrated with terrestrial biomarkers, including n-alkanes and lignin phenols, to distinguish petrogenic, soil-derived, plant-derived, and marine OC sources. A Monte Carlo mixing approach was applied to quantify the relative contributions of these sources through time. The sedimentary record indicates a pronounced reorganization of the fjord carbon system following deglaciation. Sediments deposited during the Last Deglaciation and Early Holocene contain a relatively large contribution of petrogenic OC, likely reflecting enhanced bedrock erosion and sediment transport associated with glacier retreat and catchment destabilization. During the Middle and Late Holocene, the OC assemblage shifted toward a greater marine contribution, suggesting enhanced marine productivity and/or more efficient delivery of marine-derived material to the depositional environment. Although terrestrial OC inputs generally declined from the Middle to Late Holocene, OC accumulation remained sensitive to changes in sea-ice conditions. These fluctuations likely reflect the interplay between Atlantic Water inflow and glacier-derived freshwater discharge, which modulated sea-ice cover, marine productivity, and the relative export of terrestrial and marine carbon. Our results demonstrate that the Kongsfjorden sedimentary archive records not only postglacial changes in terrestrial carbon supply but also an increasing sensitivity of OC dynamics to oceanographic forcing. This study highlights the value of Arctic fjords for tracing climate-driven shifts in carbon cycling and provides a long-term perspective on OC dynamics in the context of ongoing Atlantification.

abstracts.title: Spatial variability of pollen composition across Svalbard fjord surface sediments
affiliations: Department of Earth System Sciences, Yonsei University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
Division of Glacier and Earth Sciences, Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Pollen analysis has been established for more than a century and has been widely applied to both terrestrial and marine sediments. However, fjord sediments which are strongly influenced by glacio-marine interactions have rarely been utilized for pollen-based studies. Here, we investigate modern pollen assemblages to evaluate the potential of fjord sediments as archives of pollen records. Svalbard, a climatically sensitive Arctic region where tidewater glaciers are rapidly retreating, is characterized by numerous fjords with high sedimentation rates, providing favorable conditions for preserving environmental signals. We analyzed fjord surface samples at 39 different locations across Spitsbergen and Nordaustlandet using marine palynological protocols. Modern pollen assemblages show considerable spatial variability among fjords, although they underestimate the regional floristic diversity. Long-distance transported taxa such as Pinus, Betula (Tree Birch), and Alnus can be distinguished from local floristic signals represented by Betula nana (Dwarf Birch), Dryas, and Poaceae. Long-distance transport of extra-regional pollen can be examined in relation to atmospheric circulation, ocean currents, and biotic vectors and their effective pathways to Svalbard. By directly comparing pollen records from different fjords experiencing varying rates of tidal-glacier retreat, this study provides a unique dataset to test the space-for-time substitution method in Svalbard, specifically regarding the recent acceleration of vegetation expansion.

abstracts.title: Dinoflagellate cyst assemblages in surface sediments from Arctic Svalbard fjords: Biogeographic distribution and ecological preferences
affiliations: Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon, Republic of Korea .
Department of Earth System Sciences, Yonsei University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Svalbard represents a key transition zone between the northward-flowing Atlantic Water and the ice-covered Arctic Ocean. Ongoing Arctic warming and increasing influence of Atlantic waters are expected to profoundly alter the physicochemical and biological characteristics of fjords and coastal waters around Svalbard (Hegseth and Tverberg, 2023; Polyakov et al., 2023), with consequential effects on the composition and dynamics of aquatic plankton communities (Šupraha et al., 2022; Assmy et al., 2023; Roy et al., 2025). Dinoflagellate cysts, the fossilized resting stages of aquatic microplankton preserved in sediments, are important bioindicators of past and present aquatic conditions, such as temperature, salinity, sea-ice cover and primary productivity (Marret et al., 2020). Their high abundance in polar and subpolar regions, together with their sensitivity to environmental factors, make them powerful proxies for reconstructing past environmental changes in Svalbard and for predicting future aquatic ecosystem responses under continued climate warming. In this study, we examine the surface distribution of recent dinoflagellate cyst assemblages from 30 surface sediment samples collected across inshore and offshore Svalbard, in order to investigate their biogeographic patterns and associated environmental controls. We find distinct distribution patterns of dominant taxa (e.g., I. minutum, P. dalei, and P. glacialis) that exhibit a clear latitudinal gradient, reflecting their environmental preferences along the north–south transect. Our study also highlights the sensitivity of dinoflagellate cyst assemblages to fine-scale environmental gradients and support their application as reliable proxies for reconstructing present and past changes in Svalbard fjord systems.

abstracts.title: Late Quaternary glacial history and depositional evolution in the central Joides Trough, Ross Sea, Antarctica
affiliations: Korea Polar Research Institute
abstracts.text:
In 2019 and 2023, researchers from the Korea Polar Research Institute conducted sub-bottom profile (SBP) surveys in the central part of the JOIDES Trough in the Ross Sea, Antarctica, and recovered sediment gravity cores from 10 sites. Analysis of the SBP profiles enabled us to identify distinct acoustic units and locate grounding zones, from which we reconstructed the history of ice-sheet advance and retreat within the JOIDES Trough. The sediment cores were examined using X-ray imaging, and their magnetic susceptibility, water content, total organic carbon, calcium carbonate, and opal contents were measured to characterize sedimentary facies and infer depositional environments. To constrain the timing of deposition, 11 radiocarbon dates were obtained from foraminifera and shell fragments.

Based on the SBP data, the sedimentary succession was divided into six units. Integration of the sedimentological and chronological data allowed us to interpret the depositional environments and ages of these units as follows. The uppermost unit (Unit 1) consists of diatomaceous mud deposited under seasonally open-marine conditions during the present interglacial. It forms a thin, laterally continuous drape, generally less than 2 m thick, across the study area. Units 2 and 3 consist of diamicton associated with the most recent glaciation. The underlying Unit 3 preserves the record of the maximum ice-sheet advance, whereas the overlying Unit 2 is interpreted as diamicton deposited during ice-sheet retreat following the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). The presence of two distinct glacial units suggests that ice-sheet retreat occurred in a stepwise rather than continuous manner.

Unit 4 comprises a variety of lithologies, including diatomaceous mud, sandy mud, and gravelly mud, and exhibits well-defined stratification in the SBP profiles. This unit is interpreted to have been deposited during Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 3, when the study area was not ice-grounded and the grounding line was located closer to the study area than it is today. Unit 5 consists of massive diamicton underlying Unit 4 and is interpreted as glacial sediment deposited during MIS 4. Unit 6 represents the basement of the study area and is interpreted to comprise strata deposited during MIS 4 and earlier periods.

The distributions of Units 3 and 2 constrain the ice extent during the LGM and subsequent deglaciation, respectively, and indicate stepwise ice-sheet retreat in the JOIDES Trough. These findings provide new constraints on the Late Quaternary glacial history of the region.

abstracts.title: Controls on spatial heterogeneity in dinoflagellate cyst distribution in recent sediments off west Antarctica
affiliations: Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon, Republic of Korea
School of Environmental Sciences, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69
Instituto Antártico Chileno, Plaza Muñoz Gamero 1055, Punta Arenas, Chile
ZT, UK
abstracts.text: Here we present the study of 48 new dinoflagellate cyst assemblages from the west Antarctic shelf sediments on a wide longitudinal scale, with a greater representation of ice-proximal sites, and provide a comprehensive overview of their distributional patterns and multiple environmental forcing factors. We find a strong spatial heterogeneity in the dinoflagellate cyst distribution patterns; 1) the northern Antarctic Peninsula region is dominated by Islandinium? minutum, Selenopemphix antarctica and Brigantedinium spp. in association with meltwater-induced stratification and high diatom productivity, 2) the Bellingshausen-Amundsen Seas is dominated by Gymnodinium microreticulatum and Selenopemphix sp. 1, under influences of strong offshore winds, unstable water column and Phaeocystis blooms in austral summer, and 3) the Ross Sea shows an extreme contrast – the east-central region under vigorous vertical mixing and high Phaeocystis production is dominated by stratification is dominated by Polarella glacialis cysts together with Nucicla umbiliphora, I.? minutum and highlight melt-related hydrodynamic-meteorological coupling processes around maritime Antarctica that control physico-biological properties and overall microplankton communities therein. As the ice-shelf disintegration and sea-ice loss continue, there will be a fundamental reconfiguration of microplankton production and their community structures in a future Antarctic Ocean with greater open-water areas. This study highlights the potential of dinoflagellate cysts to monitor changes in hydrographic conditions and plankton communities in these sensitive polar marine ecosystems.

abstracts.title: Late Holocene paleoenvironmental changes and centennial-scale variability near Joinville Island, Antarctic peninsula
affiliations: Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon, South Korea
Jeonbuk National University, Jeonju, South Korea
abstracts.text: A 4.76-m-long sediment core, spanning approximately 4,000 years was recovered near Joinville Island, at the northern tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. Six AMS radiocarbon ages were obtained from carbonate shells, and sedimentological, geochemical, and micropaleontological parameters were analysed. Records of total organic carbon, diatom abundance, and diatom assemblages indicate warm, stratified, and stable conditions between 3,900 and 2,500 yr BP, followed by a cooler interval from 2,500 to 1,200 yr BP. The onset of the Neoglacial in this record is contemporaneous with that reported from Bransfield Basin and Maxwell Bay, but later than that recorded at the Firth of Tay and James Ross Island, despite their geographic proximity to the study site. Spectral and wavelet analyses of magnetic susceptibility reveal a prominent 400–500-year periodicity, particularly after approximately 3,000 yr BP. This variability is accompanied by coherent shifts in XRF-derived detrital ratios (Zr/Rb, K/Rb) and lower organic carbon content, but lacks corresponding variations in bulk grain size or gravel content. These patterns suggest episodic delivery of relatively unweathered fine terrigenous material rather than changes in the ice-rafted supply of coarse debris or bottom-current sorting. Further constraints on sediment provenance, including clay mineral assemblages, will help elucidate the processes driving this periodic variability.

abstracts.title: Orbital-scale variations of biogenic carbonate components at the Del Caño Rise (Indian sector of the Southern Ocean) during the last 400 ka
affiliations: BK21 School of Earth and Environmental Systems, Pusan National University, Busan 46241, Korea .
Graduate School of International Resource Sciences, Akita University, Akita 010-8502, Japan
Marine Core Research Institute, Kochi University, Kochi 783-8502, Japan
Université de Bordeaux, CNRS, UMR 5805 EPOC, 33615 Pessac, France
Department of Oceanography, Pusan National University, Busan 46241, Korea
abstracts.text: The Southern Ocean influences atmospheric CO₂ variability between interglacial and glacial periods by regulating air–sea CO₂ exchange, which maintains the balance of marine carbon cycling between the biological carbon pump and carbonate counter pump. Migration of Southern Ocean fronts alters the distributions of calcareous planktons and diatoms, affecting regional paleoproductivity and related marine carbon cycling. Within the subantarctic zone, the interglacial paleoproductivity has been dominated by the biogenic carbonate production, whereas the glacial paleoproductivity has been increased by the diatom production, mainly due to the front migration (Choi et al., 2025). This study evaluated the relative biogenic carbonate contributions between foraminifera or coccolithophores at orbital-time scale in the subantarctic zone of the Southern Ocean. A piston core DCR-1PC (10.16 m long) was recovered from the Del Caño Rise (46°01′S, 44°15′E; 2,632 m water depth) during the KH-10-7 cruise. About 450 samples were collected at 2-3 cm intervals. Geochemical properties (CaCO3, biogenic opal, total organic carbon (TOC), total nitrogen (TN)) were analyzed. In addition, biogenic carbonate components (foraminifera or coccolithophore) were estimated by the size fraction (<20 μm: coccolithophores, 20– 100 μm: mixture, and >100 μm: foraminifera). Matsui et al. (2022) reported that the age of DCR-1PC covers ~410 kyrs by the continuous δ¹⁸O stratigraphy. The orbital-scale change of geochemical properties of DCR-1PC follows the general pattern of subantarctic zone: the interglacial periods are characterized by higher CaCO₃ and lower biogenic opal, TOC, and TN contents. In terms of sediment mass and CaCO3 content, the relative contribution of the >100 μm fraction was higher during the interglacial periods, whereas the <20 μm fraction was more dominant during the glacial periods. It indicates that, despite the effect of biogenic opal and detrital particles, the biogenic carbonate production has oscillated between the foraminifera-dominant interglacial and coccolithophore-dominant glacial periods. Thus, such shift of biogenic carbonate production implies the different role of marine carbon cycling in the subantarctic zone at orbital-time scales, emphasizing the balance between the biological carbon pump and the carbonate counter pump.

abstracts.title: Size-dependent δ18O and δ13C variations in a planktic foraminiferal Neogloboquadrina pachyderma (sinistral) record from Chukchi Plateau: Implications for (sub)surface water conditions in the western Arctic Ocean over the past ~50 ka
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University
Byrd Polar and Climate Research Center, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH 43210, USA
abstracts.text: Oxygen and carbon stable isotopes in planktic foraminifera Neogloboquadrina pachyderma (sinistral) (Nps) have a promising potential for reconstructing (sub)surface water conditions in the Arctic Ocean. Size-dependent (63-154 µm, 154-250 µm, and >250 µm) Nps δ18O and δ13C were measured along with Ice Rafted Debris (IRD) and scanned XRF Ca and Mn contents in sediment core ARC3-P31 from the Chukchi Plateau (434 m water depth) representing paleoceanographic conditions during the last ~50 ka (Marine Isotope Stages 3-1). While the interval corresponding to the Last Glacial Maximum is represented by a hiatus, the following deglaciation is clearly marked by a strong depletion in both δ18O and δ13C in all Nps size fractions along with the peaks in detrital carbonate IRD and coal fragment indicative of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago provenance. This pronounced feature presumably indicates a collapse event of the northwestern Laurentide Ice Sheet, potentially linked to the rising sea level. In the overall record under study, average values of Nps δ18O and δ13C fluctuate in the range of 1.2-2.1‰ and 0.3-0.9 ‰, respectively. Mid-size Nps δ18O values (154-250 µm) are in average lighter by ~0.2-0.5 ‰ than those of small (63-154 µm) and large (>250 µm) Nps tests. This offset may indicate a different water-depth dwelling, possibly affected by a relatively warm subsurface Atlantic water.

abstracts.title: Sedimentary responses to ice sheet dynamics in the Chukchi-East Siberian margin based on clay mineralogy and grain size distribution
affiliations: *Department of Geology, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju 52828, Republic of Korea
Research Institute of Molecular Alchemy, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju 52828, Republic of Korea
Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon 21990, Republic of Korea
Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon 21990, Republic of Korea
Inha University, Incheon 22201, Republic of Korea
Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, 63130, United States
Department of Geology, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju 52828, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text:
The distribution of sea ice in the Arctic Ocean responds sensitively to climate change, thereby exerting a major influence on sedimentary environments. Therefore, paleoceanographic studies of sediments in the Arctic Ocean provide insights into past environmental changes associated with the extent of ice sheets. Arctic marine sediments are predominantly derived from surrounding continents, with distinct mineralogical and geochemical characteristics depending on their provenance. The transport pathways vary with grain size; fine-grained particles can be redistributed over long distances by ocean currents, whereas coarse-grained fractions such as ice-rafted debris (IRD) are transported within sea ice and icebergs across the surface circulation. Thus, reconstructing sediment provenance and transport mechanisms based on mineralogical composition and grain size distribution constrains past depositional environments during glacial-interglacial cycles.

In this study, we analyzed gravity core ARA14C-ST12 (~590 cm long; ~1,900 m water depth) from the Chukchi Basin (75°55.273′N, 172°00.508′W) using mineralogical, geochemical, and sedimentological proxies. Core ST12 preserves a sedimentary record from Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 5a to MIS 1. End-member modelling analysis (EMMA) was applied to characterize downcore variations in the grain size distribution.

Clay mineral compositions show distinct changes in sediment provenance between glacial and interglacial periods, with higher kaolinite contents indicating enhanced North American input and elevated smectite contents reflecting increased contributions from the Eurasian margin. EMMA further distinguishes the two glacial periods, with MIS 4 characterized by dominant fine-grained fractions, whereas MIS 2 shows relatively greater contributions of coarse-grained particles. These differences suggest more restricted North American sediment supply during MIS 4, associated with a more extensive East Siberian Ice Sheet/Shelf (ESIS), compared with MIS 2.

These results demonstrate that sedimentation in the Chukchi Basin was strongly affected by changes in ice sheet/shelf extent. The integrated mineralogical and grain size proxies can provide evidence for reconstructing Quaternary paleoenvironments in the northwest Arctic Ocean and understanding the interactions between Arctic ice sheet dynamics and sediment transport pathways during glacial-interglacial cycles.

abstracts.title: Glacial-interglacial variability of deepwater influenced nutrient supply and productivity in the north Pacific
affiliations: Frontiers Science Center for Deep Ocean Multispheres and Earth System, and Key Laboratory of Marine Chemistry Theory and Technology, Ministry of Education and College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, 266100, China

Frontiers Science Center for Deep Ocean Multispheres and Earth System, and Key Laboratory of Marine Chemistry Theory and Technology, Ministry of Education and College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, 266100, China
abstracts.text: The subarctic North Pacific is a key terminal region of the global overturning circulation and an important regulator of the marine carbon cycle. During glacial–interglacial cycles, changes in physical processes, such as reduced upwelling and enhanced stratification, have been widely invoked to explain variations in North Pacific nutrient supply, biological productivity and carbon exchange. Here we proposed that North Pacific biogeochemical changes were also influenced by the properties of deep waters inherited from upstream source regions. By comparing North Pacific and Southern Ocean proxies related to deep-water overturning, nutrient supply and primary productivity, we showed that variations in deep-water properties were accompanied by systematic shifts in North Pacific physical processes. The combined effects of these changes shaped nutrient availability and marine productivity in the North Pacific, revealing that its biogeochemical variability reflected the interplay between remotely sourced deep-water properties and local physical processes. Our findings revealed an interhemispheric connection between deep-water circulation and North Pacific biogeochemistry and suggested that remote changes in deep-water carbon and nutrient inventories may have contributed to glacial– interglacial CO₂ variability.

abstracts.title: Barents seaway opening and enhanced Arctic-Atlantic exchange across the mid-Pleistocene transition
affiliations: Department of Geology, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju, Republic of Korea
Univ Brest, CNRS, Ifremer, Geo-Ocean, Plouzané, France
Division of Glacier and Earth Sciences, Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon, Republic of Korea
Division of Ocean and Atmosphere Sciences, Korea Polar Research Institute, Incheon, Republic of Korea
Alfred Wegener Institute Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research, Bremerhaven, Germany
Department of Geological Sciences, Stockholm University, Stockholm, Sweden
MARUM & Faculty of Geoscience, University of Bremen, Bremen, Germany
Frontiers Science Center for Deep Ocean Multispheres and Earth System and Key Laboratory of Marine Chemistry Theory and Technology, Ocean University of China (OUC), Qingdao, China
Graduate School and Faculty of Bioresources, Mie University, Mie, Japan
Department of Earth System Sciences, Yonsei University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
National Academy of Sciences, Republic of Korea, Seoul, Republic of Korea
Marine AI Convergence Center, Inha University, Incheon, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT; ~1.25–0.70 Ma) marked a shift from predominantly 41-kyr glacial cycles to longer and more intense quasi-100-kyr cycles, without a comparable change in orbital forcing. While changes in ice-sheet dynamics and ocean carbon storage have been proposed to explain this transition, the role of Arctic–Atlantic exchange remains less understood. Here we present an authigenic neodymium isotope (εNd) record from core PS72/410-3 on the Mendeleev Ridge (western Arctic Ocean) to reconstruct changes in Arctic– Atlantic exchange over the past ~2.0 Ma and assess its climatic impacts. Our results reveal a long-term decrease in mean authigenic εNd from −8.4 before the MPT to −9.8 afterward, accompanied by larger short-term variability. We attribute this trend to an increased influence of Atlantic-derived water masses in the western Arctic Ocean and propose that this change was linked to the progressive glacial erosion and opening of the Barents Seaway across the MPT, consistent with independent paleotopographic reconstructions. In this scenario, enhanced Arctic–Atlantic exchange may have increased the export of relatively fresh Arctic waters, thereby contributing to changes in deep-water circulation and carbon storage, while increased Atlantic inflow may also have enhanced high-latitude moisture supply. Together, lower glacial atmospheric CO2 and enhanced snowfall may have favored northern ice-sheet growth and persistence through summer insolation maxima, providing a potential link between Barents Seaway opening and the establishment of 100-kyr glacial cycles. Additional Arctic proxy records and numerical modelling are required to constrain the timing and spatial extent of these changes and quantify their climatic effects.

abstracts.title: Late sulfide liquid to MSS transition at mid-ocean ridges: Implications for gold endowments in seafloor massive sulfides
affiliations: School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, 1 Gwanak-ro, Gwanak-gu, Seoul 08826, South Korea
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Seoul National University, 1 Gwanak-ro, Gwanak-gu, Seoul 08826, South Korea
abstracts.text:
The timing and nature of sulfide fractionation during the mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB) magma differentiation controls the distribution of chalcophile metals in the oceanic crust and eventually the metal grades of seafloor massive sulfide (SMS) deposits. Although the early segregation of sulfide liquid is well-documented, in MORB magma, the subsequent transition of fractionating sulfide phase to monosulfide solid solution (MSS) has remained poorly constrained, which has been constrained across other oceanic magmatic systems (Brandl et al., 2023; Li and Audétat, 2012). This transition is important because the upper oceanic crust serves as the primary metal source for SMS deposits, and the affinity of chalcophile metals differs between sulfide liquid and MSS. For example, Au strongly partitions into sulfide liquid but only weakly into MSS.

To constrain the onset of the liquid-to-MSS transition, this study utilizes the Cu-Ag systematics in MORB glasses, spanning a compositional range from basalt to dacite (MgO = 0.63–9.58 wt.%), from the Australian-Antarctica Ridge and East Pacific Rise. Both Cu and Ag similarly partition into sulfide liquid; however, Cu is more compatible with MSS than Ag (Li and Audétat, 2012). Consequently, the Cu/Ag ratio serves as an effective proxy to trace the fractionating sulfide phase. Here, we report the first Ag data in evolved MORB glasses (MgO < 4 wt.%) and the results show that Cu/Ag values remain constant during early-stage differentiation but begin to decrease at ~4 wt.% of MgO, thereby pinpointing the onset of the liquid-to-MSS transition (Fig. 1).

These observations demonstrate that MORB magmas typically undergo early sulfide liquid segregation, followed by delayed MSS crystallization, which provides useful background for understanding the Au and Ag grades of SMS deposits. This sulfide saturation history of MORB magma likely indicates the systematic depletion of Au in the upper crust and its sequestration into lower crustal cumulates, providing possibility of additional Au into ultramafic-hosted deposits relative to mafic-hosted deposits. In contrast, island arc magmas, characterized by the late sulfide saturation and rapid MSS crystallization, effectively transfer chalcophile metals into the upper crust, thereby contributing to the formation of significantly Au- and Ag-rich SMS deposits.

abstracts.title: Towards reliable resource estimation of cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts in the Korean contract area: Exploration progress and future strategy
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology
abstracts.text: Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (CFCs) are hydrogenetic deposits that grow slowly on sediment-free bedrock of seamounts and are enriched in Co, Ni, Cu, and rare earth elements. Korea holds an exploration contract with the International Seabed Authority covering 3,000 km² (150 blocks) across nine seamounts (KC-1 to KC-9) in the Magellan Seamount region, western Pacific. Resource estimation requires reliable constraints on both CFC coverage and thickness. Potential CFC-covered areas are delineated from backscatter intensity (BSI), using BSI thresholds calibrated against direct visual observations. CFC thickness is constrained by 320 cores collected between 2023 and 2025 with the KIOST Remotely Operated Coring System (KROCS). CFC abundance is then estimated for each block from mapped CFC coverage, block-averaged thickness and crust density. The main uncertainty in the current estimates is the sparse spatial coring data: most blocks are represented by only two or three cores. To improve future sampling design, we evaluated the existing core network using Voronoi gap analysis, semivariogram modelling, and kriging. Semivariogram analyses generally showed a predominantly pure nugget structure, indicating that spatial continuity in CFC thickness cannot yet be resolved at the current core spacing. At KC-1, for example, the cores suggest a broad NE–SW thickness gradient over ~44 km, whereas individual transects (≤9.4 km) still exhibit a pure nugget structure. These results suggest that regional-scale thickness trends may exist, while the characteristic scale of local spatial continuity remains unresolved. Future coring will therefore follow a two-scale strategy. New sites will be selected to reduce large sampling gaps and the maximum Voronoi-cell radius, thereby improving overall spatial coverage. Nested infill cores between selected existing core pairs will be used to determine the distance at which spatial correlation in CFC thickness becomes detectable. In parallel, additional visual surveys will refine the calibration of BSI-based CFC distribution maps. This integrated approach is designed to reduce uncertainties in both CFC distribution and thickness and progressively increase the confidence of resource estimates.

abstracts.title: Quantitative resource estimation of cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts on the KC-2 seamount, western Pacific: Intergration acoustic backscatter and ground-truth data
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology
abstracts.text: Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (CFCs) on seamounts are potential sources of commercially valuable metals. Assessing their resource potential requires information on their spatial distribution and thickness. This study estimated CFC distribution and resource abundance across 18 equal-sized blocks covering 360 km² on KC-2 Seamount in the western Pacific. Shipboard and deep-tow acoustic backscatter data were compared with remotely operated vehicle (ROV) seafloor observations to map areas of CFC exposure. CFC thickness was measured from 36 core samples collected using an ROV-mounted drilling system along four survey transects, with one to three cores collected per block. For each block, CFC resource abundance was estimated by multiplying the estimated CFC exposure area by the mean measured thickness and a dry bulk density of 1,300 kg/m³. The estimated CFC exposure area was 119.7 km², representing 33.2% of the study area. Mean CFC thickness ranged from 7.50 to 14.67 cm among blocks. Resource estimates based on these block-specific mean thicknesses ranged from 0.29 to 1.82 Mt per block. Block 33 had the largest CFC exposure area and highest estimated resource abundance, while Block 35 had the greatest mean thickness and highest mean areal abundance. Summing the estimates based on mean thickness yielded a total CFC resource abundance of 17.83 Mt, corresponding to an overall mean areal abundance of 149.01 kg/m² across the estimated CFC exposure area. Lower and upper resource estimates were also calculated for each block using its respective lower and upper thickness values. Summing these estimates yielded lower and upper totals of 15.47 and 20.19 Mt, respectively, corresponding to overall mean areal abundances of 129.25 and 168.70 kg/m². These results suggest that combining acoustic backscatter data and ROV seafloor observations with CFC thickness measurements from core samples offers a practical approach to CFC resource estimation that could also be applied to other seamounts.

abstracts.title: Hydrothermal reactivity of magnetite-bearing banded iron formations: Implications for geological hydrogen
affiliations: Ocean Georesources Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan 49111, Republic of Korea
Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Chungbuk National University,Cheongju 28644, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text:
Geological hydrogen has attracted increasing attention as a potential subsurface energy resource, yet the behavior of Fe-rich geological materials during hydrogen-related water–rock interactions remains incompletely understood. Banded iron formations (BIFs), which contain abundant Fe-bearing minerals including magnetite, represent potentially important geological materials for investigating such processes. This study examines the hydrothermal reactivity of natural magnetite-bearing BIFs and evaluates the associated H2 responses and Fe-mineral transformations under controlled temperature conditions.

Hydrothermal experiments were conducted using five natural BIF samples and a magnetite-rich lodestone reference at 150, 200, and 230 °C for 30 days. Following reaction, H2 detector responses were measured, while mineralogical and morphological changes were characterized using quantitative X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM–EDS). All reacted samples exhibited H2 detector responses above procedural blanks, with higher responses observed at higher treatment temperatures in the experimental dataset. The magnetite-rich lodestone showed the strongest response, reaching 379 ppm at 230 °C. Quantitative XRD revealed progressive decreases in magnetite abundance accompanied by increases in hematite with increasing temperature. The lodestone exhibited a 45.4 wt.% increase in hematite at 230 °C, while substantial magnetite-to-hematite transformation was also observed in several natural BIF samples. SEM observations further revealed pronounced surface alteration and the formation of secondary Fe-oxide crystals on reacted mineral surfaces.

These results demonstrate that natural magnetite-bearing BIFs undergo substantial Fe-mineral transformation under hydrothermal conditions and exhibit measurable H2-related responses. The variability among natural BIF samples further suggests that hydrothermal reactivity may depend not only on bulk magnetite abundance but also on mineralogical composition, the mineralogical occurrence of Fe2+, and mineral–fluid accessibility. Because the experiments initially contained atmospheric O2 and H2 was measured after reactor opening, the detector responses cannot be interpreted as quantitative H2 yields, and the relative contributions of water reduction and O2-driven oxidation remain unresolved. Nevertheless, the coupled observations of H2 detector responses, magnetite transformation, and surface alteration provide an experimental basis for further evaluating Fe-rich BIFs in geological hydrogen systems and highlight the importance of redox conditions, temperature, and mineralogical controls in future investigations.

abstracts.title: Effects of porosity updating on CO2 migration and geomechanical response in geological CO2 storage
affiliations: Interdisciplinary Program in Earth Environmental System Science & Engineering, Kangwon National University, Chuncheon 24341, Republic of Korea
Department of Geophysics, Kangwon National University, Chuncheon 24341, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is a technology for long-term CO2 storage through the injection of captured CO2 into deep saline aquifers or depleted oil and gas reservoirs. Reliable long-term storage requires numerical prediction of CO2 migration and geomechanical response (Rutqvist, 2012). CO2 migration and deformation associated with subsurface CO2 injection can be described using coupled two-phase flow and mechanics models. Pore-pressure changes caused by CO₂ injection induce deformation of the reservoir and surrounding formations, while volumetric strain alters porosity. Changes in porosity modify the pore space available for fluid occupancy and may influence CO2 migration and pore-pressure evolution. However, few studies have evaluated how porosity changes affect CO2 migration, pore-pressure evolution, and geomechanical response in coupled two-phase flow and mechanics simulations. We developed a porosity-updating coupling framework for two-phase flow and mechanics using the open-source finite-element platform OpenGeoSys. The coupled model was used to evaluate the effects of porosity changes on CO2 migration, pore-pressure evolution, and geomechanical response. The framework was applied to a two-dimensional finite-element model based on the reservoir structure of the Sleipner project in the Norwegian North Sea (Akai et al., 2021). The average porosity change was on the order of 10-5. Under the CO2 injection conditions considered in our model, porosity updating produced only limited changes in CO2 migration and hydro-mechanical behavior.

abstracts.title: Sedimentary and hydrodynamic responses of a tidal bar to a storm in the Geum Estuary, Korea
affiliations: Research Institute for Geological Environment and Geohazard, Chonnam National University
Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Chonnam National University
Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Chonnam National University
abstracts.text: Tidal bars are widely distributed in coastal regions around the world. They are deposited under diverse hydrodynamic and sedimentary processes, forming in a range of depositional environments such as estuaries and tidal flats. During winter season, storms are the main mechanisms of sediment transport and topography evolution in intertidal flats. We aimed to identify the impacts of storms on intertidal sedimentary processes. To better understand sedimentary process under winter storm conditions, two in-situ mooring systems were deployed simultaneously in the sandflat and the back-barrier mudflat of Seocheon tidal flat, west coast of Korea. The study area has been designated as a part of the UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site, ‘Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats’. The winter storm passed the mooring sites from January 27 to 29, 2025. The onset of this period was marked by a dramatic change in wind S to NW direction. The average wind speed was 11.4 m/s with a maximum of 15.3 m/s. At the sandflat, currents were significantly influenced by increased wind speeds, ranging from 0.01 to 1.05 m/s. At both the lower and middle sandflats, currents were significantly influenced by increased wind speeds. Bottom shear stress increased because of the storm surge and wave activities. The turbidity increased dramatically at the onset of storm and remained elevated during this period, indicating that the storm could erode bottom sediments. Overall, the results suggest that tidal bar is more susceptible to storm-induced erosion during winter season, and these processes likely lead to the development of a concave topography and an coarsening upward sediment trend. In particular, the influence of wind and waves on sediment transport varies with wind direction. At the mudflat, currents showed distinct tidal variations, ranging from 0.01 to 0.82 m/s. The turbidity peaked at the beginning of the flood tide and decreased at the high slack tide. This suggests that sediment was mainly resuspended by tidal forcing rather than by waves. Overall, the results imply that winter storm-induced erosion is more likely to occur on intertidal flat with longer immersion periods and lower sediment stability. Further studies are need to quantify the storm effects on the sediment erodibility and sediment redistribution.

abstracts.title: Wave–tide mixed-energy tidal bar at the Geum River estuary mouth, western Korea: similarity to open-coast tidal flats
affiliations: Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Korea
abstracts.text: Estuarine tidal bars are shaped by the triple interplay of tidal, wave, and river processes. Open estuary-mouth bars remain poorly understood compared to inner-estuarine counterparts. At the Geum River estuary mouth, a lobate tidal bar has developed surrounding Yubu Island, where a spit and coastal dune in the middle separates the seaward sand flat from the landward mud flat. This study aims to identify depositional characteristics of the open-estuary tidal bar and evaluate the spatial influence of wave and tidal processes on grain-size and sedimentary facies. Topographic surveys reveal that the tidal bar exhibits the highest elevation at its central portion, gradually decreasing towards both sides with gentle relief. There is little grain size change with elevation on sand flat, whereas the mud flat displays a coarsening-upward trend and strong bimodality. Seasonal variations are significant. During summer, mud content increases locally up to 90% on the sand flat, whereas sand content increases to 10–25% on average on the mud flat. Sedimentary facies analysis of box-cores indicates that the sand flat is characterized by hummocky cross-stratification (HCS) and wave ripples, indicating strong wave influence, together with current ripples, bi-directional trough cross bedding, and flaser bedding, indicating tidal influence. The barrier spits in the middle of the bar exhibit a transition from beach to overwash facies. The mud flat is dominated by lenticular bedding, indicative of tidal deposition. The sedimentary facies analysis demonstrates a spatial transition from a wave–tide mixed-energy setting on sand flat to a tide-dominated environment on the landward mud flat. Overall, the tidal bar facies closely resemble that of open-coast tidal flats, suggesting that the wave–tide mixed facies may be a key characteristic distinguishing outer from inner estuarine tidal bars.

abstracts.title: Residual tidal circulation and its influence on the morphological and sedimentary asymmetry of Yeoja Bay tidal flats, a UNESCO World Heritage site, on the southern coast of Korea
