affiliations: Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, Chonnam National University, Jeonnam-Gwangju 61186, South Korea
abstracts.text:
Mudflats along the margins of semi-enclosed bays are shaped by the interaction of tidal currents, waves, sediment supply, and residual circulation, which can produce pronounced spatial variations in morphology and sediment distribution. Yeoja Bay, located on the southern coast of Korea, is a semi-enclosed embayment and part of the UNESCO World Heritage site “Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats.” The bay is characterized by extensive muddy intertidal flats, with surface sediments predominantly composed of silt.

To investigate the hydrodynamic, morphological, and sedimentary characteristics of the tidal flats, field observations were conducted in 2024 and 2026. Mooring systems equipped with Acoustic Doppler Velocimeters (ADVs) and wave sensors were deployed during both summer and winter to obtain tidal current and wave data. The observations revealed spatial variations in tidal dynamics and sedimentary characteristics across the bay. Surface sediments are predominantly composed of silt, with mean grain sizes generally ranging from 5.7 to 8.1 phi. Distinct morphological and sedimentary asymmetry occurs between the eastern and western sectors of Yeoja Bay. The eastern sector is characterized by relatively lower tidal-flat elevations and relatively severe erosion, whereas the western sector comprises extensive, gently sloping muddy intertidal flats with relatively higher elevations.

These spatial differences are closely associated with the residual circulation and associated sediment-transport pathways. Tidal currents are ebb-dominated, ranging from 0.01 to 0.15 m s-1. The progressive vector indicates a predominantly anti-clockwise circulation with a westward residual current. This circulation pattern suggests that the western sector is characterized by sediment accumulation and lateral accretion, contributing to the development and infilling of muddy intertidal flats, whereas enhanced sediment export and erosion contribute to the relatively lower morphology of the eastern sector. The results demonstrate that residual circulation is an important factor controlling the spatial distribution of tidal-flat morphology and sediment characteristics in Yeoja Bay. This study provides baseline information for understanding the morphodynamic and sedimentary evolution of Yeoja Bay and the physical processes underlying the spatial variability of this UNESCO World Heritage tidal-flat system.

abstracts.title: Reconstructing early mid Holocene climate from Lake Suigetsu sediments using organic biomarkers
affiliations: Graduate school of environmental science, Hokkaido University, Japan
abstracts.text:
Lake Suigetsu contains one of the most continuous and well-dated lacustrine sediment records in Japan, providing an exceptional archive for investigating Holocene climate and environmental variability in East Asia. This study applies a multi-biomarker organic geochemical approach to reconstruct climate, hydrological conditions, and catchment processes during the Early to Middle Holocene using sediment samples from the SG06 core.

Sediment samples are extracted using Accelerated Solvent Extraction (ASE), followed by separation into neutral, acidic, and hydrocarbon fractions through column chromatography and Solid-Phase Extraction (SPE). Individual biomarker compounds are subsequently analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS).

The study focuses on glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraethers (GDGTs), reconstructed using the TEX86, MBT′5ME, CBT, and BIT indice, together with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and plant-derived triterpenoid methyl ethers (PTMEs). These complementary biomarkers provide information on lake temperature, hydrological variability, terrestrial organic matter input, biomass burning, vegetation dynamics, and watershed processes. By integrating multiple organic geochemical proxies, this research aims to improve our understanding of Holocene environmental evolution in East Asia and strengthen biomarker-based interpretations of the Lake Suigetsu sediment record.

abstracts.title: Three-dimensional magnetization structure of Dokdo, Simheungtaek and Isabu Tablemounts, Ulleung Basin, East Sea, from magnetization vector inversion
affiliations: Dokdo Research Center, East Sea Research Institute, Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Uljin, Republic of Korea
Division of Science Education, Kangwon National University, Chuncheon, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text:
Dokdo and the neighbouring Simheungtaek and Isabu Tablemounts form the eastern part of a volcanic chain in the Ulleung Basin, East Sea (Sea of Japan). Although the three edifices share a guyot morphology, their internal magnetization structure, and hence their construction history and the pathways of magnetic material, has remained poorly constrained. We present three-dimensional magnetization models of each edifice and of the merged Dokdo–Simheungtaek–Isabu volume.

Shipborne magnetic and bathymetric data acquired between 1997 and 2012 were combined with nearshore surveys around Dokdo (2004–2012), digitized land values and EMAG2v3 through a four-stage levelling scheme. After IGRF correction, reduction-to-the-pole and analytic-signal transforms were computed by FFT (Nabighian, 1972; Roest et al., 1992). Magnetization vector inversion (MVI), which recovers induced and remanent magnetization jointly without assuming a remanence direction, was applied to 500 × 500 × 250 m meshes extending 10 km below seafloor with Tikhonov minimum-gradient regularization (Ellis et al., 2012).

Beneath Dokdo, MVI resolves shallow susceptibility highs on the western to southern flanks and a deeper sill-like body under the summit centre; magnetization vectors there point upward while those beneath the southern flank point downward, consistent with eruptions spanning opposite polarity intervals. Simheungtaek, whose summit lies deeper at 250 m, shows highs continuous from 7 km depth to the seafloor beneath its southern and north-western bases, but neither a sill nor opposing vectors, indicating a single major episode. Its vectors parallel those of Dokdo, implying a shared polarity epoch and agreeing with reported ages of 2.76–2.94 and 2.61 Ma.

Isabu, 55 km east of Dokdo at the western margin of Oki Bank, has the deepest summit (300 m) and by far the weakest magnetization, with anomalies spanning only −300 to 300 nT and a small, weak sill beneath its centre. Opposing vectors appear faintly below the summit, hinting at multiple eruptions, but its susceptibility highs show little continuity with the Dokdo–Simheungtaek system, suggesting a separate supply.

Merged modelling recovers highs between Dokdo and Simheungtaek that single-edifice models missed, confirming the principal migration paths. The progressive weakening from Dokdo through Simheungtaek to Isabu, attributable to thermal and chemical demagnetization during dormancy, erosion and burial, implies a formation sequence of Isabu, then Simheungtaek, then Dokdo.

abstracts.title: Geoacoustic properties at the sediment-water interface
affiliations: Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources
abstracts.text:
Geoacoustic properties of seafloor sediments are essential for understanding marine geological environments and for interpreting acoustic reflection and propagation at the seafloor. In particular, physical properties such as grain size, density, porosity, and water content can vary significantly across the sediment-water interface and within the shallow sub-bottom sediments, resulting in corresponding variations in acoustic properties. This presentation aims to characterize the geoacoustic properties near the sediment-water interface by integrating in situ acoustic measurements with laboratory measurements of acoustic and physical properties.

In situ acoustic data were acquired using the KISAP (KIGAM Seafloor Acoustic Probe) and M-KISAP (Multiple-KISAP) systems. These measurements were used to investigate acoustic properties and their vertical and horizontal variations within the shallow seafloor sediments. Sediment samples collected at the same or adjacent sites were also analyzed in the laboratory to determine sound speed and major physical properties, including density, porosity, water content, and grain-size characteristics.

The in situ measurements obtained from KISAP and M-KISAP were compared with laboratory-derived acoustic and physical properties to evaluate the relationships between sound-speed variations and sediment characteristics near the sediment-water interface. Particular attention was given to the vertical sound-speed structure immediately below the seafloor, its relationship with changes in sediment physical properties, and potential differences between in situ and laboratory measurements.

The results of this study are expected to improve our understanding of geoacoustic variability at and immediately below the sediment-water interface and to provide a basis for establishing quantitative relationships between acoustic and physical properties of marine sediments. The integrated dataset may also contribute to improving the reliability of geoacoustic parameters used in seafloor acoustic reflection and underwater sound propagation models and to advancing field-based approaches for geoacoustic characterization of shallow marine sediments.

abstracts.title: Numerical modeling of the effects of fault location and permeability on hydrothermal circulation at the outer rise
affiliations: Interdisciplinary Program in Earth Environmental System Science & Engineering, Kangwon National University, South Korea
Department of Geophysics, Kangwon National University, South Korea
abstracts.text:
Subducting oceanic plates experience extensional stress associated with slab bending at the outer rise, where normal faults, or bend faults, develop in the upper part of the plate. Bend faults formed at the outer rise provide pathways for seawater infiltration into the oceanic lithosphere. Seawater infiltration through these faults may reactivate hydrothermal circulation. Reactivated hydrothermal circulation redistributes heat within the lithosphere through advective heat transport, potentially modifying the thermal structure of the oceanic plate. Changes in the thermal structure of the oceanic plate may appear as observable variations in geophysical data, including heat flow and magnetic anomalies.

The development and thermal effects of hydrothermal circulation depend on fault location and permeability. We constructed a two-dimensional finite-element model to investigate these effects within the oceanic plate. The model couples Darcy flow in a porous medium with heat transport. The model represents fault zones as high-permeability zones, with different fault locations and permeability conditions considered in the numerical experiments.

The numerical models examine variations in the penetration depth and spatial extent of hydrothermal circulation. The analysis also evaluates the magnitude and spatial distribution of seafloor heat flow. Finally, we aim to compare modeled heat-flow variations with geophysical observations to evaluate the contribution of hydrothermal circulation to observed heat-flow anomalies.

abstracts.title: Influence of initial mantle thermal heterogeneity on segment linkage during rift propagation
affiliations: Department of Geophysics, Kangwon National University, Chuncheon, Republic of Korea
Department of Geophysics, Kangwon National University, Chuncheon, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text:
Rifting involves lithospheric thinning and rupture in response to extension driven by plate motions, trench retreat, or plume ascent. Continued extension may lead to oceanic crust formation. Rift propagation along spatially distributed lithospheric weak zones proceeds through the growth and linkage of individual segments. Segment linkage depends on lithospheric rheology, initial offsets, and extension direction. Previous studies have identified connected, overlapping but unlinked, and independently propagating segments at different initial offsets. At a fixed offset, variations in lithospheric strength control deformation localization along major boundary faults or across the crust between segments.

The initial thermal structure influences lithospheric strength and asthenospheric flow. With an imposed along-axis mantle temperature gradient, previous modeling by the authors demonstrated transport of hot asthenospheric material in the direction of rift propagation. Axis-parallel asthenospheric flow potentially affects rift propagation and the distribution of partial melting ahead of the rift tip. However, the earlier simulations considered a single rift axis without analyzing linkage between offset segments. The influence of initial mantle thermal heterogeneity on segment linkage therefore requires evaluation with identical weak-zone configurations.

Three-dimensional thermo-mechanical models using ASPECT simulate rifting along two offset lithospheric weak zones. The analysis examines the influence of initial mantle thermal heterogeneity on segment linkage across different weak-zone offsets and positions. Model pairs with identical weak-zone configurations allow quantitative comparisons of deformation localization and the timing, geometry, and location of segment linkage for different initial mantle temperature gradients. The analysis also examines the occurrence and velocity of axis-parallel asthenospheric flow, together with temperature and partial melt fraction distributions. Changes in lithospheric effective viscosity and strength are evaluated alongside deformation localization and asthenospheric flow during segment linkage. The study investigates the relationship between segment linkage during rifting and the thermal state of the asthenosphere.

abstracts.title: Rapid finite source inversion using pre-calculated Green’s functions and spatially optimized GNSS networks for faults in Western Japan
affiliations: Department of Interdisciplinary Program in Earth Environmental System Science and Engineering, Kangwon National University Chuncheon, Republic of Korea
Department of Geophysics, College of Natural Sciences, Kangwon National University, Chuncheon, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: The slip distribution on the fault plane is estimated through finite source inversion. The estimated slip distribution is crucial input data for various subsequent earthquake studies, including tsunami and post-seismic deformation modeling. In particular, estimating the slip distribution through rapid inversion enables the early forecasting of tsunami wave arrival times and heights. To reduce the computational time required for finite source inversion, we generated pre-calculate Green’s function matrices for major faults models of the western coast of Japan provided by the Japanese Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT). We constructed a 3D numerical model incorporating the MLIT faults of the western coast of Japan and GNSS station information. Using pre-calculated matrices during the inversion process reduces computational time. Real-time GNSS observation data are used to quickly determine slip distributions. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that both the accuracy and computational efficiency of the inversion are maximized when selectively utilizing data from GNSS stations located within a specific radius (e.g., 100, 200, 300, and 400 km) from the epicenters. Excluding coseismic deformation data from far-field stations effectively mitigates the observational errors and noise. This study is expected to contribute to the establishment of rapid seismic hazard assessment systems in western Japan.

abstracts.title: AI-assisted integrated multisensor maritime surveillance architecture
affiliations: University of Science and Technology, Daejeon, Korea (Republic of)
Korean Institute of Ocean Science and Technology, Busan, Korea (Republic of)
Dominican Navy (ARD, Armada de Republica Dominicana), Santo Domingo, Dominican (Republic of)
abstracts.text:
Maritime authorities must transform heterogeneous and asynchronous observations into actionable information before deploying limited patrol resources. Automatic Identification System (AIS), coastal radar, geospatial data, electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensors, and unmanned aerial vehicles provide complementary evidence, but differences in coverage, update rate, accuracy, and reliability complicate their operational integration. This study proposes a design and evaluation framework for an explainable, AI-assisted multisensor maritime surveillance architecture adapted to preventive patrol operations in the Dominican Republic.

The architecture comprises four interconnected stages. First, AIS and radar observations are normalized in space and time, associated through spatial, temporal, and kinematic compatibility, and represented as a consolidated maritime contact enriched with geospatial context and explicit uncertainty. Second, behavioral features, including speed variation, course changes, loitering, route deviation, contact encounters, sensitive-zone entry, and AIS irregularities, are analyzed using Isolation Forest. The model produces a continuous anomaly score representing statistical deviation rather than a determination of threat or illegality. Third, the proposed Maritime Anomaly Risk Index (MARI) combines normalized behavioral and contextual indicators into an auditable priority score, allowing operators to identify the factors that raised a contact’s operational relevance. Fourth, selected contacts may undergo EO/IR or UAV verification before the complete evidence record is presented to command and control for human-authorized assessment.

The methodology combines available institutional and public observations, controlled simulations, and representative maritime scenarios. Evaluation is conducted at both component and system levels using track-association accuracy, contact continuity, anomaly-detection performance, false-alarm rate, MARI ranking stability, visual-detection metrics, processing latency, and changes in operational uncertainty.

The principal contribution is a modular and testable framework that links multisensor correlation, explainable anomaly prioritization, selective visual verification, and human decision support. The proposed architecture seeks to improve the evidential basis for preventive maritime patrol without automating interdiction or replacing competent operational authority. Keywords: Maritime domain awareness; multisensor data fusion; AIS–radar association; anomaly detection; Isolation Forest; MARI; EO/IR; UAV; preventive maritime patrol; Dominican Republic.

abstracts.title: Regional-to-local modelling of storm surge and wave conditions around Tongatapu during tropical cyclone Gita
affiliations: Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST), Busan, Republic of Korea
University of Science and Technology (UST), Daejeon, Republic of Korea
Ministry of Lands, Survey, Planning and Natural Resources, Nuku ‘alofa, Tonga
abstracts.text: Tongatapu, Tonga, is highly exposed to tropical-cyclone coastal hazards because settlements, infrastructure, and essential services are concentrated on low-lying land bordered by reefs and a shallow lagoon. This study developed a nested Delft3D FLOW–SWAN modelling framework to examine storm-related water-level and wave conditions around Tongatapu during Tropical Cyclone Gita in February 2018. A regional hydrodynamic model represented astronomical tides and large-scale cyclone forcing, while a higher-resolution nested model resolved Tongatapu, ‘Eua, surrounding reefs, and the lagoon. This regional-to-local configuration was designed to retain the large-scale ocean response while representing the complex nearshore controls that are important for small reef-fringed islands. Regional tidal boundaries were derived from TPXO 7.2, and ERA5 supplied wind and atmospheric pressure fields. Because ERA5 smoothed the compact cyclone core, the atmospheric forcing was corrected using best-track position, central pressure, and maximum-wind information before being blended with the regional background. Regional tide simulations were evaluated against observations at Neiafu and Lifuka, producing mean absolute errors of 0.082 m and 0.080 m, respectively. Matched tide-only, meteorological, and coupled FLOW–SWAN simulations were compared to isolate the storm-related contribution from the astronomical tide. This controlled experiment matrix allowed the tidal, meteorological, and wave-related signals to be interpreted consistently rather than attributing the total water level to a single process. At Station S6, the coupled storm-related residual reached approximately 0.51 m during Gita’s passage. Spatial results showed both positive and negative residuals around Tongatapu, indicating that the coastal response was not uniform and reflected the combined influence of wind direction, bathymetry, reef passages, and lagoon geometry. The model also reproduced strong offshore wave conditions and spatially variable wave transformation near the island. These findings demonstrate the importance of transferring regional cyclone forcing consistently into a local coastal model in reef-fringed island settings. They also provide a physically based foundation for improving local coastal-flood assessments where direct storm observations remain limited. The present results represent water-level residuals rather than inundation depths; subsequent work will incorporate wetting and drying with higher-resolution topography to estimate flood depth and extent for coastal hazard planning in Tonga. Tropical Cyclone Gita; Delft3D FLOW–SWAN; storm surge; wave transformation; Tongatapu; coastal hazards

abstracts.title: Planktonic-benthic foraminiferal isotope differentiation and sedimentary carbon variability on the Hupo Basin slope, southwestern East Sea
affiliations: Library of Marine Samples, Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Geoje 53201, Republic of Korea
Marine Environment Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Busan 49111, Republic of Korea
Sea Power Reinforcement· Security Research Department, Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology, Busan 49111, Republic of Korea
University of Science and Technology (UST), Daejeon 34113, Republic of Korea
abstracts.text: Marine sediments preserve interactions among biological carbon production, water column structure, and sedimentary carbon composition, yet the relationship between vertical water-column differentiation and sedimentary carbon variability remains poorly constrained in the southwestern East Sea. This study integrates sedimentary facies, bulk geochemical proxies, including total organic carbon (TOC), CaCO₃, C/N ratios, δ¹³Corg, and TOC/TIC ratios, and planktic and benthic foraminiferal stable isotopes from core E09-05 recovered from the Hupo Basin slope to evaluate the relationship between sedimentary carbon variability and vertical water column structure. The analyzed interval was divided into five geochemical–lithological units (GLUs). GLU III is characterized by high CaCO₃ contents and low TOC/TIC ratios, representing a carbonate-rich interval, whereas GLU IV marks a transition toward increasing organic carbon contents. GLU V is characterized by high TOC and TOC/TIC ratios, low C/N ratios, and higher δ¹³Corg values, indicating organic carbon enrichment and a greater relative contribution of marine-derived organic matter. Planktic δ¹⁸O generally decreases and δ¹³C increases toward the upper part of the core, whereas benthic isotope records show no comparable directional changes. Consequently, planktic–benthic δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C offsets increase markedly in GLU V, indicating greater surface– bottom isotopic differentiation, consistent with stronger vertical hydrographic and biogeochemical differentiation. The enriched planktic δ¹³C values, together with the organic geochemical characteristics of GLU V, further suggest enhanced biological carbon utilization and potentially enhanced surface-water productivity. The co-occurrence of greater surface–bottom isotopic differentiation and organic carbon enrichment reveals a close stratigraphic association between vertical water-column differentiation and sedimentary carbon variability. This association provides a framework for interpreting the potential roles of marine organic matter supply and preservation in shaping sedimentary carbon composition on the Hupo Basin slope.

abstracts.title: Paleoceanography and paleoclimatology of the North Pacific over the past 10 million years
abstracts.text: Previous studies document a transition from a warm Neogene climate with relatively high-carbon dioxide toward strong glacial–interglacial climate regime changes of the Pleistocene with the lower-carbon dioxide. Global compilations of sea surface temperature reconstructions support general cooling trends over the past 10 million years. The temperature changes can be strongly linked to ocean and atmospheric circulation changes. However, there is no long-term high-resolution temperature record from the middle-latitude northwestern Pacific where it is very important regarding climate changes. Here we present a new, extremely high-resolution (1-3 kyr), continuous alkenone sea surface temperature record spanning the past 10 million years from the subarctic front region of the Northwest Pacific. Our results reveal that temperature changes responsed to climate forcing were significantly large at the climatologically-sensitive middle latitude North Pacific region compared to the tropical western Pacific over the period. On glacial-interglacial timescale, alkenone temperature variance and its dominant frequencies changed stepwise, defining three phases: strong-amplitude variability (~5–9°C) at 0–1.7 Ma, moderate variability (~2–5°C) at 1.7–5.6 Ma, and weak variability (~1–2°C) at 5.6–9 Ma. Band-pass filtering isolates 405, 100, 41 and 21/19 kyr components, revealing pervasive orbital pacing and reproducing the three-phase structure. On long-term timescale, our results exhibit multistage process of the North Pacific cooling with related climate changes over the time period. During the warm period, significant warming at the middle latitude and reduced equator-to-middle latitude meridional thermal gradient were associated with a weakened Hadley circulation and weaker, poleward-displaced westerlies. In contrast, during the cooling period and the intensification of Northern Hemisphere glaciation interval, significant low temperature at the middle latitude and strengthened meridional gradient was likely accompanied by stronger, more equatorward westerlies. This atmospheric reorganization likely linked to a southward displacement of the North Pacific subarctic frontal system and modified the northern extent and circulation of the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre.

abstracts.title: Submarine landslides and associated gravity flow deposits around the Japanese islands
abstracts.text:
Submarine landslides are major submarine geohazards that can cause great damage to coastal area. The Japanese islands locate along the NW Pacific subduction margins, where many large earthquakes have been occurred. Large earthquakes are a trigger for submarine landslides along the submarine slopes, and the movement of a large amount of sediment mass by submarine landslide has the potential for generating tsunami. Therefore, it is crucial for hazard mitigation to understand the nature, trigger mechanism and recurrence of submarine landslides. However, our knowledges on their tsunamigenic potential remain limited.

Unexpectedly shallow and large coseismic slip to the trench by the 2011 CE Tohoku-oki earthquake contributed to the large tsunami (Kodaira et al., 2021). Post-earthquake bathymetric profiles indicated large (>50 m) change compared with pre-earthquake profile (Fujiwara et al., 2011). Shallow coseismic slip during the 2011 CE earthquake caused deformation of the trench-fill basin stratigraphy (Kodaira et al., 2012). Coring campaign and seafloor observation at the lowermost trench slope suggested the occurrence of a kilometer-scale rotational slump by the 2011 CE earthquake (Strasser et al., 2013; Ueda et al., 2023). Thick (>7 m) mass transport deposits (MTDs) containing well-preserved calcareous benthic foraminifera were obtained in cores from the hadal trench basins at the northern Japan Trench below the CCD (Usami et al., 2021). Thickness of the correlative MTDs in IODP Exp 386 cores exceeded 10 m (Strasser et al., 2024). Benthic foraminifera assemblages suggested that the origin of the MTD mud is the upper slope at a water depth of ~600 m. Kioka et al. (2019) correlated the MTDs among several trench basins suggesting huge amount of sediment transported from upper slope to hadal trench basins.

In the Beppu Bay, an actively subsiding coastal basin with high sedimentation rate, bathymetric and sub-bottom profiling data indicated the repeated occurrence of submarine landslides along the coastal slope. Core analyses suggested that the submarine landslides were likely triggered by two historical earthquakes. Correlative event layers of the two landslide events in nearby cores were composed of submarine debris flow deposits and turbidites, suggesting flow transformation from submarine landslide to turbidity current through submarine debris flow occurred. The submarine landslides occurred at the coastal slope located at the major submarine discharge sites of underground hot-spring water near the active Asami-gawa Fault. The submarine hot-spring water discharge along the slope likely produces preferable precondition for coastal submarine landslides off Beppu City.
affiliations: Geological Survey of Japan, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, Tsukuba, Japan
Department of Paleontology and Anthropology, National Museum of Nature and Science, Tokyo, Tsukuba, Japan
Center for Integrated Research and Education of Natural Hazards, Shizuoka University, Shizuoka, Japan

abstracts.title: Deep-sea sedimentary dynamic processes crossing active to passive continental margins: Fifteen consecutive years of mooring observations in the South China Sea
abstracts.text: Deep-sea currents regulate transport and settling processes of terrigenous and marine particles across various temporal, spatial, and dynamic scales, forming deep-sea sedimentary dynamics. These dynamic processes are crucial for reshaping distribution configuration of deep-sea sediments, tracing sediment source-to-sink transport processes, and understanding global material cycles. Despite some important progress made over the past half-century through field observations and simulations, consecutive long-term in-situ observations of deep-sea sedimentary dynamics are still lacking. This study selects the South China Sea, which features contrasting tectonic and ocean current backgrounds, with submarine canyons on active margin (off Taiwan) and sediment drifts on passive margin (off South China), both running through by the same contour currents. Deep-sea sedimentary dynamic process observation systems were deployed, consisting of 12 sets of current profile/sediment trap moorings. The systems have been incrementally improved and successfully operated since 2011, with the longest consecutive mooring observation reaching 15 years (2011–2026), making it the world’s longest-running integrated observation systems for deep-sea currents and sediment transport. This presentation will introduce the longest in-situ observational studies on along-slope sediment transport by contour currents, cross-slope sediment transport by turbidity currents in submarine canyons, and interactions between terrigenous lithogenic material and marine particulate organic carbon. This study identifies the characteristics of marginal sea sediment dynamics, featuring transport by canyon turbidity currents on the active margin, transport by contour currents on the passive margin, and regulation of terrigenous lithogenic material on the settling of marine particulate organic carbon.
